sections.title: Digest — at a glance
sections.note: short summary; full detail below

items: The access layer of India’s mobile networks: radios, Massive-MIMO active antenna units and baseband, plus the RF front-end and silicon inside them.
India now assembles and designs the equipment but still imports the parts — 4–5% of a RAN BOM is domestic while 52% of parts imports come from China. Scope: India, NSE/BSE universe.
SMT assembly of radio and baseband boards, RF alignment and power testing, then environmental burn-in — the same spine at Tejas, ITI, Dixon and at Nokia Chennai and Ericsson’s Pune line.
Key machinery: SMT lines, RF test benches, anechoic chambers and OTA testers, environmental chambers; RAN silicon is bought in, not made.
AAUs are the harder node: the antenna array and the radio are one part, so assembly, calibration and beamforming test happen together.
Certification test capacity (TSTLs under MTCTE and ITSAR) is itself a queue that gates every launch.
RF front-end and power amplifiers — GaN/LDMOS devices and transceivers from a US/Japan/EU oligopoly, no Indian fab. Resilience: YEARS.
RAN silicon — L1-PHY FPGAs, SoCs and ASICs (AMD/Xilinx, Altera, Marvell, Qualcomm). Resilience: YEARS to STRUCTURAL.
Parts-level China dependence — 52% of parts imports, antennas 69%, populated PCBs 55%, even as finished Chinese gear is excluded. Resilience: MONTHS–YEARS.
Demand concentration — 98% of demand is private operators who buy global OEMs; the BSNL order that built Indian RAN capability was a one-off. Resilience: CYCLICAL.
Backhaul — only ~44–46% of base stations are fibre-connected, capping 5G-Advanced and densification. Resilience: YEARS (right-of-way bound).
Value sits with the RF device makers, the silicon vendors and the global OEM brands; India captures assembly, integration and an increasing share of design.
Tejas is the proof point and the warning: it built a 1-lakh-site network, then revenue fell 87% in FY26 when that order ended, and it is loss-making on ₹2,315 cr of backlog.
The export seam is real: Ericsson now ships India-made antennas to Europe with over half the antenna content local, and Tejas has its first international 5G wins.
Component localisation is the next pool — ECMS was doubled to ₹40,000 cr in Budget 2026 and now covers antennas, filters and coils.
The annuitisation pool (AMC, software upgrades, managed services) is under-monetised on a 5.6-lakh-site installed base.
India TANE market $25 bn (FY25) → $50 bn (FY32F): 10.4% 7-year CAGR, value nominal, no volume series [CALCULATED]. 5-year and 3-year CAGR [UNAVAILABLE].
Last year is not one number: HFCL revenue +21.8% (FY26) while Tejas fell 87% on the BSNL base effect — growth is being reallocated, not just added. [REPORTED-T1]
Global equipment market 5.3% CAGR (FY23–FY30F) — India grows about twice as fast, but off a 4–5% localisation base.
5G subscriptions: 430 mn (Ericsson, Oct 2026) vs 465 mn (tele.net, Mar 2026) — [CONFLICTING DATA]; scopes differ, and both exceed the 5G BTS count in per-site terms.
Dec 2026 — BSNL’s commercial 5G target, on software upgrade of the indigenous 4G stack (Kerala and AP circle CGM statements, Aug 2026).
31 Dec 2026 — NCCS security-certification exemption for cloud IP routers and Wi-Fi CPEs expires; MTCTE relaxation package also ends.
31 Mar 2027 — the ₹12,195 cr telecom PLI ends; the successor (reported ₹6,000–7,000 cr, component-focused) is targeted for Q1 FY28 with Cabinet approval still pending as of 08-Oct-2026.
Rolling — whether any private operator awards a material 5G-Advanced or Open-RAN refresh to an Indian OEM; that, not BSNL, is the demand question.
No NSE/BSE-listed company exists in RF front-end devices, filters, RAN silicon, RAN power supplies or antennas as a pure-play.
Nearest listed exposures: Tejas (RAN OEM), HFCL (antennas, cable, telecom products), ITI (contract manufacture, ODC, turnkey), Dixon (Open-RAN PLI), TCS (integration).

sections.title: Bottlenecks — Risk & Opportunity
sections.note: dual-readable: every risk is a substitution play

risk.title: The dependence moved inside the box
risk.text: Trusted-source rules cut Chinese finished equipment to 13.4% of equipment imports, but 52.3% of telecom parts imports are still Chinese — antennas 69.3%, populated boards 55.4%. Localisation of a 4G RAN BOM is 4%, of a 5G RAN BOM 5%.

opp.title: A component policy now exists
opp.text: ECMS was doubled to ₹40,000 cr in Budget 2026 and covers PCBs, passives, antennas, filters and coils; the proposed PLI successor (₹6,000–7,000 cr, reported) is explicitly component- and design-focused. That is the first policy aimed at the 52%, not the assembly.

risk.title: RAN silicon dependency
risk.text: L1-PHY FPGAs, SoCs and ASICs are almost fully imported (AMD/Xilinx, Altera, Marvell, Qualcomm). India imported ~$30 bn of electronic ICs in FY26 and its first fab is targeted for 2028.

opp.title: Disaggregation lowers the silicon lock-in
opp.text: Jio virtualised L1 on general-purpose processors; C-DoT with WiSig and VVDN built an indigenous 5G RAN on BSNL spectrum, live-tested at Ambala. Software-defined radio is the one route that does not need a domestic fab.

risk.title: Demand concentration, not capability
risk.text: 98% of equipment demand is private operators buying global OEMs. Tejas proved world-scale delivery, then revenue fell 87% in FY26 and losses ran to ₹909 cr once the BSNL order ended.

opp.title: Exports are the second customer
opp.text: Ericsson now ships India-made antennas to Europe with over half the antenna content local; Tejas has an NEC Massive-MIMO supply contract and an end-to-end 5G network order in South America. Global imports of antennas, RRHs and BBUs alone exceeded $219 bn in 2024 against under $1 bn of Indian exports.

risk.title: Cost disability at the component layer
risk.text: NITI Aayog puts Indian manufacturers 26–29% above global peers on fiscal disability, and Nokia reports a 20–80% price gap on locally sourced components versus Vietnam or China.

opp.title: The narrow, under-capitalised seam
opp.text: Antennas, RF front-ends and populated boards are where a domestic substitute is most plausible, and Ericsson’s local antenna line shows the 50%-plus local-content threshold is reachable. The next ₹40,000 cr of ECMS money is aimed here.

risk.title: Certification gatekeeping is tightening
risk.text: MTCTE and the ITSAR/ComSec regime gate every product; a graded ComSec 2026 scheme is being notified and the Pro Tem relaxation runs to 31 Dec 2027. Huawei and ZTE remain excluded. Every exemption expiry is a queue at India’s limited TSTL labs.

opp.title: A certification moat in India’s favour
opp.text: Approved Indian vendors — Tejas, HFCL, Dixon — and foreign OEMs that manufacture locally clear the gate first, and NITI Aayog explicitly recommends stronger domestic testing and certification capacity as a build-out.

risk.title: The 5G capex cycle has turned
risk.text: Coverage is largely built (5.63 lakh BTS, 99.9% of districts); Ericsson expects incremental, not 2023-style, capex. Only ~44–46% of sites are fibre-connected, so the next spend is backhaul and intelligence, not more radios.

opp.title: Annuitising the installed base
opp.text: AMC, managed services, 5G-Advanced software and RIC apps convert 5.6 lakh 5G sites plus ~1.75 lakh BSNL 4G BTS into a recurring stream, and the fibre gap is itself a multi-year order book for HFCL and Sterlite. Deepest hidden import dependency: the RF front-end and RAN silicon — power amplifiers, filters/duplexers and the L1-PHY FPGAs/SoCs that do the baseband maths — plus the populated boards and antennas that carry them. These sit below the OEM assembly layer India has localised, are almost entirely imported, and remain majority-Chinese by value even as the trusted-source wall keeps Chinese finished gear out.

sections.title: Value pools & cost waterfall
sections.note: where value is captured · and which pool leaks to imports

items: Value sits with RF device makers, silicon vendors and the global OEM brands.
India captures assembly, integration, and a rising share of design and software.
Indian RAN value-add is lumpy: one BSNL order built the capability, its completion produced a ₹909 cr loss.
Export and component localisation are the two pools growing fastest.
Aftermarket (AMC, software upgrades, RIC apps) is the least-monetised pool.
Tejas Networks NSE/BSE: TEJASNET — RAN OEM for ~1 lakh BSNL sites; FY26 revenue ₹1,103 cr, PAT −₹909 cr; Q2FY27 order book ₹2,315 cr [REPORTED]
HFCL NSE/BSE: HFCL — FY26 revenue ₹4,949 cr (+21.8%), PAT ₹329 cr, order book ₹21,206 cr, exports 41% [REPORTED]
ITI Limited NSE/BSE: ITI — FY26 revenue ₹2,184 cr; ODC, RRU/BBU contract manufacture, West Zone turnkey ₹856 cr [REPORTED]
Tata Consultancy Services NSE/BSE: TCS — BSNL consortium lead, ~1 lakh sites integrated plus ₹2,903 cr add-on PO [REPORTED]
Dixon Technologies NSE/BSE: DIXON — PLI-approved for Open-RAN (RU, DU, CU, RIC); no disclosed RAN revenue yet [INFERENCE]
Reliance Industries (Jio Platforms / Radisys) NSE/BSE: RELIANCE — in-house 5G SA stack, virtualised L1, RAN software licensing [REPORTED]
Sterlite Technologies NSE/BSE: STLTECH — optical fibre and cable into fronthaul and backhaul [REPORTED]
RF front-end devices, filters, RAN silicon and RAN power supplies: no listed Indian pure-play at all.
52.3% of telecom parts imports by value are Chinese; antennas 69.3%, populated PCBs 55.4%.
Nokia’s own read: locally sourced components cost 20–80% more than Vietnam or China.

sections.title: Bottlenecks — Risk & Opportunity
sections.note: dual-readable: every risk is a substitution play

risk.title: RAN & modem silicon
risk.text: RFICs, baseband SoCs and FPGAs are almost fully imported (Qualcomm, AMD/Xilinx, Marvell, Analog Devices); India has no listed RAN-silicon pure-play and no commercial fab.

opp.title: Design-led manufacturing + OSAT
opp.text: The Design-Linked Incentive, MosChip/Saankhya design houses and the new OSAT build-out (CG Semi, Kaynes Semicon, Suchi) let India capture design and packaging value without a leading-edge fab.

risk.title: Sub-THz devices & test equipment
risk.text: There is no commercial domestic supply of sub-THz front-ends or sub-THz test gear; capability sits in R&D (SAMEER, IITs). This is the least mature, most import-dependent node.

opp.title: First-mover on the SAMEER THz testbed
opp.text: India's 6G THz testbed (SAMEER + IIT-M/G/P) already demonstrated a 6,400 Mbps link at 270 GHz; TTDF funding can turn a testbed lead into component capability.

risk.title: Spectrum timing and coexistence
risk.text: The 6 GHz band is contested between licensed IMT and de-licensed Wi-Fi, and satellite incumbents constrain sub-THz use; WRC-27 (Oct-2027) decides the bands, delaying any operator capex decision.

opp.title: A predictable national spectrum pipeline
opp.text: India's Spectrum Roadmap gives 10-year visibility (upper-6 GHz ~700 MHz identified; 400 MHz readied for auction). Predictability is itself the enabler of an indigenous 6G equipment market.

risk.title: GaN/GaAs RF front-end
risk.text: Power amplifiers and MMICs are imported; indigenous GaN (AGNIT, GAETEC) is at pilot/low-volume scale and most semiconductor-grade materials and substrates are still imported.

opp.title: Compound-semiconductor fabs under ISM 2.0
opp.text: GaN foundry and compound-semi capacity (Crystal Matrix, AGNIT's planned fab, GAETEC) can seed an indigenous RF front-end supply as 5G/6G base stations all use GaN PAs.

risk.title: Standards & IP leadership
risk.text: India contributes to 3GPP/ITU/oneM2M but holds a small share of 6G core patents; its 10%-by-2030 target implies a very steep climb from today's base.

opp.title: A seat at the standard-setting table
opp.text: The Bharat 6G Alliance (90 members, 7 working groups) and the TDIP scheme fund standards participation; standards influence is the cheapest route to value capture in a pre-commercial market.

risk.title: A zero-revenue window to ~2030
risk.text: No 6G revenue exists until roughly 2030, so any 6G exposure is a multi-year option, funded by 5G-Advanced and export revenue in the meantime; the TTDF outlay (₹271–542 cr) is small against the task.

opp.title: Sell the 5G bridge, then the 6G upgrade
opp.text: The proven indigenous 4G/5G stack (100,000+ BSNL sites) is already exportable to Africa, SE Asia and Latin America; the installed base annuitises into software upgrades as standards evolve toward 6G. Deepest hidden import dependency: the RF/baseband silicon and the sub-THz test-and-measurement stack. These sit below the OEM assembly layer India has begun to localise, are almost entirely imported, and gate the ability to design, qualify and manufacture any 6G radio. No listed Indian company provides pure-play exposure to either.

sections.title: Bottlenecks — Risk & Opportunity
sections.note: dual-readable: every risk is a substitution play

risk.title: China dependence — intermediates & KSM
risk.text: Roughly half of technical-grade inputs and ~70% of key intermediates come from China; supply shocks, export curbs or factory shutdowns create price spikes. Resilience: months–years.

opp.title: Backward integration
opp.text: Integrated chemistry (Aarti, Atul, Jubilant, SRF, GFL) and the ACFI-proposed ₹5,000–7,500 cr PLI-style programme target the leak; chemical parks/clusters de-risk it.

risk.title: Off-patent price collapse
risk.text: When a molecule goes off-patent, Chinese scale floods the market — chlorantraniliprole prices fell ~80% after its Aug-2022 expiry, hitting technical and intermediate margins. Resilience: structural.

opp.title: First-to-register & CDMO pivot
opp.text: Early registrants of recently off-patent molecules capture the 15–20% margin window; innovators’ contracts (CDMO) move value to lower-volatility, higher-margin work.

risk.title: Regulatory drag & data protection
risk.text: A new molecule costs ₹2,000 cr+ and 10–12 years; registration is slow and data-protection rules uncertain, muting R&D (1–2% of turnover vs 5–10% abroad). Resilience: years.

opp.title: Pesticides Management Bill, 2025
opp.text: Proposed digital, time-bound registration, decriminalisation of petty offences and a CROP portal could compress approval times and reward compliant innovators.

risk.title: Biologicals regulatory transition
risk.text: Biostimulants moved under FCO Schedule VI and biopesticides under CIB&RC; thousands of products, few approvals, compliance costs squeezing MSMEs. Resilience: months.

opp.title: Consolidation to organised players
opp.text: Science-backed, compliant players (PI, Rallis, Coromandel, UPL) gain share as the grey market is cleaned up.

risk.title: Imported adjuvants & process equipment
risk.text: Surfactants, emulsifiers and specialty reactors/continuous-flow systems are largely imported — a quiet cost and capability leak. Resilience: years.

opp.title: Formulation-chemistry & machinery localisation
opp.text: Domestic specialty-chemistry and equipment firms can substitute imports as scale grows.

risk.title: Monsoon & channel cyclicality
risk.text: Domestic demand tracks the monsoon and pest pressure; channel destocking and price wars whipsaw volumes and realisations. Resilience: cyclical.

opp.title: Branded formulations & export diversification
opp.text: Brand equity and geographic spread (Latin America, US, Japan) smooth the domestic cycle. Deepest hidden dependency: the imported intermediate layer. India’s manufacturing and export strength sits on a base of China-sourced KSMs and advanced intermediates (pyridine, chloro-aromatics, organophosphorus, fluorinated blocks) — plus imported adjuvants, catalysts and process equipment. The capital and chemistry to close it sit with a handful of integrated specialty players; the fastest value creation is in off-patent actives, export CDMO and backward integration.

items.h: Snapshot India's commercial fleet is set to triple to ~2,250 aircraft by 2035, but MRO is a services business and civil components a discrete-manufacturing one. India is competent at line and base airframe checks and is scaling component manufacturing, yet ~80% of MRO value still flies to Singapore, Dubai and Europe — because engines and components, not hangars, hold the value. Process & equipment

Components: forging, investment casting, HIP, vacuum heat-treat, 5-axis machining, surface treatment.

Engine & component MRO value leaks to OEM shops (Safran, GE, P&W, RR) and global hubs.

sections.title: Bottlenecks — Risk & Opportunity
sections.note: dual-readable: every risk is a substitution play

risk.title: Engine MRO & OEM-controlled parts
risk.text: ~50% of MRO value, ~80% of engine cost is OEM materials; entry needs an OEM licence. Resilience: years .

opp.title: OEM-partnered engine shops
opp.text: Safran SAESI (300 LEAP visits/yr) and IndiGo–CFM make the OEM the partner, not the competitor.

risk.title: Component MRO 'missing middle'
risk.text: Fuel systems, pneumatics, actuation, avionics LRUs, landing-gear accessories — 'nearly hundred per cent' abroad. Resilience: years .

opp.title: Component repair depth
opp.text: Wheels/brakes, NDT and landing-gear shops (Sika, Horizon, Haveus, Magnum) are the nearest domestic step.

risk.title: Avionics LRUs & software
risk.text: High-end LRUs, FADEC modules and data licences remain outside India. Resilience: months–years .

opp.title: Avionics repair + DOA
opp.text: Thales Gurugram, and India's avionics houses (Data Patterns, BEL) plus DGCA Design Organisation Approvals.

risk.title: Certification & skills
risk.text: CAR-66 engine-CRS anomaly and 25–30% attrition; certified engineers cannot be bought quickly. Resilience: years .

opp.title: DGCA/EASA work-share & training
opp.text: Safran trains 100 technicians/yr; 87+ DGCA AMOs; mutual-recognition is the lever.

risk.title: Aerospace-grade materials
risk.text: Ti sponge, superalloy and composite prepreg were largely imported. Resilience: months–years .

opp.title: Melt–cast–forge integration
opp.text: PTC/Aerolloy (VIM+VAR+4,500t press), MIDHANI and Bharat Forge's ring mill close the loop. Deepest hidden dependency: the OEM-controlled engine parts, avionics LRUs and their data licences. India is building hangars and test cells faster than it is building component and software sovereignty — infrastructure without control of the maintenance pipeline.

items.h: Snapshot Grid-scale battery energy storage (BESS) in India — cells to containerised systems, PCS, EMS, grid interface, EPC and the developer layer. India has ~10–14 GWh commissioned against a 47 GW / 236 GWh need by 2031-32; cells are ~90% imported. Process & equipment
items: Cell making is a coating→calendering→stacking→formation line; India mostly assembles cells into modules, racks and containers.
Key machinery — electrode coaters, stackers, formation cabinets, laser welders — is imported, largely Chinese.
Container & pack assembly is India’s live value-add (Waaree, Pace Digitek, Premier, Vikram).
Cells & cell materials — ~90% imported; China controls 97–99% of anode.
BMS (~90% imported) — now behind a UL 1973 Ed.3 gate.
PCS & power semiconductors — imported power electronics.
Battery price rebound in 2026 vs tariffs struck on lower costs (Crisil: 8–9 GWh delay risk).
Cells (40–55% of cost) leak to imports — Ola, Exide, Amara Raja, Reliance, Waaree are building.
Pack/container assembly, EMS software and TMS are the pools that stay domestic — and meet the 20% DCR.
Grid interface (transformers, switchgear, cables) is a domestic oligopoly (Hitachi, CG, GE Vernova).
Developer/BOO annuity (12–15 yr BESPA) sits with NTPC Green, Tata Power, Adani, JSW.
Recycling is a new incentive-backed pool under the National Critical Mineral Mission.
CEA draft (Sep-2026): mandatory grid-forming PCS + 10% co-located storage for RE plants from Jul-2027.
MNRE draft (May-2026): ≥60% localisation of PCS/EMS for ≥100 MW grid-forming BESS tenders from 2027.
20% domestic-content rule on VGF BESS; rising to 40% and beyond.
PLI-ACC disbursements expected from FY28; customs-duty exemption extended to Mar-2029.
No listed pure-play for BMS, EMS, power semiconductors, thermal management or fire suppression.

risk.title: Cells & cell materials
risk.text: ~90% of cells and nearly all cathode, anode, separator and electrolyte are imported; China controls 97–99% of anode and has used export controls on graphite (2023) and LFP technology (Jul-2025). Resilience: years.

opp.title: Domestic gigafactories
opp.text: Ola, Exide (EESL), Amara Raja, Reliance (Jamnagar, 40→120 GWh) and Waaree are building; PLI-ACC disbursements begin FY28; a PLI for cell materials is being framed.

risk.title: BMS & control electronics
risk.text: ~90% of BMS is imported — a safety-critical, cybersecurity-sensitive layer — and now gated by MNRE’s UL 1973 Ed.3 + ISO 15118-20 import rule (Sep-2026).

opp.title: Indigenous BMS & EMS
opp.text: MNRE now mandates India-developed EMS software; private players (Xbattery, Maxwell, Kalkitech) are scaling — an unlisted pure-play gap a listing could fill.

risk.title: PCS & power semiconductors
risk.text: PCS is 10–18% of cost and largely imported; there is no Indian power-semiconductor fab for high-power IGBT / SiC devices.

opp.title: Localising power electronics
opp.text: Hitachi Energy, CG Power, Waaree, Vikram and Premier are building PCS capability; CG Semi (OSAT, Sanand) is the route toward a domestic device line.

risk.title: Project economics & battery-price rebound
risk.text: Battery prices rebounded in 2026 while many tariffs were struck on lower costs; Crisil flags 8–9 GWh of the pipeline at delay risk, and a 5 GWh cell plant runs at negative EBITDA.

opp.title: Downstream is where the money is
opp.text: Wood Mackenzie: near-term value sits in containers, EMS, SCADA and packs — exactly the 20% DCR-compliant layers Indian firms already own.

risk.title: Skilled manpower & certification
risk.text: Cell-process engineers are scarce; Chinese-technician visa delays and accredited-lab test slots slow every ramp — people and test slots cannot be bought.

opp.title: Qualification moat
opp.text: NABL/ARAI-accredited testing and process-engineering depth carry durable pricing power as DCR rises toward 40% and beyond. Deepest hidden import dependency: the cell-line machinery itself — electrode coaters, stackers, formation cabinets, laser welders and high-voltage test rigs — is dominated by Chinese and Korean equipment OEMs and is subject to Chinese export-control measures, making it the true gate on how fast India can localise cells.

sections.title: Digest — at a glance
sections.note: short summary; full report in chat

items.h: Snapshot The BMS monitors and protects every cell in a pack — a small share of cost (~5% of BESS capex, 8–12% of container cost) but safety- and cyber-critical. India imports ~90% of BMS units, and the ICs inside are near-totally imported. Process & equipment
items: Three-tier architecture: BMU (module) → BCU (rack) → BAU (container/system); a 5 MWh container is ~1 BAU + 12 BCUs + 48 BMUs over ~5,000 cells.
Boards are SMT-assembled in India (Napino, Dixon, Syrma, Kaynes) using imported silicon.
1500 V designs need reinforced isolation and isolated daisy-chain comms.
AFE/MCU/isolation ICs — a four-supplier global oligopoly (TI, ADI, NXP, ST); no Indian fab.
Firmware & cybersecurity — safety-critical talent thin; BMS security flaws documented.
Container-scale propagation testing not available in India.
Chinese BMS price competition undercuts indigenous R&D.
ICs are 30–40% of BMS BOM cost — the pool that leaks abroad.
Design, firmware and assembly stay domestic — Endurance/Maxwell, HBL, Amara Raja (Nuvation MoU).
EMS software is mandated domestic (Kalkitech, Statiq, Tuva) — 5–7% of project value.
PCB/laminates are ~85% imported — an ECMS-backed localisation target.

risk.text: India lacks full-scale container thermal-runaway propagation testing; IS 17387 certification runs 6–12 weeks; the UL 1973 Ed.3 + ISO 15118-20 gate bites imported BMS from Sep-2026. Resilience: low-to-medium.

items.h: Snapshot Component MRO is India's 'missing middle' — the highest-value node it does not control. Aircraft may be checked and even engines overhauled in India, but the fuel systems, avionics LRUs, landing gear, APUs and hydraulics still fly abroad. sections.title: Digest — at a glance
sections.note: short summary; full detail below

items.h: Snapshot The condenser and heat-rejection system — the turbine-island equipment that condenses exhaust steam and rejects its latent heat. BHEL builds 660/800 MW surface and air-cooled condensers and the 700 MWe nuclear condenser; condenser performance follows ASME PTC 12.2. The live cycle is the supercritical / ultra-supercritical thermal build-out plus the 10×700 MWe PHWR fleet, with dry (air) cooling now the growth vector as water norms tighten. Process & equipment
items: Titanium or stainless / cupro-nickel condenser tubing, tubesheet plate, water boxes and hotwell, LP heaters in the condenser neck, circulating-water pumps, vacuum / air-extraction systems and online fouling / salinity instrumentation.
Titanium condenser tubing is the gating imported input; the air-cooled condenser (finned-tube bundles + fans) is the machinery-intensive dry-cooling alternative.
Titanium condenser tubes are imported (erosion/corrosion-resistant, standard for seawater cooling); no listed Indian maker. Resilience: months–years.
Large-scale air-cooled condensers: BHEL floated a GLOBAL tender (Aug-2026) for the 3.2 GW Darlipali + Telangana ACC package — signalling the 800 MW ACC node is not fully in-house. Resilience: months.
Fouling, salinity and air ingress degrade condenser performance; monitored by specialty instrumentation BHEL developed in-house (ASME PTC 12.2). Resilience: months.

Cooling-tower norm rollback risk: the Environment (Protection) Third Amendment Rules, 2025 let MoEF&CC exempt plants from mandatory cooling towers — a drag on forced wet-cooling retrofits, but not on water-scarcity-driven ACC build. Resilience: structural.
BHEL NSE: BHEL — surface condensers and ACC for thermal and nuclear turbine islands (HEEP Haridwar); outstanding OB ₹2.58 lakh cr (Sep-2026).
Larsen & Toubro NSE: LT — condensers, bleed condensers and heat exchangers incl. nuclear-grade; ACC within its 2×800 MW Lara-III EPC (LNTP Jul-2026).
Thermax NSE: THERMAX — India’s leading dry-cooling / air-cooled-condenser supplier; TBWES boiler package ₹1,600 cr (1×800 MW USC, Mar-2026).
Walchandnagar NSE: WALCHANNAG · ISGEC NSE: ISGEC — bleed condensers, shell-and-tube heat exchangers and pressure parts.
KSB NSE: KSB · Kirloskar Brothers NSE: KIRLOSBROS · WPIL NSE: WPIL — CW and auxiliary pumps; KSB nuclear OB ₹1,235 cr (Jun-2026).

India steam condensers for thermal power (scope: steam condensers for thermal power plants, India): CAGR ~6.4% , 2025→2034 — India is the fastest-growing Asia-Pacific market [REPORTED-T3, HTF Market Intelligence]. Value (nominal); volume [UNAVAILABLE].

India air-cooled heat exchangers (scope: dry-cooling / heat-rejection, India): $271.5 mn (2024) → $450.8 mn (2029) , CAGR 10.7% [REPORTED-T3, MarketsandMarkets] — the dry-cooling growth vector. Value (nominal); volume [UNAVAILABLE].

[CONFLICTING DATA] on the wider condenser space (different scopes): global steam condensers for thermal power $4.1 bn (2025)→$6.2 bn (2034) 4.8% [marketintelo]; Asia-Pacific $2,980 mn (2025)→$4,760 mn (2034) 5.3% [HTF]; global surface condensers $1.71 bn (2025)→$2.82 bn (2034) 5.7% [GrowthMarketReports] — the spread is scope-driven.

Demand driver: India thermal capacity ~242 GW (Jun-2025), with ~47.5 GW under construction (30-Jun-2026); water norms (3–3.5 m³/MWh) push dry cooling. Growth is capacity / unit-count led (physical), with a mix shift toward higher-value dry cooling — value is nominal by default [INFERENCE].
BHEL ACC package global tender (Enquiry B/4222/6/0669V1, 04-Aug-2026) for 1×800 MW Darlipali + 3×800 MW Telangana (3.2 GW); bid deadline extended to 30-Oct-2026. [LIVE]
BHEL Q2 FY27 (14-Oct-2026): revenue ₹9,300 cr (+23.8%), consolidated PAT ₹821 cr (+119%), OB ₹2,57,571 cr (+17.3% YoY); board approved ₹500 cr for thermal + nuclear sets at HEEP Haridwar. [CYCLICAL]
CEA advisory (02-Sep-2026) asking thermal plants to run comprehensive annual water audits — reinforces dry-cooling and efficiency demand. [LIVE]
L&T Energy CarbonLite LNTP from NTPC for 2×800 MW Lara-III (Chhattisgarh), ~₹10,000–15,000 cr, ACC within scope (30-Jul-2026). [CYCLICAL]
Titanium condenser tubing has no NSE/BSE-listed maker (imported; NEOTISS India, Hyderabad, is an unlisted producer). Nearest listed proxy: MIDHANI (titanium alloys / mill forms, not condenser tube).

risk.text: The erosion/corrosion-resistant titanium tube (standard for seawater cooling) is a specialty import item; a supply disruption is hard to re-route and retubing cycles create recurring demand. Resilience: months–years.

opp.title: Specialty-tube qualification
opp.text: NEOTISS India (Hyderabad, unlisted) already makes welded titanium condenser tubes locally; a listed entrant — or a MIDHANI downstream tube line — would close the page’s central import gap and capture the retubing stream.

risk.title: Large-scale air-cooled condensers
risk.text: BHEL floated a GLOBAL (ICB) tender in Aug-2026 for the 3.2 GW Darlipali + Telangana ACC package, signalling that 800 MW-class ACC design/supply is not fully in-house. Resilience: months.

opp.title: ACC capability at scale
opp.text: Thermax (India’s dry-cooling leader) and L&T (ACC within its Lara-III EPC) can scale domestic 800 MW ACC capability for India’s water-stressed thermal fleet — the fastest-growing heat-rejection pool.

risk.title: Fouling, salinity and air-ingress
risk.text: Condenser performance degrades with tube fouling, salinity ingress and air ingress — monitored by specialty instrumentation BHEL has developed in-house. Resilience: months.

opp.title: Instrumentation & O&M services
opp.text: Online fouling / salinity / air-ingress systems and cleaning services are a recurring, defensible value pool — reinforced by the CEA’s Sep-2026 water-audit advisory.

risk.title: Cooling-tower norm rollback
risk.text: The Environment (Protection) Third Amendment Rules, 2025 let MoEF&CC exempt thermal plants from mandatory cooling-tower installation, which could slow the forced wet-cooling retrofit pipeline. Resilience: structural.

opp.title: Water-scarcity demand is the real driver
opp.text: The exemption is case-by-case; sites with no water still need dry cooling, so the ACC / dry-cooling pool keeps growing independently of the mandate. Where value sits: the condenser is India’s most mature heat-rejection node — BHEL, L&T, Walchandnagar, ISGEC and Thermax cover the body, ACC and heat exchangers, and Kirloskar Brothers, KSB and WPIL cover the CW pumps. The single import gap is the titanium tube ; the live watch item is the 800 MW ACC package BHEL is sourcing globally.

digest.h: Snapshot The condenser and heat-rejection system — the turbine-island equipment that condenses exhaust steam and rejects its latent heat. BHEL builds 660/800 MW surface and air-cooled condensers and the 700 MWe nuclear condenser; condenser performance follows ASME PTC 12.2. The live cycle is the supercritical / ultra-supercritical thermal build-out plus the 10×700 MWe PHWR fleet, with dry (air) cooling now the growth vector as water norms tighten. Process & equipment
items: Titanium or stainless / cupro-nickel condenser tubing, tubesheet plate, water boxes and hotwell, LP heaters in the condenser neck, circulating-water pumps, vacuum / air-extraction systems and online fouling / salinity instrumentation.
Titanium condenser tubing is the gating imported input; the air-cooled condenser (finned-tube bundles + fans) is the machinery-intensive dry-cooling alternative.

Larsen & Toubro NSE: LT — condensers, bleed condensers and heat exchangers incl. nuclear-grade; ACC within its 2×800 MW Lara-III EPC (LNTP Jul-2026).

sections.title: Digest
sections.note: short summary · full detail below

items: A cryocooler is a closed-cycle refrigerator reaching ~2–80 K without liquid cryogens, used wherever infrared detectors, superconducting magnets or quantum processors must stay cold.
India has no listed cryocooler OEM — the machine is imported; domestic capability sits at unlisted labs (RRCAT, IISc) and defence/space programmes.

Spine: rare-earth regenerator fill → precision linear compressor (flexure bearings + clearance seals) → thermo-mechanical unit → cold finger + vacuum interface → drive electronics → multi-day characterisation.
Key machinery: micron-tolerance CNC, vacuum brazing furnaces, laser welding, helium leak detectors, thermal-vacuum chambers, laser vibrometers and helium liquefiers.
Space/defence units add screening, exported-vibration and life testing.
Rare-earth magnetic regenerator compounds (HoCu2/Er3Ni/GOS) — heavy-RE concentration in China. Resilience: years.
Helium-4 charge gas — India imports 100%, Qatar-dominated. Resilience: months (re-routeable, price-shocky).
Helium-3 for sub-K dilution — rate-limited by tritium decay; no substitute. Resilience: structural.
Helium compressor / flexure-seal know-how and the dilution-refrigerator duopoly (Bluefors, Oxford Instruments). Resilience: years.
The linear compressor is ~40–50% of system cost; the rare-earth regenerator and helium charge are the next cost drivers.
Value is captured upstream (regenerator compounds, precision compressors) and in systems integration — not in final assembly.
India today captures only the cryostat/vacuum-vessel and gas-distribution segments, plus downstream IR/EO integration.
Pools that leak to imports: cold head, regenerator, compressor, magnets and the dilution refrigerator — where no listed pure-play exists.
Global cryocooler: ~$2.8–3.5 bn (2025) ; headline 5-yr CAGR 7.1% (MarketsandMarkets 2025–30) to 13.4% (Mordor 2026–31). Value (nominal); volume [UNAVAILABLE]. [CONFLICTING DATA — scope-driven].
Last-year growth: [UNAVAILABLE] — the sources publish no clean 2024→2025 series; 3-yr CAGR: [UNAVAILABLE] .
Mix: Stirling ~32% of 2025 share; pulse-tube fastest at ~14.9% CAGR; GM ~33% on a hardware-only scope.
End-markets: military/defence largest (~21%), healthcare (cryogen-free MRI) large, quantum the fastest-growing. India has no discrete cryocooler market series.
RRCAT built a GM cryocooler (30 K) with an indigenous oil-free helium compressor (Sep-2026). [LIVE]
DRDO–Zero mK India 20 mK dilution refrigerator under the ₹500 cr TDF (Sep-2026). [LIVE]
REPM sintered-magnet scheme (₹7,280 cr) beneficiary award still pending (Q4 2026). [LIVE]
India national helium-reserve and domestic-recovery debate (Rajmahal/Cambay pilots). [LIVE]

No NSE/BSE pure-play for the cold head, rare-earth regenerator, helium compressor, helium-3 or dilution refrigerator — exposure is via INOX India (cryostat), Linde India (helium) and downstream IR/EO names.

sections.title: Bottlenecks — Risk & Opportunity
sections.note: same facts, read both ways

risk.title: Rare-earth regenerator compounds (HoCu2 / Er3Ni)
risk.text: Heavy-rare-earth separation is China-dominated; ~100 t of holmium would be needed to convert ~100k MRI units against ~10 t/yr global output. Resilience: years.

opp.title: Domestic RE separation + rare-earth-free regenerators
opp.text: IREL (unlisted) plus the ₹7,280 cr REPM scheme build adjacent capacity; frustrated-magnet regenerators (CuFeAlO2, MnNbTaO6) are a lab-stage decoupling route.

risk.title: Helium — He-4 sourcing and He-3 scarcity
risk.text: India imports 100% of helium, Qatar-dominated, ~7–10 days stock; He-3 output is rate-limited by tritium decay (~8,000 l/yr, spot >$2,000/l).

opp.title: Helium recovery, reserve and He-3-free sub-K routes
opp.text: Reliquefaction/recovery services, a national reserve, and funded He-3-free sub-K cooling research; Linde India and INOX Air Products are the distribution layer.

risk.title: Compressor know-how & dilution-refrigerator duopoly
risk.text: Flexure-bearing + clearance-seal engineering is concentrated in a few OEMs; sub-K stacks come from Bluefors and Oxford Instruments. Resilience: years.

opp.title: Indigenous helium compressor & dilution refrigerator
opp.text: RRCAT's oil-free helium compressor is the seed; DRDO–Zero mK (20 mK) and Amaravati Quantum Valley (4 K reached) are the frontier.

sections.title: Digest — at a glance
sections.note: short summary; full detail below

items.h: Snapshot India’s data-centre and AI-compute stack — land, power, cooling, servers and the subsea/fibre connectivity that ties them to the world. Installed IT capacity has gone from ~375 MW (2020) to ~1.8 GW (H1 2026), with a committed pipeline several times that, driven by hyperscalers and AI. The build is India’s largest capital-formation story, but the supply side stays import-heavy: GPUs, HBM memory, liquid cooling and high-end electricals are the deep dependencies. Scope: India, NSE/BSE. Process & equipment
items: A data centre is built power-first : grid feed → HV/MV substation & transformers → switchgear → UPS → rack PDUs, with gensets + BESS for backup. Electrical systems are ~40–45% of capex.
Cooling is the second spine: air (chillers / CRAH) for conventional racks, liquid (direct-to-chip / immersion, CDU, cold plates) for AI racks above ~25–40 kW.
Compute is assembled in India (SMT, integration, burn-in) around imported GPU/memory — Netweb, Dixon, Syrma and Kaynes are the domestic integration layer.
Builds are vertical and complex (land cost): a DC goes live in 12–18 months, but the transmission that must feed it takes 3–4 years.
Power & transmission: 26.3 GW of DC load by FY32 vs ~1.8 GW today; HV substations/transmission take 3–4 years, DCs 12–18 months. Resilience: years.
Transformers / switchgear / HV GIS: global queue, 2–5-year lead times; CRGO steel mostly imported until ~FY28. Resilience: years.
GPU accelerators + HBM memory: import-only (Nvidia/AMD; Samsung/SK Hynix/Micron); prices repriced sharply in 2026. Resilience: structural.
Liquid cooling: largely import-dependent, thin domestic base (Refroid, KuhlTherm nascent). Resilience: months–years.
Subsea: ~95% of international bandwidth lands in a ~6 km Mumbai stretch; repair vessels/depot absent. Resilience: months.
Power equipment (transformers, switchgear, UPS, gensets, cables) is the largest domestic capture — ~40–45% of capex, served by listed Indian makers. Value stays home.
The compute pool (GPU + memory) leaks almost entirely to imports — up to ~90% of an AI server’s value.
Colocation/operator economics are annuity-like and high-margin (FY26 EBITDA: Nxtra 40%, Sify 45%, AdaniConneX 63%) but almost entirely unlisted.
Localisation plays: liquid cooling (Refroid, KuhlTherm), DCIM/orchestration software and optical interconnect (Dixon–Gemtek, Tejas, HFCL).
India DC market (scope: DC services, India): ~$1.7 bn (FY26) → ~$6.8 bn (FY30) , implied ~41% value CAGR (nominal) [CALCULATED from KPMG]. Volume/capacity series below.

Installed capacity (scope: IT load): ~1.9 GW (FY26) → 7.0–7.5 GW (FY30) [REPORTED-T2, KPMG] — capacity CAGR ~35–40%. [CONFLICTING DATA]: Axis Capital sees only ~2.8–3 GW operational by 2030; C&W pipeline 3.9 GW; Economic Survey ~8 GW by 2030; govt target 9 GW.
Operator revenue (scope: third-party colo): ~20–22% CAGR to ~₹20,000 cr by FY28 [REPORTED-T1/T2, CRISIL].
Last-year: FY26 saw ~500+ MW added; H1 2026 absorption 101 MW, 82% pre-committed hyperscale [REPORTED-T2, JLL/CBRE]. Growth is mostly physical volume; the value CAGR is lifted by the AI/GPU mix.
DPDP Rules notified 14-Nov-2025 ; full compliance deadline 13-May-2027 — a data-sovereignty tailwind for domestic capacity. [LIVE]

IndiaAI Mission — C-DAC RFE C-DAC/GPU/01/2026 (published 07-Oct-2026) seeks up to 10,000 AI compute units in clusters of ≥512 at one Indian data centre; bids close 29-Oct-2026, 15:30 IST , technical bids open 30-Oct. Correction from the prior run: the RFE read here requires all infrastructure, data, logs and backups to stay in India and does not say global resale is allowed — that line is unconfirmed. [REPORTED-T1]

DC IPOs — Sify Infinit’s ₹3,700 cr issue stays on hold (seeking ~₹40,000 cr valuation against ₹22,000–25,000 cr offered); Yotta now targets a Jan–Mar 2027 listing of up to US$1.5 bn , draft papers in Oct-2026. Correction from the prior run: the Yotta issue was carried at ₹6,000–8,000 cr. [REPORTED-T2]
UP Data Centre Policy 2026 (Aug-2026): ₹2 lakh cr / 2 GW target, AI-compute booster, dual-grid power. [CYCLICAL]

No listed pure-play for GPU/AI silicon, HBM memory, liquid cooling, DCIM software or the colocation operator layer — nearest proxies are the EMS/ODM integrators (Netweb, Dixon, Syrma, Kaynes), industrial-cooling names (Blue Star, Voltas, Amber) and the conglomerates (Reliance, Adani, Airtel).

sections.title: Bottlenecks — Risk & Opportunity
sections.note: dual-readable: every risk is a substitution play

risk.title: Power & transmission
risk.text: The power ministry projects data centres adding 26.3 GW of grid load by FY32 against ~1.8 GW of operational capacity today. Transmission infrastructure takes 3–4 years to build versus 12–18 months for a DC; Mumbai’s next 5 GW would need new 400/765 kV substations and lines. In Q1 FY26 India curtailed ~300 GWh of renewables the grid could not carry. Resilience: years.

opp.title: A ₹9.6 lakh cr transmission cycle
opp.text: India has committed ~₹9.6 lakh crore of transmission capex through 2032; data centres are being added to the Harmonised Master List of infrastructure. Substation, transformer, GIS, HVDC and grid-automation orders flow to Hitachi Energy India, CG Power, GE Vernova T&D, ABB and Siemens — a structural multi-year order book that sits almost entirely with listed Indian makers.

risk.title: Transformers, switchgear & CRGO steel
risk.text: Global lead times for high-power transformers have stretched to ~5 years with prices doubling; HV gas-insulated switchgear is predominantly imported. CRGO electrical steel — the transformer core material — is almost entirely imported from Japan, Korea and China. Resilience: years.

opp.title: Domestic capacity build-out
opp.text: Siemens Energy approved a 30,000 MVA transformer plant (~₹2,060 cr, by FY30–32); JSW Steel’s Thyssenkrupp Nashik CRGO expansion (~3.5 lakh t) lands ~FY28; CG Power, Voltamp and Atlanta Electricals are adding dry-type/PDU-transformer capacity. Localisation of the electrical stack is the deepest near-term value shift.

risk.title: GPU accelerators & HBM memory
risk.text: AI silicon is import-only (Nvidia/AMD/Intel) and accounts for up to ~90% of an AI server’s value; HBM memory is a three-player global oligopoly. GPU and memory prices repriced sharply through 2026 (Blackwell +15–23%, HBM doubling in Q1), directly hitting the IndiaAI Mission and every server build. Resilience: structural.

opp.title: Integration, not fabrication
opp.text: India cannot fab GPUs, but it can capture the integration layer: Netweb (Nvidia OEM partner), Dixon and Syrma (server JV/boards) and Kaynes (OSAT). MeitY is redesigning the IT-hardware PLI because GPUs make up ~90% of AI-server cost — shifting incentives toward design, system integration and thermal engineering rather than assembly.

risk.title: Liquid cooling
risk.text: AI racks at 25–40 kW (rising past 100 kW) make air cooling insufficient; direct-to-chip and immersion cooling are almost entirely import-dependent, with a thinner domestic base than transformers and far less policy attention. Resilience: months–years.

opp.title: A sovereign thermal stack
opp.text: Refroid (DLC/immersion, BPCL dielectric fluids, Technavious/TierX partnerships) and KuhlTherm (RDHx/CDU, India’s first liquid-cooling validation lab, 300 MW→2 GW target) are building an indigenous loop; Navin Fluorine is making two-phase immersion fluid with Chemours at Surat. An SSRN screen flags liquid-cooling balance-of-plant as structurally reachable by small entrants.

risk.title: Subsea concentration
risk.text: ~95% of India’s international bandwidth lands within a ~6 km stretch of Mumbai’s coast; India has ~1% of the world’s cable landing stations and no domestic cable-repair vessel or depot. Cable planning takes 3–4 years plus up to 2 years to lay. Resilience: months.

opp.title: A second and third coast
opp.text: Google’s America-India Connect and Meta’s Waterworth are adding Visakhapatnam; Airtel is building a Vizag landing station; Tata Communications is investing $152 mn in MIST/Project CS. New landing points, TRAI’s call for cable depots and the 2026 telecom-authorisation reform all widen the connectivity pool. Deepest hidden dependency: the two inputs that decide whether an Indian data centre can run at all — power delivered at the site (transmission, transformers, HV switchgear, CRGO steel) and silicon delivered into the rack (GPU accelerators and HBM memory). Both are gated abroad or by grid build-out, and both reprice the whole industry when they tighten.

sections.title: Digest — at a glance
sections.note: short summary; full detail below

items.h: Snapshot India’s data-centre liquid-cooling stack — direct-to-chip cold plates and manifolds, coolant distribution units (CDUs), quick-disconnects, dielectric / water-glycol coolants and the heat-rejection loop that AI racks above ~25–40 kW require. A drill-down of Data Centres & AI-Compute Infrastructure → “Liquid Cooling — DLC, Immersion, CDU” . Demand is pulled by the AI rack-density step-change (10 kW → 40–130 kW) while supply stays import-heavy and largely unlisted. Scope: India, NSE/BSE. Process & equipment
items: Cold plates are machined (multi-axis CNC / skiving) from C11000 copper or 6061 aluminium, with a brazed cover and a leak/pressure test — flatness across the die footprint is the hard part.
CDUs assemble pumps, a plate heat exchanger, manifolds, filtration and controls into a skid that isolates the rack loop from facility water.
Fluids are synthesised (fluorochemical two-phase / single-phase PAO-hydrocarbon-ester; water-glycol blends) — a chemistry business, not an assembly one.
Heat rejection uses dry coolers, chillers and cooling towers; the fluid network is SS/corrugated hose with dry-break quick-disconnects.
Dielectric fluids: two-phase immersion was PFAS-dependent; 3M’s Novec exit completed end-2025 and no at-scale non-PFAS two-phase fluid is qualified. Resilience: years .
Cold plates / CDUs / quick-disconnects: import-dependent (Boyd, CoolIT, Vertiv, Schneider/Motivair, CPC, Staubli); thin domestic base. Resilience: months–years .
Commissioning skills: certified liquid-cooling technicians and loop-chemistry know-how are scarce. Resilience: months–years .
Standards: no Indian liquid-cooling certification regime yet — specs set by OCP / ASHRAE / Nvidia. Resilience: structural .
Chemistry & cleanliness: mixed-metal galvanic corrosion and particulate in cold-plate channels are the dominant long-run failure mode.
Fluids & chemistry is the highest-margin node and the one place a listed Indian play exists — Navin Fluorine (two-phase, with Chemours at Surat), with Castrol India and Gulf Oil Lubricants in trials.
Heat rejection (chillers, dry coolers, plate HX) is the largest domestic capture — Voltas, Blue Star, Thermax, with KRN Heat Exchanger as the component supplier.
Cold plates and quick-disconnects carry high value but are imported; the machining capability to localise exists (CNC/skiving) but is not yet dedicated to DC cold plates.
CDUs are integration-heavy and mid-value — foreign-led, but Indian entrants (RDP, Dynetics, Neometrix, KuhlTherm) and HVAC OEMs (Blue Star, Voltas) are building.
Aftermarket (fluid service, filtration, coolant recycling) is a recurring annuity and almost entirely unlisted.

India DC cooling market (scope: all cooling, India): ~$2.4 bn (2025) → ~$7.7 bn (2030) , implied ~26% value CAGR (nominal) [CALCULATED from techcircle, T3]. Liquid-based segment ~$0.6 bn (2024) [REPORTED-T3, Technavio].

[CONFLICTING DATA]: IMARC sees the whole cooling market at only ~$0.69 bn (2025) → ~$2.23 bn (2034), ~13.5% CAGR; Stratview sees India liquid cooling at just ~$0.3 bn by 2030 — far below Technavio’s $0.6 bn for 2024. Scope differs (all cooling vs liquid only; product vs service).
Volume: India DC capacity ~1.4 GW (mid-2025) → ~2 GW (end-2025) → 4.5–12 GW (2030) [CONFLICTING DATA]; rack density 10 kW → 40–130 kW; ~70% liquid / 30% air in new builds [JLL, T2].

3-year / last-year: liquid cooling is the fastest-growing cooling segment and rack-based cooling the fastest-growing type. Growth is predominantly physical volume (kW) ; the value CAGR is lifted by a price/mix shift toward immersion and two-phase.
3M Novec exit completed end-2025 ; US EPA TSCA 8(a)(7) PFAS reporting window opens to 31-Jan-2027. [LIVE]

Chemours – Navin Fluorine two-phase immersion fluid (Opteon-class) plant at Surat, Gujarat: ~US$14 mn capex (US$5 mn from Chemours), commissioning guided to Jul–Aug 2026 after slipping from 1QFY27; ~75% utilisation targeted by end-FY27, with phase-2 capex potentially ~10x. Correction from the prior run: start-up moved out of 1QFY27. [REPORTED-T2]
Schneider Electric Motivair liquid-cooling factory in Bengaluru (CDUs, RDHx, cold plates for 100 kW+ racks) — India’s 3rd global hub, Feb-2026. [CYCLICAL]
Blue Star liquid-cooling / CDU models “commercially ready within ~12 months”; Gulf Oil and Castrol fluids in India trials. [CYCLICAL]

No listed pure-play for cold plates, quick-disconnects, CDUs, immersion tanks, leak detection or liquid-cooling service . Nearest proxies are the fluids names (Navin Fluorine, Castrol India, Gulf Oil), the heat-rejection OEMs (Voltas, Blue Star, Thermax, KRN), the fluid-network play (Aeroflex) and HVAC components (Amber).

sections.title: Bottlenecks — Risk & Opportunity
sections.note: dual-readable: every risk is a substitution play

risk.title: Dielectric fluids & the PFAS trap
risk.text: Two-phase immersion was built on 3M’s Novec fluorochemicals, which 3M withdrew over PFAS regulation and completed exiting at end-2025 — cutting approved chemistries from roughly seven to four and triggering a ~40% secondary-market price rise. No at-scale, non-PFAS two-phase fluid is qualified; Schneider and Microsoft both flag two-phase chemistries as PFAS by current definitions. Resilience: years.

opp.title: India as a fluid-chemistry supplier
opp.text: Navin Fluorine is producing two-phase immersion fluid with Chemours at Surat (from ~1QFY27), and Castrol India and Gulf Oil Lubricants are in trials — putting the highest-margin node of the stack on Indian soil. A non-PFAS two-phase molecule, or a qualified single-phase hydrocarbon/ester family, is the single biggest open prize in the whole ecosystem.

risk.title: Cold plates, CDUs & quick-disconnects
risk.text: The thermal-capture and distribution hardware — cold plates, manifolds, CDUs, dry-break quick-disconnects — is dominated by foreign OEMs (Boyd, CoolIT, Vertiv, Schneider/Motivair) and connector houses (CPC, Staubli, Parker, Danfoss), with essentially no listed Indian pure-play. Resilience: months–years.

opp.title: A machining-and-skids localisation
opp.text: The capability to localise cold plates (multi-axis CNC, skiving, brazing, leak test) and fluid-network skids already exists in India’s heat-exchanger and precision-machining base (KRN, Amber). Aeroflex already holds an exclusive India liquid-cooling contract with a US hyperscaler and has tripled skid capacity; RDP, Dynetics and Neometrix build CDUs; Blue Star and Voltas are moving in from HVAC.

risk.title: Skills, commissioning & standards
risk.text: Advanced liquid loops — CDUs, RDHx, immersion tanks — need specialised commissioning and loop-chemistry expertise, and India’s certified talent pool is thin relative to the build pace. There is no Indian liquid-cooling certification regime; specs are set by OCP, ASHRAE and Nvidia (GB200 NVL72). Resilience: months–years.

opp.title: A sovereign thermal-service layer
opp.text: KuhlTherm has stood up India’s first liquid-cooling validation lab; RDP ships CDUs with pan-India onsite SLAs on GeM. Commissioning, validation, leak-test and coolant-service capability is a defensible services annuity — and a natural extension for the HVAC/MEP contractors (Blue Star, Voltas) and the operators building the halls. Deepest hidden dependency: the two inputs that decide whether a high-density Indian AI hall can run at all — the dielectric fluid chemistry (PFAS-constrained, two-phase supply rebuilding after 3M’s exit) and the precision thermal hardware (cold plates, CDUs, quick-disconnects). Both are gated abroad today; both are the localisation prizes the AI build-out has made urgent.

sections.title: Regulatory calendar
sections.note: standing, dated decision windows that move this industry

head: Date / window
Item
What it does
Label
rows: 3M completes its exit from PFAS / Novec manufacturing

Ends supply of the Novec 7000-series that anchored commercial two-phase immersion; forces a procurement rebuild across fluorinated, hydrocarbon, ester and water-glycol chemistries, and a 6–9-month requalification per fluid.
US EPA TSCA 8(a)(7) PFAS reporting deadline
Operators holding legacy Novec inventory and any fluorinated-fluid use must report; state rules (NJ, ME, MA, MN, WA) add overlapping disclosure. Shapes which chemistries can be deployed at scale.
Chemours – Navin Fluorine two-phase immersion-fluid plant (Gujarat)

Domestic production of Opteon-class two-phase fluid (~US$14 mn investment, US$5 mn from Chemours); commissioning guided to Jul–Aug 2026; phase-2 capex under discussion at potentially ~10x. The first scaled Indian dielectric-fluid capacity.
Schneider Electric Motivair liquid-cooling factory, Bengaluru
India’s first Motivair production site (3rd globally) — CDUs, RDHx and cold plates for 100 kW+ racks; reduces lead times for Indian hyperscalers and sets the domestic benchmark.
Blue Star liquid-cooling / CDU commercialisation; Castrol & Gulf Oil fluid trials
Blue Star targets liquid-cooling/CDU models commercially ready within ~12 months; Castrol and Gulf Oil are validating DC fluids in India. Watch for commercial contracts, not just trials.
National Data Center Mission; IndiaAI GPU tenders
Targets 100 green-certified data centres and subsidised GPU access — a demand floor that pulls high-density, liquid-cooled capacity into India.

sections.title: Digest
sections.note: short summary · full detail below

items: Defence electro-optics & thermal imaging (EO/IR) is the sensing layer of the modern battlefield: hand-held thermal imagers, weapon and tank sights, naval EO/IRST, airborne/UAV payloads, missile IIR seekers and counter-drone optics.

India's military EO/IR market is ~$1.19 bn (2026), heading to ~$1.78 bn by 2030 (10.4% CAGR); the wider defence-sensor market is ~$1–1.5 bn, ~80% imported. BEL (with BELOP) and DRDO (IRDE/CHESS/DEAL/SSPL) are the design-and-production spine; a private layer (Data Patterns, Paras, Ideaforge, Zen) is climbing.
The catch: the two deepest nodes — the IR detector/FPA and the germanium IR optics — are the most import-bound, so system value sits downstream of the chokepoint.

Spine: detector material growth (MCT/InSb/microbolometer) → FPA fabrication & indium-bump hybridisation to a ROIC → dewar + cryocooler (IDDCA) → diamond-turned, coated IR optics → LRU/electronics assembly in cleanrooms → integration → blackbody/MTF/thermal-vacuum qualification → DGQA acceptance.

Key machinery: MBE/MOCVD reactors, wafer fabs, single-point diamond-turning lathes, magnetron-sputter/ion-beam coaters, vacuum dewars, flip-chip/wire bonders, cryocooler assembly, cleanrooms, blackbody + collimator + MTF benches and thermal-vacuum chambers.
Night vision runs a parallel spine: photocathode deposition → microchannel-plate and fibre-optic assembly → tube vacuum processing (BELOP, Pune).
IR detector / FPA fabrication — cooled MCT/InSb and uncooled microbolometer dies are ~100% imported; DRDO SSPL/SCL output is limited. Resilience: years.
Germanium IR optics — ~100% imported, China-controlled, price ~5× since 2023. Resilience: years (chalcogenide substitution is the emerging escape).
Cryocoolers (Stirling/JT) — imported from Israel/Europe. Resilience: years.
ROIC/readout silicon and high-speed FPGA/DSP — imported. Resilience: months–years.
Test & calibration gear (blackbodies, collimators, MTF benches, diamond-turning machines) — ~90–100% imported. Resilience: years.
Prime integration and system engineering is the largest domestic pool and is captured by BEL (listed) as DRDO's productionisation partner; night-vision tubes add a near-monopoly pool via BELOP.
IR optics and opto-mechanical assembly is a climbing private pool (Paras Defence) — and the node most exposed to the germanium chokepoint.
Readout/processing electronics and software/AI fusion is the highest-margin, fastest-appreciating pool (Data Patterns, BEL, Zen).
The pools that leak to imports are the deepest: detector/FPA dies, germanium and chalcogenide optical blanks, cryocoolers, ROIC silicon and test gear.
Localisation opportunity sits at the detector/fab, IR-optics-material and cryocooler layers — where no listed pure-play exists today.

India military EO/IR: $1.04 bn (2025) → $1.19 bn (2026) → $1.78 bn (2030) ; headline 5-yr CAGR 10.4% (2026–2030, source) or ~11.4% (2025–2030, [CALCULATED]). Value (nominal); volume [UNAVAILABLE]. [REPORTED-T2]
Last-year growth 2025→2026: +14.4% [CALCULATED]. 3-yr CAGR: [UNAVAILABLE] — the sourced series carries no 2023 base.
Defence-sensor market (broader scope): ~$1–1.5 bn today → $3.5–4 bn by 2030. [REPORTED-T2, different scope — not additive]

Growth is value/mix-led (more UAV payloads, vehicle awareness, counter-drone, seekers) rather than unit-count-led; India captures ~30% of sensor value domestically today, targeted toward ~$1 bn by 2030.
Rival-scope datapoint: the wider Indian surveillance market is put at ~$4.3 bn → >$15 bn by 2029 [REPORTED-T2, includes civil/commercial].

Nimmaluru Advanced Night Vision factory (₹362 cr) dedicated 16-Oct-2025 — thermal imaging, IR seekers and anti-drone; ramping output. [LIVE]

No NSE/BSE pure-play for the IR detector/FPA, cryocoolers, IR-optical blanks or EO/IR test gear — exposure is via unlisted DRDO fabs, startups (Tonbo, EON Space Labs, Tempsens/Pyrosens) and foreign-listed OEMs.

sections.title: Bottlenecks — Risk & Opportunity
sections.note: dual-readable

risk.title: IR detector & focal-plane array
risk.text: The FPA — cooled MCT/InSb or an uncooled microbolometer die — is the single highest-value part of any EO/IR system and is ~100% imported; DRDO SSPL and SCL output is lab-scale. Resilience: years.

opp.title: Indigenous microbolometer FPA fab
opp.text: An iDEX challenge already calls for indigenous microbolometer FPAs and dewar-detector-cooler assemblies; a domestic FPA line unlocks every sight, payload and seeker at once. No listed pure-play yet.

risk.title: Germanium IR optics
risk.text: Germanium is the standard LWIR lens material; India is ~100% import-dependent, China controls supply, and the price has ~5×'d since 2023 with >40-week lead times. Resilience: years.

opp.title: Germanium-free & chalcogenide optics
opp.text: Chalcogenide glass replaces germanium in LWIR lenses and is easier to make domestically — EON Space Labs' germanium-free payload (2026) is the template; NCMM backing is the catalyst. Capturable by optics houses (Paras).

risk.title: Cryocoolers & ROIC silicon
risk.text: Stirling/JT micro-coolers and the ROIC readout silicon behind cooled detectors are imported, gating every high-performance (cooled) system. Resilience: years.

opp.title: Cooler & readout localisation
opp.text: A domestic micro-cooler and ROIC line would lift the cooled-detector ceiling for tanks, naval EO/IRST and seekers — high entry barriers, captive demand, no incumbent.

risk.title: Test, calibration & optical-fab equipment
risk.text: Blackbodies, collimators, MTF/MRTD benches, thermal-vacuum chambers and single-point diamond-turning lathes are ~90–100% imported — the deepest hidden dependency in a 'localised' product. Resilience: years.

opp.title: Metrology & optical-fab tooling
opp.text: Every EO/IR line needs this gear; a greenfield Indian optical-fabrication and EO/IR-metrology play has no incumbent. High barriers, but it is the 'mother' dependency of the whole chain.

risk.title: Export controls (SCOMET / Wassenaar)
risk.text: SCOMET and Wassenaar end-use controls limit export of high-resolution thermal and multispectral EO/IR gear, constraining Indian OEMs' export growth even as domestic capability rises. Resilience: months–years (policy).

opp.title: Export-compliance & certification play
opp.text: A unified EO/IR test/qualification framework and export-compliance capability would let Indian OEMs convert domestic wins into exports — Tonbo already earns ~65% of revenue abroad.

sections.title: Digest — at a glance
sections.note: short summary; full detail below

items: Flat-panel display manufacturing — LCD and OLED/AMOLED panels plus the module layer that bonds, lights and tests them — the single largest input India imports for its electronics.
India has no front-end panel fab: the country assembles modules and integrates systems, importing almost all open cells and every upstream material.
Front-end spine (all offshore): glass substrate → TFT-array (deposition, photolithography, etching) → cell (liquid-crystal fill / OLED deposition + encapsulation) → open cell.
Back-end (increasingly Indian): open-cell in → polariser lamination → driver-IC bonding (COG / COF) → backlight assembly → module test → LCM out.
Key machinery — lithography / steppers, CVD & sputter, dry / wet etch, inkjet OLED printers, laser lift-off, bonding and AOI — is imported; India has no display-equipment maker.
Front-end fab (TFT-array / cell) — absent; no commercially operational fab expected before 2031 (Omdia). Resilience: structural.
Glass substrate — no domestic supplier; Corning / AGC imported; the collapse of the Adani–Hon Hai Gen 10.5 plan (Jan 2026) cited exactly this. Resilience: structural.
Display driver ICs (DDIC) — no Indian design or fab; Korea / Taiwan-concentrated; 16–20 week lead times on automotive-grade. Resilience: structural.
Polariser, liquid crystal and OLED emitter materials — ~100% imported, concentrated in Japan / Korea / China. Resilience: structural.
Open cell — China is 90%+ of India's LCD-module imports. Resilience: months→years (single-origin).
Value sits upstream of assembly: array + cell processing is 30–35% of module cost and entirely offshore; glass / materials 20–25%; driver IC 15–20%.
Module assembly is 15–20% of cost and thin-margin — but it is the layer India is actually building (Dixon, Minda Instruments, TXB, Samsung Display Noida, TCL CSOT, Visteon).
The ₹40,000 cr ECMS is redirecting value into display modules and the components beneath them; the front-end panel fab remains unclaimed by any listed company.
Listed capture is narrow: only Dixon holds a display-module line directly; Minda and SJS hold it via wholly owned subsidiaries.

sections.title: Bottlenecks — Risk & Opportunity
sections.note: dual-readable: every risk is a substitution play

risk.title: No front-end panel fab
risk.text: India has no TFT-array / cell fabrication; open cells are imported. Omdia sees no commercially operational front-end fab before 2031. Resilience: structural.

opp.title: Display Fab Scheme + Semicon 2.0
opp.text: 50% capex support (pari-passu) sits unclaimed; display fabs are a named Semicon 2.0 category (guidelines 16-Sep-2026). A Gen 6 (mobile) + Gen 8.5 (TV / IT) pair is the standing plan — ~$1–2 bn (LCD) to $3–5 bn (OLED) each.

risk.title: Glass substrate
risk.text: No domestic supplier; Corning / AGC / NEG imports. The collapse of the Adani–Hon Hai Gen 10.5 LCD plan (Jan-2026) cited the missing glass-substrate base and equipment cost premium. Resilience: structural.

opp.title: AvanStrate (Vedanta)
opp.text: Vedanta acquired Japan's AvanStrate (Gen 4–8 TFT-LCD glass substrates, ~$500 mn, 2024) — an unlisted asset that is India's only display-glass foothold. A domestic glass plant is the precondition for any front-end fab.

risk.title: Display driver ICs (DDIC)
risk.text: No Indian design or fab; Korea (Samsung, LX Semicon) and Taiwan (Novatek) concentrated; automotive-grade lead times of 16–20 weeks. Resilience: structural.

opp.title: India's OSAT & design base
opp.text: New OSAT capacity (ATMP) plus a growing fabless-design pool could host DDIC packaging — but the wafer and the design IP stay offshore. A medium-term, not near-term, play.

risk.title: Polariser, liquid crystal & OLED materials
risk.text: ~100% imported and highly concentrated (Japan / Korea / China); OLED emitters are effectively a patented duopoly. Resilience: structural.

opp.title: Specialty-chemicals adjacency
opp.text: India's dye, polymer and specialty-chemical base (deep in Gujarat / Maharashtra) is the natural host for polariser film and LC blends — a licensed-partnership opening, not a greenfield one. Deepest hidden import dependency: the substrate beneath the panel — the fusion-drawn display glass and the polariser film laminated onto it. Even a “localised” module plant imports both, plus the driver IC bonded to the glass and the backlight behind it, so domestic value-add at the module stage is capped at roughly 15–20% of module cost until the upstream layer exists.

sections.title: Bottlenecks — Risk & Opportunity
sections.note: dual-readable: every risk is a substitution play

risk.title: XLPE insulation system
risk.text: The technology core of the cable. HV/EHV-grade XLPE and semiconductive compounds are a genuine material bottleneck — super-clean grades come from a handful of global producers, not from India. No NSE/BSE pure-play.

opp.title: XLPE insulation system — localisation play
opp.text: No NSE/BSE pure-play; domestic qualification of super-clean HV/EHV compound is the substitution play, with ~50% of EHV consumption still imported. [DERIVED]

risk.title: XLPE compound (HV/EHV grade)
risk.text: NO COVERAGE IN SELECTED UNIVERSE. Borouge/Borealis (now Borouge International), Hanwha (foreign); BLS Polymers and Ankit Polymers are unlisted. Nearest listed proxy: none.

opp.title: XLPE compound (HV/EHV grade) — localisation play
opp.text: No NSE/BSE pure-play; Havells is bringing XLPE ≤33 kV in-house, but HV/EHV super-clean grades remain the open substitution play. [DERIVED]

risk.title: Semiconductive compound
risk.text: NO COVERAGE. Supplied by the same global compound majors (Borouge/Borealis Antwerp semicon upgrade completed 2025). No listed Indian pure-play.

opp.title: Semiconductive compound — localisation play
opp.text: No NSE/BSE pure-play; domestic qualification of this node is the substitution play. [DERIVED]

risk.title: Joints, terminations & accessories
risk.text: Pre-moulded joints and terminations are a certification-heavy, historically imported layer. Raychem RPG (private) is the localiser (CPRI-approved 245 kV). No listed pure-play.

opp.title: Joints, terminations & accessories — localisation play
opp.text: Universal Cables sources via Viscas (Japan); a listed Indian pre-moulded-accessory maker is the missing link. [DERIVED]

risk.title: CCV / VCV line & equipment
risk.text: NO COVERAGE. Catenary / vertical continuous vulcanisation lines come from Troester, Maillefer, Scholz (Europe) and Chinese OEMs; X-ray gauges from Sikora. Every new Indian EHV line is gated on imported equipment.

opp.title: CCV / VCV line & equipment — localisation play
opp.text: No listed Indian equipment maker; a domestic VCV-line builder would unlock the whole EHV ramp. [DERIVED]

risk.title: Submarine cable & lay vessels
risk.text: NO COVERAGE IN SELECTED UNIVERSE — and no Indian manufacturer at all. Global supply is concentrated (Prysmian, Nexans, NKT, Sumitomo, LS, Taihan) and only ~20 cable-lay vessels exist worldwide; India also has no subsea repair ship. The single largest localisation gap in the chain.

opp.title: Submarine cable & lay vessels — localisation play
opp.text: PGCIL’s 220 kV undersea export-cable package (Gujarat offshore wind Phase-I) is the first real demand signal; KEI has announced plans for a Gujarat subsea plant (potential 2029–30). [DERIVED] Where value sits: Cable OEMs — Polycab, KEI, Universal, Apar, Finolex, RR Kabel, Havells. EPC — KEC, L&T, Kalpataru. Copper/aluminium recovery; submarine cables and super-clean XLPE compound are the open prizes.

sections.title: Digest — at a glance
sections.note: short summary; full detail below

items.h: Snapshot Two chains in one sector: heavy electrical (grid-linked, policy-driven) and electronic (export-led, mobile-anchored). Demand is de-risked by a decade-long ₹9.16 L cr T&D capex plan; supply-side value leaks to imports. Process & equipment
items: Transformer spine: CRGO core cutting → coil winding → core-coil assembly → oil/vacuum impregnation → tank & bushing fitment → routine + impulse testing.
Cable spine: wire drawing → stranding → XLPE/PVC extrusion → armouring → HV/EHV type-testing.
Electronics spine: SMT (printer, pick-and-place, reflow) → AOI/X-ray → box-build → burn-in; semiconductor back-end is OSAT (assembly, test, package).
Core machinery (core-cutting, HV winding, CCV extrusion, SMT lines, OSAT handlers) is largely imported from Europe, Japan, Korea and China.
CRGO steel — ~90% imported; BIS-gated; live anti-dumping probe (Jun 2026). Resilience: months–years.
Power semiconductors — ~100% of valves imported; domestic OSAT only now starting. Resilience: years.
PCBs — ~90% of demand imported; laminates the upstream gap. Resilience: months–years.
Certified skills & HV test labs — bind tighter than materials.
Grid execution — right-of-way / forest-clearance delays run 3–18 months.
Transformers & HV switchgear — strong order books, pricing power at 765 kV/HVDC; value stays with the domestic builder.
Cables & wires — largest pool; new conglomerate entrants compress the moat.
EMS/ODM — huge revenue, thin margin; value migrates up only via backward integration.
Smart meters — annuity-like AMISP cash flows; most visible domestic pool.
Leakage — CRGO, power semis, PCBs, passives and machinery sit offshore; ECMS/ISM exist to pull them onshore.
CRGO anti-dumping probe (initiated 22 Jun 2026) — resets transformer input cost.
ECMS outlay raised to ₹40,000 cr (Budget 2026-27).
Semicon 2.0 (₹1,27,500 cr, Jul 2026) — equipment / materials / design-IP.
BEE star-label upgrade for distribution transformers (Jan 2025).
Passive components & specialty chemicals — no listed NSE/BSE pure-play; nearest proxies are EMS players building backward integration.
Insulators — thin listed coverage; the largest domestic maker is unlisted.

sections.title: Bottlenecks — Risk & Opportunity
sections.note: dual-readable: every risk is a substitution play

risk.title: CRGO electrical steel
risk.text: ~90% imported; BIS certification gates suppliers; a live anti-dumping probe (Jun 2026) could raise transformer costs. Resilience: months–years.

opp.title: Domestic GOES
opp.text: JSW–JFE scaling 50 → 250 ktpa at Nashik and 62 → 100 ktpa at Vijayanagar (~350 ktpa by FY28) — a protected import-substitution franchise.

risk.title: Power semiconductors (IGBT / SiC)
risk.text: ~100% of valves and ~90% of wide-bandgap devices imported; no domestic fab. Resilience: years.

opp.title: OSAT & SiC
opp.text: Kaynes Semicon (Sanand) already shipping India-packed power modules; CG Power OSAT and RIR SiC under construction — the largest untapped pool (~US$140 bn global).

risk.title: PCBs
risk.text: ~90% of demand imported; laminates are the binding upstream gap; anti-dumping duty on ≤6-layer PCBs since H1 CY24. Resilience: months–years.

opp.title: ECMS-backed PCB lines
opp.text: Amber, Syrma, Kaynes and Dixon are building multi-layer / HDI / flex capacity under ECMS with local-laminate incentives.

risk.title: Certified skills & HV test labs
risk.text: HV winding, NDT and fab process engineers, plus impulse/short-circuit test capacity, bind tighter than materials.

opp.title: Training & testing infrastructure
opp.text: Slowest to fix, so qualification-gated roles and certified labs carry durable scarcity value.

risk.title: Grid execution
risk.text: Right-of-way, forest-clearance and land delays run 3–18 months, gating equipment offtake timing.

opp.title: EPC & project management
opp.text: Multi-year order books for T&D EPC players; execution capability is itself scarce. Deepest hidden import dependency: the machinery that builds the equipment — CRGO core-cutting lines, HV winding machines, CCV/VCV cable extrusion lines, SMT lines and OSAT handlers. Procurement lead times run into years, and this gap sits below every other node in the tree.

items: India's EMS sector is ~USD 40–45 bn (FY25), projected to exceed USD 150 bn by FY30 (KPMG, Jun 2026).

items.h: Snapshot Engine MRO is the largest, hardest and most OEM-controlled pool in aviation maintenance. A shop visit is ~60–70% material and ~80% of engine maintenance cost is OEM-controlled parts — so India's low labour cost buys little here. India's commercial engine overhaul is effectively one government shop (AIESL) plus Safran's new Hyderabad LEAP centre; ~80% of demand still goes overseas. Process & equipment
items: Disassembly to modules → clean → NDT → repair → heat-treat/coat → machine → balance → assemble → test-cell run.
Gating inputs: LLPs, HPT/HPC airfoils, OEM parts data and the Engine Shop Manual.
Equipment: test cells, balancing rigs, vacuum furnaces, 9-axis plasma spray, CMM, engine stands.
OEM-controlled parts, data & LLP monopoly — years .
Test-cell capacity and critical mass (needs 2,000–2,500 aircraft) — years .
CAR-66 engine-CRS licence anomaly — years .
Part lead times >12 months — cyclical.
OEM shops (CFM/GE/Safran, P&W) capture the material margin.
Premier/licensed MROs (LHT, AFI-KLM, MTU) capture shop-visit value.
USM/PMA/DER economy is the independents' margin lever.
India's domestic pool is thin: AIESL + Safran SAESI + IndiGo (building).

India: engine + APU ~60% of MRO outlay; ~80% of engine MRO overseas [REPORTED-T2].

sections.title: Digest — at a glance
sections.note: short summary; full report in chat

items.h: Snapshot Everything between the battery and the wheel: traction motor, inverter/motor controller, reduction gear or e-axle, control software and the thermal and test layers around them. In a battery-electric vehicle these systems plus thermal management are 25–30% of vehicle value, and 60–70% once the battery is included. India assembles most of what it sells but still imports the two inputs that decide performance — rare-earth magnets and power semiconductors. Process & equipment
items: Motor build: lamination stamping and annealing → stator winding or hairpin insertion → varnish/potting → rotor magnet insertion and magnetisation → balancing → end-of-line dyno.
Inverter build: SMT board assembly → power-module mounting and sintering → cold-plate and HV connector fitment → potting → firmware flash → high-voltage and EMC test.
E-axle: gear cutting and grinding, heat treatment, shaft and bearing fitment, then motor + inverter + reducer assembly and a system-level dyno run.
Almost all of this machinery — winding lines, stamping presses and dies, magnetisers, vacuum potting, EOL dynos — is imported.
Rare-earth magnets: ~90% of world output and ~80% of India's imports from China; resilience YEARS for a new magnet grade, STRUCTURAL for a licence embargo.
Power modules and control ICs: 60–70% of module consumption imported; no Indian traction-grade module line at scale — MONTHS to YEARS.
Thin high-grade CRNO electrical steel: domestic capacity arriving, top grades still imported — MONTHS.
Test capacity: high-voltage dyno and high-power EMC slots are the quiet constraint on launch timing — MONTHS.
Design IP: controller and motor platforms are licensed from Gtake, Inovance, EVR Motors and AEM — a commercial dependency, not a physical one.
Power module and control silicon is the largest single value pool in the inverter and it leaks abroad almost entirely.
Magnets are under ~5% of vehicle cost but gate the whole motor — the cheapest bottleneck in the industry and the hardest to substitute.
Gear, shaft and differential forging/machining is where Indian suppliers already capture real value — Sona Comstar's BEV revenue was ₹1,154 crore in FY26, 35% of automotive product revenue.
Motor and controller assembly is domestic and competitive, with thin margins and heavy OEM price pressure.
Integrated e-axle assembly is the migrating pool: whoever assembles motor + inverter + reducer captures the system margin, which is why Bosch–Tata AutoComp, Uno Minda and Valeo are all building it.
Localisation is not the same as value capture — a motor assembled in India from imported magnets and modules can be 50–60% local by process and far less by value.
Value: India's EV powertrain components and traction-motor manufacturing was ~USD 1.82 billion in 2024, forecast to grow at 22–28% CAGR over 2026–2035 (nominal) [REPORTED-T3].
5-year: [UNAVAILABLE] — no reliable FY21 base in the sourced set; do not quote a five-year CAGR for this layer.
3-year volume: e-2W registrations 7,83,400 (FY23) to 14,53,953 (FY26) is a 22.9% CAGR [CALCULATED].
Last year: 2.45 million EVs retailed in FY26, +24.6% — e-2W +21.8%, e-3W +19.0%, e-PV +83.6%, e-CV +122% [REPORTED-T2].
Price versus physical: EV penetration rose only to 8.3% of all vehicles because ICE price resets after GST 2.0 in Sep-2025 narrowed the gap — value growth is outrunning unit growth.
1 Apr 2027 — PMP full-domestic traction motor and inverter for e-bus and e-truck; already slipped three times.
China REPM export licensing — no Indian automotive licence approved as of Sep-2026 [LIVE]; re-check each run.
REPM scheme — 6,000 MTPA target, RFP issued Mar-2026; watch bidder selection as the first real localisation signal.
FY2027-28 — last PLI-Auto performance year, with under 10% of the outlay disbursed so far.
No NSE/BSE-listed company in magnets (REPM), control ICs, power modules at traction scale, test/homologation, or powertrain production equipment. Proxies are named on each node.
