sections.title: Bottlenecks — Risk & Opportunity
sections.note: dual-readable: every risk is a substitution play

risk.title: Rare-earth magnets (REPM)
risk.text: China holds ~90% of global sintered-magnet output and supplied over 80% of India's ~540 tonnes of magnet imports. Export licensing since Apr-2025 has left Indian automotive applications unapproved; Bajaj halved Chetak output in Jul-2025 and redesigned motors onto light rare-earth grades. Resilience: YEARS to requalify a new grade, STRUCTURAL against a licence embargo.

opp.title: Magnet-free and light-rare-earth motor design
opp.text: Synchronous reluctance and ferrite-assisted designs are now a commercial route, not a science project — Sona Comstar developed a RE-free SynRM in Q2 FY26, Sterling licensed AEM's magnet-free technology, and Greaves partnered Chara Technologies. Whoever qualifies a magnet-free traction motor for Indian duty cycles owns the substitution.

risk.title: Power modules and control ICs
risk.text: 60–70% of module consumption is imported; SiC comes from Europe and the US, low-cost IGBT from China. No Indian line makes traction-grade modules at scale, and automotive-qualified MCUs remain allocation-constrained. Resilience: MONTHS for a re-source, YEARS for a domestic qual.

opp.title: Module packaging and OSAT
opp.text: India's semiconductor mission is funding assembly, testing and packaging rather than fabs, which is exactly the right entry point for power modules: Kaynes Semicon, CG Power's packaging venture and RIR's SiC line in Odisha can capture module-level value without needing a leading-edge fab.

risk.title: Design IP licensed, not owned
risk.text: Controller platforms, motor topologies and even firmware come from Gtake, Inovance, EVR Motors and AEM. Localisation of assembly without ownership of the design caps both margin and the ability to redesign around a supply shock. Resilience: STRUCTURAL until IP is built.

opp.title: IP as the last localisation step
opp.text: L&T's ₹5,000 crore auto-electronics entry with EVR-licensed traction motors claims ~98% component localisation and ~70% indigenous value by cost — the template for how licensed IP converts into domestic value. Design ownership is the next, and hardest, layer.

risk.title: Test capacity and homologation slots
risk.text: High-voltage traction dynos, high-power EMC chambers and abuse-test rigs are scarce and booked; ARAI, ICAT and NATRAX are the gate. A launch can slip on a test slot rather than on a part. Resilience: MONTHS.

opp.title: Test infrastructure as a service
opp.text: The ₹780 crore PM E-DRIVE allocation for upgrading testing agencies, plus private dyno capacity, is a small but real services pool — and a moat for whoever owns certified capacity. Deepest hidden dependency: the two smallest-value items in the stack — a few hundred grams of sintered magnet and a palm-sized power module — decide whether an Indian EV can be built at all. Everything else in the powertrain can be re-sourced in months; these two take years.

items: Power module and control silicon — the largest single pool in the inverter, and it leaks abroad almost entirely.
Integrated e-axle assembly — the migrating pool; system margin accrues to whoever assembles motor + inverter + reducer.
Gears, shafts and differentials — where Indian suppliers already earn real margin; Sona Comstar BEV revenue ₹1,154 crore in FY26.
Motor and controller assembly — domestic, competitive, thin-margin, exposed to OEM price pressure.

Uno Minda — EV systems and EDUs inside a ₹1,388 crore Green Mobility segment, 7% of group revenue.
Sterling Tools — India's largest MCU maker through a 100%-owned subsidiary, a small slice of a fastener-led listed entity.
JSW Steel and Precision Wires India — the two materials pools that stay domestic.
Sintered NdFeB magnets — ~80% imported, no listed Indian maker.
Power modules and control ICs — 60–70% and near-total import respectively.
Thin high-grade CRNO steel, DC-link capacitors, resolvers and thermal interface materials.
Licensed design IP — royalty value that never enters the Indian BOM.

sections.title: Digest — at a glance
sections.note: A short summary. Structure and inputs live on the tree; process, value pools and watch items are summarised here.

items.h: Snapshot Reading DNA/RNA into base sequence — the instruments, the reagent chemistry, the clinical labs that run the tests, and the upstream synthesis + bioinformatics layer. India is a fast-growing demand market (~20% value CAGR) and a near-zero supply market: the machines and chemistry are imported, while Indian companies capture the service layer. Process & equipment
items: Spine: sample collection → DNA/RNA extraction → library prep → sequencing run → base-calling → alignment/variant-calling → interpretation & counselling.

Key machinery: the sequencer (Illumina NovaSeq/MiSeq, Thermo Ion Torrent/Genexus, PacBio, Oxford Nanopore, MGI), automated liquid handlers (Tecan, Hamilton, Mosquito, Dragonfly), thermal cyclers, capillary-electrophoresis fragment analyzers, −80°C and liquid-N2 storage, HPC/GPU compute.
Sequencers — effectively 100% imported; Illumina + Thermo ~75–85% of the installed base. Resilience: YEARS–STRUCTURAL.
Sequencing chemistry, enzymes & flow cells — imported, 70–80% of kit value; single-source flow cells. Resilience: YEARS.
Indian reference / interpretation data — GenomeIndia is a state asset; global interpretation databases (ClinVar, gnomAD) are foreign.
Skills — bioinformaticians and certified genetic counsellors bind tighter than materials.
Instruments and sequencing chemistry — the largest, most defensible pools — leak almost entirely to Illumina, Thermo Fisher, PacBio, Oxford Nanopore and MGI.
Consumables are the recurring pool (49.6% of market value per one scope; 92.1% per another) and 70–80% imported.
The pool India does capture is the clinical-service layer — Metropolis, Dr Lal PathLabs, Thyrocare, Suraksha, Krsnaa.
Domestic kit-making is nascent and private (Genes2Me, Decipher Genomics); bioinformatics is partly domestic (Strand, Genes2Me CliSeq, Haystack).
Localisation opportunity sits in kits/panels, an indigenous sequencer (Bayosthiti, private) and Indian reference data.
India NGS: ~$284 mn (IMARC) to ~$298 mn (GrandView) in 2025 → ~$1.34–1.43 bn by 2033–34; ~20% CAGR, value (nominal). [REPORTED-T2]
Volume: installed base ~400–500 high-throughput sequencers (2026) → ~1,000–1,400 by 2035 ≈ ~11.5% CAGR. [CALCULATED]
Growth is price/mix-and-adoption led: falling cost (whole genome <$200) plus clinical transition; India is ~2.6% of the global NGS market. [REPORTED-T2]
Oct-2026: proposed ₹8,000 cr genome corpus + Section 8 company; scale-up of GenomeIndia and IndiGen. [LIVE]
GenomeIndia target raised to 10 mn genomes; NITI roadmap proposes expanding to 50,000 then 1 lakh. [REPORTED-T2]
Illumina guides India demand to grow 4–5x over five years; MGI gaining share on price. [LIVE]
BioE3 policy + Biofoundry network (8 institutions) and 11 biomanufacturing platforms. [REPORTED-T1]
No NSE/BSE pure-play in sequencing instruments, library-prep kits, enzymes, flow cells, oligo synthesis or bioinformatics. Nearest listed proxies are the diagnostic chains and Tarsons (labware).

sections.title: System Overview
sections.note: Four subsystems. Gold-bordered nodes are the HIGH-priority subsystems carried into the drill-down tree — the sequencer itself, the flow cell, the library-prep kits and enzymes, the sequencing chemistry, the bioinformatics and interpretation steps, and the Indian reference data. The industry is a hybrid : discrete manufacturing (instruments, kits) feeding a service industry (the labs).

sections.title: Value-Chain Ladder & Supplier Tiers
sections.note: Raw material → aftermarket, with the Tier-4 → OEM supplier bands. The instruments and the sequencing chemistry — where the IP and the margin sit — are almost entirely outside India; the country's listed exposure is concentrated downstream in the service layer.

rungs.label: Tier 4 · Raw
rungs.body: Enzymes (biological) · nucleotides · specialty chemicals · PP / PC resins (labware) · silicon & CMOS sensors · optical glass / quartz · fluorophores · rare earths (lasers & optics) almost all imported

rungs.label: Tier 3 · Specialty
rungs.body: Library-prep kits · SBS sequencing chemistry · flow cells · capture probes / gene panels · oligonucleotides · magnetic beads Genes2Me, Decipher (private) begin here

rungs.label: Tier 2 · Component
rungs.body: Sequencers · automated liquid handlers · capillary-electrophoresis analyzers · thermal cyclers / qPCR · fragment analyzers

rungs.label: Tier 1 · Instrument & reagent OEMs
rungs.body: Illumina · Thermo Fisher · Pacific Biosciences · Oxford Nanopore · MGI · Element · Qiagen · NEB all foreign-listed / unlisted in India

rungs.label: OEM / Downstream
rungs.body: Genomics service labs & diagnostic chains — Metropolis · Dr Lal PathLabs · Thyrocare · Suraksha · Krsnaa · Apollo · Fortis/Agilus · MedGenome (pvt) · Strand (RIL) — where India captures value

rungs.label: Aftermarket
rungs.body: Recurring consumables pull-through · instrument AMC / service · re-analysis & re-reporting · biobanking & data the durable pool; the instrument is the razor, the reagents the blade

sections.title: Bottlenecks — Risk & Opportunity
sections.note: dual-readable: every risk is a substitution play

risk.title: Sequencing instruments & platforms
risk.text: NO COVERAGE IN SELECTED UNIVERSE. Illumina and Thermo Fisher account for an estimated 75–85% of the Indian instrument installed base and Illumina alone holds ~80% of the NGS market; instruments are effectively 100% imported. A single-vendor installed base is the deepest structural dependency in the chain.

opp.title: Sequencing instruments — localisation play
opp.text: No NSE/BSE pure-play. The substitution play is an indigenous benchtop sequencer — Bengaluru's Bayosthiti (C-CAMP, private) is the visible attempt — plus a domestic service/AMC layer. [DERIVED]

risk.title: Flow cell / chip & sequencing chemistry
risk.text: NO COVERAGE. Flow cells and SBS chemistry are proprietary, single-source and imported; the consumable is the recurring razor-blade that locks labs into a platform. No listed Indian pure-play.

opp.title: Flow cells & sequencing chemistry — localisation play
opp.text: No NSE/BSE pure-play; platform-agnostic kit makers (Genes2Me, private) are the nearest domestic capability. [DERIVED]

risk.title: Library-prep kits & enzymes
risk.text: NO COVERAGE IN SELECTED UNIVERSE. Import dependence is estimated at 70–80% of kit value; high-fidelity polymerases, engineered ligases and custom probe panels are still early in domestic scale-up. Foreign kit makers (Illumina, Thermo, Qiagen, NEB) dominate.

opp.title: Library-prep kits & enzymes — localisation play
opp.text: Genes2Me (LeoNext, CE-IVD, Manesar) and Decipher Genomics (Ahmedabad) are the domestic entrants, both private; this is the most addressable import-substitution node. [DERIVED]

risk.title: Bioinformatics & interpretation
risk.text: Alignment and variant-calling are largely open-source, but the interpretation databases (ClinVar, gnomAD, HGMD) are foreign and the bioinformatician talent pool is thin. Clinical interpretation must be signed off by scarce molecular pathologists and genetic counsellors.

opp.title: Bioinformatics & interpretation — localisation play
opp.text: Domestic platforms exist — Strand Life Sciences (Reliance subsidiary), Genes2Me's CliSeq, HaystackAnalytics (private) — and the GenomeIndia reference is a sovereign data moat for India-specific variant interpretation. [DERIVED]

risk.title: Indian reference data & interpretation databases
risk.text: Global reference databases are Eurocentric; ~44 mn GenomeIndia variants are absent from global databases. Access to raw FASTQ is restricted (gVCF only, ~35 TB) under the FeED protocol, which can slow downstream product development.

opp.title: Indian reference data — localisation play
opp.text: GenomeIndia / IndiGen give India a differentiated asset for India-specific gene panels and pharmacogenomics; the proposed ₹8,000 cr corpus would scale it to 50,000–1 lakh genomes. [DERIVED]

risk.title: Lab plasticware & consumables
risk.text: Mostly importable and increasingly domestically served — the least binding node. Cold chain, −80°C and liquid-N2 biobanking remain infrastructure dependencies.

opp.title: Lab plasticware & consumables — localisation play
opp.text: Tarsons Products (NSE: TARSONS) is the listed domestic labware supplier into molecular-biology and genomics workflows — a modest but real listed exposure. [REPORTED-T1] Where value sits: the instruments and the sequencing chemistry — the two most defensible pools — sit with Illumina, Thermo Fisher, PacBio, Oxford Nanopore and MGI, all offshore. India's listed value capture is downstream, in the clinical-service layer (Metropolis, Dr Lal PathLabs, Thyrocare, Suraksha, Krsnaa) and, marginally, in labware (Tarsons) and point-of-care molecular diagnostics (Molbio).

nodes.name: Electrolyser Stack
nodes.fn: The stack itself — cells, electrodes, membrane/diaphragm, bipolar plates and end-plates — where water is split. 24–32% of electrolyser cost but the IP- and material-dense core; most technology is licensed in from abroad.
nodes.importDep: High — stack IP and key components largely imported
nodes.conc: Consolidating — Reliance, Adani, L&T, Waaree, Advait lead

companies.m: L&T Electrolysers — 300 MW SIGHT T-I; pressurised alkaline under McPhy licence at Hazira
Reliance Electrolyser Manufacturing — 300 MW SIGHT T-I; Nel alkaline licence; Jamnagar giga complex
Adani New Industries — 198.5 MW T-I + T2; tie-ups with Cavendish and Hydep; 5 MW off-grid pilot, Kutch
300 MW SIGHT T2; 1 GW alkaline plant at Dungri, Gujarat (₹676 cr, commissioning FY27)
300 MW PLI; 30 MW alkaline assembly live at Mehsana (Mar-2026), scaling to 1 GW
Dual tie-ups — thyssenkrupp nucera (alkaline) and Hystar (PEM); seeking manufacturing partner
HydrogenPro alkaline partnership (exclusive India rights); Ceres SOEC; SOEC demo plant

nodes.name: Membrane / Diaphragm
nodes.fn: PFSA (Nafion) membranes for PEM and Zirfon (ZrO2 + PPS) diaphragms for alkaline — the ion-conducting separator. The single largest domestic-value gap.
nodes.importDep: Very high — ~0% domestic; Nafion (Chemours) and Zirfon (Agfa) proprietary
nodes.near: Nafion (Chemours, US) and Zirfon (Agfa, Belgium) are proprietary. A domestic PFSA/Zirfon alternative is an unlisted white space flagged as an R&D priority by CEEW/MNRE. India imports ~65–70% of the green-hydrogen value chain.

nodes.name: Catalyst (Ir / Pt / Ni)
nodes.fn: Anode/cathode catalysts — iridium oxide and platinum for PEM, Raney-nickel for alkaline. Iridium is the hardest global constraint: ~7.5 t/yr world supply, a by-product of platinum mining.
nodes.importDep: Very high — India has no Ir/Pt/Ni reserves; near-total import
nodes.conc: Monopoly-ish (South Africa PGMs; China for other minerals)
nodes.near: Global PGM supply dominated by Anglo American Platinum, Impala, Sibanye-Stillwater, Northam (South Africa >60%) and Norilsk (Russia). Low-loading catalyst design and PGM recycling are the mitigation paths; alkaline/AEM avoid Ir entirely.

nodes.name: Porous Transport Layer
nodes.fn: Sintered titanium (PEM) or nickel foam (alkaline) that transports gas/water and conducts current; PEM PTL is gold- or Pt-coated. Highest single indigenisation headroom (0→60% per CEEW).
nodes.importDep: High — Ti powder and Ni foam imported; coating can be done in India
nodes.gap: NO LISTED PURE-PLAY IN SELECTED UNIVERSE.
nodes.near: Titanium feedstock imported; compaction, sintering and gold coating are localisable in India. No NSE/BSE exposure; supplier base is unlisted or foreign.

nodes.name: Bipolar Plates
nodes.fn: Nickel- or gold-coated stainless-steel plates that distribute water, conduct current and clamp the stack. Blanking/stamping is present in India; high-grade coating is not fully localised.
nodes.importDep: Partial — SS blanking/stamping domestic; high-grade sheet and coating imported
nodes.gap: NO LISTED PURE-PLAY IN SELECTED UNIVERSE.
nodes.near: Context (weak): Graphite India and HEG make graphite, a potential plate material, but not electrolyser BPPs. Domestic capability is at unlisted fabricators (~15% DVA).

nodes.name: Rectifiers & Transformers
nodes.fn: IGBT/thyristor rectifiers and converter transformers that turn grid AC into the precise low-ripple DC the stack needs — 30–50% of electrical-system cost and a real domestic strength.
nodes.importDep: Low–partial — power electronics largely domestic; some semiconductors imported

sections.title: Digest — at a glance
sections.note: short summary; full detail below

items.h: Snapshot India is trying to build a green-hydrogen economy — splitting water with renewable power — anchored by the National Green Hydrogen Mission (2023). The supply chain is electrolyser → renewable power → water → storage/transport → green ammonia / refinery / steel offtake . Policy has awarded capacity far ahead of delivery: 862,000 t/yr of green H₂ and 3,000 MW/yr of electrolysers, but only ~8,000 t/yr and ~2 GW are commissioned. Process & equipment
items: Two dominant stack routes: pressurised alkaline (workhorse) and PEM ; SOEC and AEM are pilot-stage.
Alkaline stack = Ni-coated SS plates, Raney-Ni electrodes, Zirfon diaphragm, KOH lye, nickel foam.
PEM stack = PFSA (Nafion) membrane, IrO₂ anode / Pt cathode, gold-coated Ti PTL, gold-coated SS plates.
Stack is only 24–32% of cost; balance of plant (68–76%) — rectifiers, transformers, separators, DM water, purification, compression — is where India is strongest.
Membranes — Nafion (PFSA) and Zirfon are proprietary, near-100% imported; ~0% domestic.
Catalysts — iridium (global supply ~7.5 t/yr) and platinum; India has no reserves. Resilience: structural.
Critical minerals — nickel, zirconium, titanium, Mo, rare earths; China controls up to ~95% of some. Resilience: years.
Stack manufacturing — assembly is localising, but stack IP is licensed from Nel, McPhy, thyssenkrupp nucera, HydrogenPro, Hystar.
Demand — green H₂ is 2–3× grey on cost; SIGHT itself names demand creation the key bottleneck.
BoP & integration is India's real, near-term value pool — 68–76% of electrolyser cost, already ~45% domestic (pumps, vessels, power systems).
Stack manufacturing is the contested prize — L&T, Reliance, Adani, Waaree, Advait, BHEL; most IP is licensed in.
Downstream molecules (green ammonia, methanol, SAF) capture the export value — Reliance's 15-yr Samsung C&T green-ammonia SPA (US$3bn+) is the template.
Project/EPC & the RTC-power annuity sits with NTPC Green, Adani Green, Tata Power, JSW.
Leaking to imports: membrane, catalyst, PTL, Ti/Ni feedstock, stack IP, and most mfg equipment.
Green-hydrogen market est. ~US$1.4bn today, ~ 40%+ CAGR FY26–30E value (nominal), off a low base — [REPORTED-T3].
Volume growth is policy-led and lumpy: commissioned capacity ~8,000 t/yr vs 862,000 t/yr awarded — conversion, not demand, is the constraint.

Electrolyser-equipment market estimates conflict on scope — India electrolyser market put at US$57m (2026) by one house and ~US$100m by another; a third puts it at US$620m by 2030. [CONFLICTING DATA].
3-yr and last-year splits: [UNAVAILABLE] in this pass — base series too thin and scope-inconsistent.
SIGHT Tranche-I electrolyser SCDs were 9–10 Aug 2026 ; Tranche-II 26-Mar-2027 . As of Jul-2026, no SIGHT plant fully commissioned; several slipped to 2027. [LIVE]
ISTS transmission-charge waiver — 25 years, for projects commissioned on/before 31-Dec-2030 .
Green-ammonia GAPA/GASA signed 31-Mar-2026 at ₹49.75–64.74/kg to 13 fertiliser units (724,000 t/yr).

sections.title: Bottlenecks — Risk & Opportunity
sections.note: dual-readable: every risk is a substitution play

risk.title: Membranes (Nafion / Zirfon)
risk.text: PFSA and Zirfon diaphragms are proprietary, made by a handful of global firms; India's domestic value add here is ~0%. Needed at PEM & alkaline scale. Resilience: structural–years.

opp.title: Indigenous membrane programme
opp.text: MNRE/CEEW flag advanced membrane technology as a priority; a domestic PFSA/Zirfon alternative is a defensible white space — currently unlisted.

risk.title: Iridium & platinum catalysts
risk.text: Global iridium supply is ~7.5 t/yr, a by-product of Pt mining (South Africa >60% of PGMs). Net-zero PEM build-out could need ~30% of global supply; shortages flagged as early as 2030. India has no reserves. Resilience: structural.

opp.title: Low-loading & recycling
opp.text: Cutting Ir loading (target

risk.title: Critical minerals
risk.text: Nickel, zirconium, titanium, molybdenum and rare earths are near-100% imported; China controls up to ~95% of some. ~1 t of nickel per MW of alkaline electrolyser. Resilience: years.

opp.title: Process-here, import-ore
opp.text: Import the mineral, do compaction/sintering/coating in India — CEEW sees this adding ~10 pts of indigenisation; Ti PTL → stainless-steel substitution cuts cost too.

risk.title: Stack IP & manufacturing equipment
risk.text: Stack technology is licensed from Nel, McPhy, thyssenkrupp nucera, HydrogenPro, Hystar; the R2R casting, coating and sintering tooling is imported. Resilience: years.

opp.title: Assembly-led localisation is already happening
opp.text: Advait (30 MW, Mehsana), Waaree (Dungri), L&T (Hazira) are real; the next step is stack-component and tooling localisation.

risk.title: Demand & cost gap
risk.text: SIGHT itself names demand creation the key bottleneck; green H₂ is ₹397/kg vs grey ₹150–200/kg. Awarded 862,000 t/yr but ~8,000 t/yr commissioned (Feb-2026). Resilience: months–years.

opp.title: Blending mandate + export offtake
opp.text: Refinery/fertiliser HPO mandates would aggregate demand; green-ammonia export (Reliance–Samsung C&T, US$3bn+) monetises early. Deepest hidden import dependency: the electrolyser stack itself — membrane, catalyst and stack IP — not the balance of plant. BoP is 68–76% of cost and already ~45% domestic, so headline "localisation" flatters India: the value-dense, IP-heavy 24–32% of the machine is where dependence is structural. Green H₂ is ~65–70% import-dependent along the value chain.

digest.h: Snapshot India is trying to build a green-hydrogen economy — splitting water with renewable power — anchored by the National Green Hydrogen Mission (2023). The supply chain is electrolyser → renewable power → water → storage/transport → green ammonia / refinery / steel offtake . Policy has awarded capacity far ahead of delivery: 862,000 t/yr of green H₂ and 3,000 MW/yr of electrolysers, but only ~8,000 t/yr and ~2 GW are commissioned. Process & equipment
items: Two dominant stack routes: pressurised alkaline (workhorse) and PEM ; SOEC and AEM are pilot-stage.
Alkaline stack = Ni-coated SS plates, Raney-Ni electrodes, Zirfon diaphragm, KOH lye, nickel foam.
PEM stack = PFSA (Nafion) membrane, IrO₂ anode / Pt cathode, gold-coated Ti PTL, gold-coated SS plates.
Stack is only 24–32% of cost; balance of plant (68–76%) — rectifiers, transformers, separators, DM water, purification, compression — is where India is strongest.
Membranes — Nafion (PFSA) and Zirfon are proprietary, near-100% imported; ~0% domestic.
Catalysts — iridium (global supply ~7.5 t/yr) and platinum; India has no reserves. Resilience: structural.
Critical minerals — nickel, zirconium, titanium, Mo, rare earths; China controls up to ~95% of some. Resilience: years.
Stack manufacturing — assembly is localising, but stack IP is licensed from Nel, McPhy, thyssenkrupp nucera, HydrogenPro, Hystar.
Demand — green H₂ is 2–3× grey on cost; SIGHT itself names demand creation the key bottleneck.
BoP & integration is India's real, near-term value pool — 68–76% of electrolyser cost, already ~45% domestic (pumps, vessels, power systems).
Stack manufacturing is the contested prize — L&T, Reliance, Adani, Waaree, Advait, BHEL; most IP is licensed in.
Downstream molecules (green ammonia, methanol, SAF) capture the export value — Reliance's 15-yr Samsung C&T green-ammonia SPA (US$3bn+) is the template.
Project/EPC & the RTC-power annuity sits with NTPC Green, Adani Green, Tata Power, JSW.
Leaking to imports: membrane, catalyst, PTL, Ti/Ni feedstock, stack IP, and most mfg equipment.
Green-hydrogen market est. ~US$1.4bn today, ~ 40%+ CAGR FY26–30E value (nominal), off a low base — [REPORTED-T3].
Volume growth is policy-led and lumpy: commissioned capacity ~8,000 t/yr vs 862,000 t/yr awarded — conversion, not demand, is the constraint.

Electrolyser-equipment market estimates conflict on scope — India electrolyser market put at US$57m (2026) by one house and ~US$100m by another; a third puts it at US$620m by 2030. [CONFLICTING DATA].
3-yr and last-year splits: [UNAVAILABLE] in this pass — base series too thin and scope-inconsistent.

risk.title: Propellants & primers

opp.text: The same gap is an explicit, policy-flagged opportunity: building NC/NG, ball-powder and primer capacity is a captive, subsidy-backed market with export pull.

risk.text: Barrel/alloy steel is domestic, but antimony (100% imported), copper ore and lead constrain cartridge and case supply. Resilience: months.

opp.title: Materials localisation
opp.text: MIDHANI and Kalyani Steels already make qualified barrel steel; closing the antimony/copper/lead chain is an import-substitution play at the base of the BOM.

risk.title: Barrel-forging & CNC machinery
risk.text: Cold-hammer forging machines, mandrel rods and high-end CNC/EDM are largely imported — the deepest hidden import dependency in a 'localised' industry. Resilience: months–years.

opp.title: Machine-tool localisation
opp.text: Every new small-arms and artillery line needs this equipment; domestic machine-tool builders (and Yantra India's forging base) can capture it.

risk.title: Proof & test throughput
risk.text: Proof-testing and DGQA acceptance are concentrated and can gate output as private production scales. Resilience: months.

opp.title: Test-capacity build-out
opp.text: New firing ranges and in-process quality (moving from end-of-line inspection) widen throughput and cut the return/defect rate flagged by the PAC.

risk.title: Harmonic / strain-wave reducers
risk.text: Effectively 100% imported — no robotics-grade domestic producer. Every joint needs one. Resilience: years / structural.

opp.title: Domestic reducer industry from zero
opp.text: Leaderdrive's 500k+/yr scale shows the shape; India's humanoid ambitions would need reducer volumes exceeding any single Chinese supplier.

risk.title: RV / cycloidal reducers
risk.text: Heavy base axes rely on Nabtesco-class cycloidal units; ~60% global share. Precision domestic production absent. Resilience: years.

opp.title: Heavy-axis localisation
opp.text: High torque/stiffness niche; a natural first product for a domestic precision-gearing entrant.

risk.title: Flexspline steel & heat treatment
risk.text: The thin-wall forged cup needs proprietary forming and tight-atmosphere heat treatment; the metallurgy is a decade-long transfer to master. Resilience: structural.

opp.title: Materials & process know-how
opp.text: The hard part is process, not the drawing — a genuine moat once built.

risk.title: Gear grinding machines & metrology
risk.text: The grinders (Klingelnberg, Gleason, Nidec, Höfler) and CMMs (ZEISS, Mitutoyo) that make reducers are fully imported. Resilience: years / structural.

opp.title: Machine-tool build-out
opp.text: Without domestic gear grinding and metrology, no reducer plan can qualify — see the Machine Tools entry.

risk.title: Price competition from China
risk.text: Chinese units at ~half the landed cost (₹65–90k vs ₹1.3–1.5 L) make domestic entry hard on price alone. Resilience: years.

opp.title: Reliability premium + policy support
opp.text: Indian buyers value lifecycle reliability; a National Robotics Mission demand anchor could bridge the gap. Deepest hidden dependency: the precision gear-grinding machines and metrology behind the reducer — and the sub-micron flexspline process. India can design a reducer on paper; making one that survives 10,000 hours of robot duty is a machine-tool and metallurgy problem.

risk.title: Converter valves & control code
risk.text: A 3-player global oligopoly (Hitachi / GE / Siemens) owns the valve and the proprietary control software; Indian assembly is not sovereignty. Resilience: years.

opp.title: Domestic valve lines
opp.text: BHEL supplies thyristor valves from Bengaluru for Khavda–Nagpur and Bhadla–Fatehpur; Hitachi Energy assembles HVDC valves in Chennai and is adding a line at Chengalpattu (₹1,000 cr, Jul-2026); GE Vernova is building an LCC/VSC valve line in Chennai (early-2027). Local content 30% → 60% by FY35.

risk.title: Power semiconductors
risk.text: No Indian fab for high-power thyristors / IGBT / SiC; ~60–65% of converter silicon imported; a Chinese export control would bite directly.

opp.title: OSAT today, SiC fab next
opp.text: CG Semi OSAT (Sanand) began commercial production Jul-2026; SiCSem's ₹2,067 cr SiC fab (Odisha) signed with ISM in May-2026; CDIL is expanding high-power discrete capacity; MeitY + MoP + POWERGRID launched an indigenous SiC-MOSFET drive for VSC-HVDC (Sep-2026, 36-month development).

risk.title: Converter transformers
risk.text: Custom-built, individually tested, 18–36 month lead times; only a handful of Indian plants are qualified for HVDC-grade units. Global OEM order books are full to 2030.

opp.title: A widening Indian club
opp.text: TARIL became the first Indian-origin private maker to win an HVDC converter-transformer order (₹53.33 cr, Dec-2025) and is scaling 40,000 → 75,000 MVA; BHEL, Hitachi and CG hold capability.

risk.title: HVDC cables (XLPE DC)
risk.text: The DC-rated XLPE insulation compound and the joints/terminations have no domestic production; heavy import reliance, and no domestic subsea cable capability.

opp.title: Greenfield cable plants
opp.text: Sterlite Electric (Vadodara, up to 400–550 kV HVDC/HVAC), KEI (Sanand Phase-II EHV by Mar-2027; HVDC-ready, full spectrum by FY27) and Polycab (EHV by 2027) are building the domestic base.

risk.title: EHV bushings, insulators & CRGO
risk.text: Bushings have only 2–3 suppliers worldwide; CRGO electrical steel runs a ~30% national shortfall. These gate converter-transformer and switchgear output.

opp.title: Import relief + localisation
opp.text: The Centre granted a two-year exemption (Jul-2026) for select Chinese transformer-component suppliers (bushings, insulators) with India plants, to hold schedules; TARIL and others are backward-integrating CRGO processing.

risk.title: Skilled manpower & test capacity
risk.text: HVDC commissioning engineers and HV type-test bays (CPRI-led) are named binding constraints; capacity can be bought, people and test slots cannot.

opp.title: Qualification moat
opp.text: Scarce, qualification-gated roles and NABL/CPRI test slots carry durable pricing power; Hitachi's GTIC and GE Vernova's Noida lab deepen the talent base. Deepest hidden import dependency: the machine tools, vacuum/oil-processing plants and HV test bays used to build HVDC converter transformers and valves themselves — procurement lead times of 2–4 years for high-end manufacturing systems, and effectively the true gate on how fast India can localise.

sections.title: Digest — at a glance
sections.note: short summary; full detail below

items.h: Snapshot India's industrial-gas industry sells oxygen, nitrogen and argon made by cryogenic air separation, plus hydrogen, CO2, acetylene, helium and specialty blends — delivered three ways: on-site build-own-operate plants (48% of value), merchant liquid by tanker, and packaged cylinders . It is the invisible input to steel, refining, pharma, solar and now semiconductors. Process & equipment
items: Spine: filter → main air compressor → molecular-sieve prepurification → cold box (brazed aluminium plate-fin exchangers) → turboexpander → double-column cryogenic distillation → argon column → liquid storage → tanker or cylinder filling.
Hardware that matters: oil-free centrifugal compressors, turboexpanders, PFHEs, distillation columns, cryogenic pumps, vacuum-brazing furnaces, helium leak detectors.
Non-cryogenic routes: PSA/VPSA for small N₂/O₂; SMR and electrolysis for H₂; recovery plants for CO₂.
Process IP and cold-box hardware — design ownership sits with Linde, Air Products, Air Liquide; no Indian turboexpander or PFHE capability. Resilience: years.
Helium — 100% imported, no substitute, 7–10 days of inventory. Resilience: structural.
Electronic specialty gases — ~25 of ~50 gases will stay import-only. Resilience: years.
Power price — ~24% of supplier revenue; the single largest controllable cost. Resilience: weeks.
Rare gases (Ne/Kr/Xe) — Indian ASUs mostly lack recovery skids; import from China/Ukraine/Russia. Resilience: structural.
On-site BOO contracts are the annuity: 15–20-year take-or-pay, ~23% of the leader's revenue but the most durable cash flow.
Merchant liquid carries the pricing power when regional supply is tight; distance-limited to roughly 200–300 km.
Specialty and electronic gases earn the highest margin per cubic metre and are the least localised — the open white space.
Cryogenic equipment is India's genuine export win: INOX India earns ~59% of revenue abroad at ~24% EBITDA margin.
Leaking to imports: helium, rare gases, ~38 specialty gases, cold-box internals, turboexpanders and large centrifugal compressors.
Value (nominal): 6.7% 5-yr CAGR (2020–25), 6.9% 3-yr , +7.6% last year — [CALCULATED] from a US$1,020m→1,410m series.
Volume: 4.4% 5-yr CAGR , +4.2% last year (10.0→12.4 mn tonnes) — so roughly a third of value growth is price and mix.
Forecasts cluster at 6–7.5% to 2028–31; published market sizes conflict on scope from US$1.31bn to US$3.81bn. [CONFLICTING DATA]
Qatar Ras Laffan helium force majeure (Mar-2026); repairs guided at 3–5 years. [LIVE]
Gas Cylinder (Third Amendment) Rules 2026 notified 21-Sep-2026 — CNG/CBG mobile refuelling units. [REPORTED-T1]
Linde India's SEBI / Supreme Court related-party and business-allocation matter — NSE valuation report dated 16-Mar-2026, impact indeterminate. [LIVE]
INOX AP's ₹500 cr Dholera electronic-specialty-gas hub, targeted live 12–18 months from Oct-2025. [LIVE]
No NSE/BSE pure-play in helium, electronic specialty gases, rare-gas recovery or ASU process design — the four highest-value import nodes are unlisted or foreign.
The market leader, INOX Air Products (₹3,048 cr revenue, ~50% operating margin), is a 50:50 INOX–Air Products JV and is not listed.

sections.title: Bottlenecks — Risk & Opportunity
sections.note: dual-readable: every risk is a substitution play

risk.title: ASU process IP, cold box and turboexpander
risk.text: India runs thousands of tonnes per day of ASU capacity but Linde, Air Products and Air Liquide own the design of almost all of it. There is no Indian cryogenic turboexpander capability and no brazed aluminium plate-fin heat exchanger capability; domestic designers reach only about 5,000 Nm³/h against the 2,000–5,250 TPD units built at steel mills. Resilience: years.

opp.title: Fabricate-here, license-the-process
opp.text: Linde India already fabricates columns up to 7 m wide, 45 m long and 170 t at Taratala, and INOX India builds large cryogenic tanks on its own technology. The realistic play is cold-box and column fabrication plus erection for licensed designs, then turboexpander and PFHE joint ventures — a pool worth the rotating-equipment share of every new ASU.

risk.title: Helium — 100% imported, no substitute
risk.text: India consumed about 3.4 million cubic metres in 2025 with zero domestic production; over half traditionally comes from Qatar, whose Ras Laffan complex suffered force majeure in March 2026 and is guided at 3–5 years to repair. Inventories are 7–10 days because of boil-off, and prices rose 35–50% within weeks. Resilience: structural.

opp.title: Multi-origin contracts, recovery and recycling
opp.text: Stallion India's January-2026 tie-up with Sharjah Oxygen for RAS Gases product is the template for a listed helium-import franchise. Zero-boil-off MRI technology, on-site reclamation and closed-loop recovery at fabs turn scarcity into a service business; domestic extraction from West Bengal and Jharkhand gas is below the ~0.2% economic threshold and 5–10 years away.

risk.title: Electronic specialty gases
risk.text: A fab needs more than 50 ultra-high-purity gases; INOX Air Products makes about 12 and is adding 10, leaving roughly 25 that will stay import-only. Purity runs to parts per billion, the gases are toxic, flammable or corrosive, and no fab can afford a millisecond of downtime. Resilience: years.

opp.title: The one node with a live policy subsidy and a live build
opp.text: Semicon 2.0 (Cabinet, July 2026) extends incentives to semiconductor materials, chemicals and gases; INOX AP's ₹500 cr Dholera hub is under construction. Purification, packaging, analysis and audit-readiness — not molecule synthesis — are the bankable first steps, and India's first UHP nitrous oxide plant already exists.

risk.title: Power price
risk.text: Electricity is roughly 24% of supplier revenue and the dominant cash cost of an ASU; Linde India spent ₹129.7 cr on power and fuel against ₹694.4 cr of revenue in Q1 FY27. A tariff revision or a lost open-access approval moves merchant margins immediately. Resilience: weeks for on-site contracts (pass-through), months for merchant.

opp.title: Captive renewables and open access
opp.text: Linde India has taken stakes in renewable SPVs (Avaada, FPEL Surya, Zenataris) purely to buy power; Air Water's Chennai plant covers ~40% of its electricity with solar. Green-power-linked ASUs become both a cost hedge and a selling point for green-hydrogen and green-steel customers.

risk.title: Rare gases (neon, krypton, xenon)
risk.text: These come out of the same cold box, but Indian ASUs mostly do not have recovery skids, so the country imports from China, Ukraine and Russia — three jurisdictions with active export-control or conflict risk. Xenon and krypton are ~36% and ~67% semiconductor-use gases globally. Resilience: structural.

opp.title: Retrofit recovery onto every new ASU
opp.text: Rare-gas recovery is a small incremental capex on a ₹750 cr plant and yields the highest value per cubic metre in the industry. With roughly 20 large ASUs announced or under construction, attaching recovery skids is a near-term, high-return localisation play — currently with no Indian supplier.

risk.title: Demand concentration in steel
risk.text: Steel and metals are the largest end-use, and on-site contracts are anchored on SAIL, Tata Steel, JSW and AM/NS expansions. A steel capex pause idles multi-thousand-tonne plants that cannot be relocated. Resilience: months–years (contract-backed, take-or-pay).

opp.title: Diversify into solar and semiconductors
opp.text: INOX AP already supplies Tata's TP Solar, ReNew and Waaree, and Air Water reads semiconductor nitrogen demand as the next leg. Each new demand cluster — PV, OSAT, display, food cold chain, data-centre cooling — is a chance to re-price merchant gas upward. Deepest hidden import dependency: not the gas — the machine that makes the gas . India can fabricate tanks, tankers and cylinders competitively and even exports them, but the cold box internals (PFHE), the turboexpander and the large oil-free centrifugal compressor that decide an ASU's efficiency and lead time are all imported, as is the process design itself. A 2,150 TPD plant is ₹750 cr of which the value-dense core is foreign; the same is true of the specialty-gas packages that a fab needs.

sections.title: Digest
sections.note: short summary

items.h: Snapshot India's basic inorganic chemical complex — the alkali and acid backbone that feeds alumina, glass, textiles, water treatment, steel and agriculture. A process industry , so the BOM is a recipe and energy balance, not an assembly tree. It spans chlor-alkali, soda ash, industrial gases, mineral acids and phosphate fertilisers. Process & equipment
items: Chlor-alkali: brine purification → membrane-cell electrolysis; ~2,150–2,200 kWh/t; electricity is the dominant cost .
Soda ash: Solvay route, then compaction to dense grade; emerging electric calciners for low-CO₂ ash.
Gases: cryogenic air-separation units (ASU) and PSA; acids: DCDA sulphur-burn and smelter by-product plants.
Rock phosphate / phosphoric acid — imported; MONTHS–YEARS to substitute.
Potash — 100% imported; STRUCTURAL, no localisation path.
Chlorine imbalance — weak chlorine offtake can force caustic output cuts; MONTHS.
Soda-ash import surge — protected only by MIP / anti-dumping; MONTHS.
Turnkey equipment (ASU, cells, acid plants) — YEARS.
Caustic soda is a thin-margin commodity; the value is migrating downstream into chlorine derivatives , where India is under-integrated.
Soda ash value is policy-set — MIP and anti-dumping determine realisations; solar glass is the new demand pool.
Industrial gases are contract-locked and the most attractive pool — but the bulk leaks to unlisted MNC JVs.
In phosphate fertilisers the pool is captured by the subsidy , not the market; importers absorb losses.
Smelter by-product acid is a genuine domestic-cost hedge against imported sulphur.
Localisation prize sits in rock-phosphate / phosphoric-acid capacity and in downstream chlorine integration.

Correction from the prior run: soda-ash MIP ₹20,108/t lapsed 31-Dec-2025 and was not renewed; imports from China rose ~5× in Q1 FY26. AD duties recommended; the live instrument is the fresh safeguard-QR probe initiated 16-Mar-2026.
NBS subsidy rabi 2025-26: P ₹47.96/kg, S ₹2.87/kg.
Rock-phosphate price-linkage notification (IBM formula) — draft, gazette pending.
GHCL ₹6,500 cr greenfield and Tata Mithapur +350 kt dense soda-ash timetables.

sections.title: Digest — at a glance
sections.note: short summary; full report in chat

items.h: Snapshot Li-ion cell manufacturing is the single largest value pool in the battery chain and India's deepest import gap: ~2 GWh installed against a ~260 GWh tender pipeline, with cells 25–40% costlier to make locally. Chemistry is LFP-dominant for BESS; NMC serves higher-energy uses. Process & equipment
items: Process train: slurry mixing → coating & drying → calendering → slitting/die-cutting → stacking or winding → tab welding → electrolyte filling → formation → ageing → grading.
Cell-line equipment is ~55–60% of a 5 GWh plant's cost and >75% of global capacity is Chinese (Wuxi Lead, Yinghe, Hangke, Hymson).
India's live value-add is module/pack/container assembly (Semco, Itech), not cell making.
Cathode & anode — China ~90% of LFP CAM and >90% of graphitisation; LFP tech on China's restricted-export list (Jul-2025).
Separator & copper foil — near-100% / 80–85% imported.
Cell-line machinery — on China's dual-use list; the 10 Nov 2026 suspension expiry is a live cliff.
Scale economics — a 5 GWh plant runs at ~−10% EBITDA; breakeven ~10 GWh.
Cathode CAM (35–45% of material cost) — Himadri (HSCL), Gujarat Fluorochemicals (FLUOROCHEM), Tata Chemicals.
Anode AAM (12–18%) — HEG, Himadri; Epsilon/TACC unlisted.
Separator & electrolyte — TCPL (TCPLPACK) separator; Neogen (NEOGEN) + GFL electrolyte/salts.

risk.title: Cathode & anode (CAM / AAM)
risk.text: China holds ~90% of LFP cathode and >90% of graphitisation; LFP technology and graphite/anode equipment are under Chinese export control. Resilience: structural.

opp.title: Domestic CAM & anode
opp.text: Himadri, GFL, HEG/TACC and Epsilon are commissioning CAM/AAM; a ~₹12,000–13,000 cr component scheme is in final approval.

opp.title: Machinery duty relief
opp.text: ~85 categories of cell-making machinery are BCD-exempt to 31 Mar 2029, and Indian pack/module-line integrators (Semco, Itech) are scaling.

risk.title: Scale economics
risk.text: A 5 GWh plant runs at ~−10% EBITDA; breakeven ~10 GWh and positive margins need ≥20 GWh; domestic cells cost 25–40% more than imports. Resilience: years.

opp.title: Policy-pulled demand
opp.text: CEA's storage mandate, the 20% DCR on VGF BESS and grid-forming rules create captive volume; PLI-ACC disbursements begin FY28.

risk.title: Technology licences & skilled manpower
risk.text: Nearly all players rely on Chinese/Korean technology licences, now restricted; Chinese-engineer visa delays slow commissioning; LFP process know-how is tacit. Resilience: structural.

opp.title: In-house development
opp.text: Agratas developed LFP in-house after concluding Chinese licensing was near-nil; Indian process-engineering depth is building with each line commissioned. Deepest hidden dependency: the cell-making machinery itself — electrode coaters, stackers, formation cabinets and HV test rigs — is Chinese-dominated and export-control exposed, so it is the true gate on how fast India can localise cells, ahead even of the materials.

Flight-tested at ITR Chandipur and Abdul Kalam Island; new ranges at Junput and Nagayalanka.

Test-range throughput — new ranges under construction; months.
Solid-propellant capacity — near-duopoly; months.
Integration and electronics (BDL, BEL) capture system value.
Propulsion (Solar, Premier) and warheads are the fastest-growing private pools.

sections.title: Digest — at a glance
sections.note: short summary; full detail below

items.h: Snapshot India is the world’s second-largest mobile-phone maker by volume and now its top exporter of finished phones — ₹6.27 lakh cr produced and ₹2.60 lakh cr exported in FY26, with 99.2% of domestically used phones made locally. But the value sits in imported components: domestic value addition is only ~23% against ~38% in China, and non-localised parts (chipset, memory, display, camera) are ~55–60% of a phone’s bill of materials. Scope: India, NSE/BSE. Process & equipment
items: Assembly spine: SMT/PCBA → sub-assembly (display, camera, battery bonding) → final assembly–test–pack (FATP), across 300+ Indian assembly units.

Key machinery: SMT lines (printer, pick-and-place, reflow, AOI, X-ray), display bonding lines (COG/COF), camera-module lines (COB/CSP), injection moulding for enclosures, automated optical/electrical test.
Component fabs are only now starting: display module sub-assembly (Dixon–HKC, Minda), camera modules (Dixon Q-Tech), Li-ion cells (ATL; Munoth–Cosmx), PCB (Kaynes, AT&S, BPL) — all ECMS-funded.
Semiconductors — SoC, memory, PMIC, RF front-end: ~fully imported; ICs are 23.7% of India’s electronics import basket (~$30 bn in FY26). Resilience: structural.
Display assembly — no front-end panel fab; ~$4.4 bn imported; module sub-assembly only just starting. Resilience: years.
Camera modules — ~25% localised; module sub-assembly beginning (Dixon Q-Tech). Resilience: months–years.
Memory price shock — DRAM/NAND +40–50% YoY on AI demand is the live cost driver. Resilience: structural (global).
Li-ion cells & chargers — consumer cells ~fully imported; charger leader (Salcomp) is unlisted.
Final assembly is high-volume, thin-margin (Dixon’s mobile & EMS: ~₹44,257 cr revenue at ~3.5% operating margin) — value leaks upstream.
Biggest import pools: chipset/memory/RF (structural), display assembly (~13.5% of BOM) and camera (~10%) — together ~55–60% of BOM, mostly imported.
Value that stays home: PCBA (96% DVA), battery packs (95%), vibration motors (80%), USB cables (60%), mechanics (20%), chargers (20%).
Localisation wave (ECMS): display module (Dixon–HKC, ~₹5,500–6,000 cr potential), camera modules (Dixon Q-Tech, ₹2,500 cr target), enclosures (Tata, Motherson, Hindalco), PCB, passives, magnets.
Policy now pays for localisation: MPMS gives +1.5% for domestic sourcing and +3% for Indian-brand design — the first scheme rewarding components, not just assembly.
Accessories (~$7.5 bn, growing) and the ~1 bn-device installed base are the durable domestic pools.

India smartphone shipments: ~153 mn CY2025 → forecast ~125–133 mn CY2026 (−13 to −18%), Q3 CY2026 −26% YoY (decade low) — a memory-driven price shock, not lost demand. ASP $282 (2025, +8%); replacement cycle 3.5→4.3 yrs [REPORTED-T2, Omdia/IDC].
Production & export (value): mobile production ₹6.27 lakh cr FY26; exports ₹2.60 lakh cr [REPORTED-T1, PIB].
Accessories: USD 6.86 bn (2025) → 14.66 bn (2034); 5-yr CAGR ~8.5% [CALCULATED] from USD 4.56 bn (2020) [REPORTED-T3, IMARC].
[CONFLICTING DATA] on the handset trajectory (different scopes): IMARC 163.72 mn (2025)→295.92 mn (2034), 6.53% CAGR vs Omdia/IDC/Counterpoint forecasting a 2026 decline.
MPMS notified Aug-2026 — FY27–31, ₹62,500 cr; first claims from FY27. [LIVE]
ECMS outlay raised to ₹40,000 cr (Budget 2026-27); 106 projects; further tranches expected. [CYCLICAL]
PLI-LSEM ended 31-Mar-2026 — margin headwind as benefits phase out (Dixon guided ~50–70 bps). [CYCLICAL]
Memory price cycle — normalisation not expected before H1-2027 (Omdia). [LIVE]

No NSE/BSE pure-play for: SoC/chipset, memory, RF front-end, consumer Li-ion cell, charger/adapter, image sensor, front-end display panel, and test/certification. Nearest listed proxies are the EMS/component integrators (Dixon, Kaynes, Syrma, Centum); the rest are foreign or private (Foxconn, Tata Electronics, Bhagwati, Salcomp, ATL, Munoth).

sections.title: Bottlenecks — Risk & Opportunity
sections.note: dual-readable: every risk is a substitution play

risk.title: Semiconductors — SoC, memory, PMIC, RF
risk.text: The highest-value parts of every handset are ~fully imported; ICs are 23.7% of India’s electronics import basket (~$30 bn in FY26), and industry estimates put Chinese firms at 70–75% of components used in India. No Indian listed pure-play exists. Resilience: structural.

opp.title: Fab, OSAT & design
opp.text: Semicon India (Semicon 2.0 approved 15-Jul-2026), the C2S/TTDF design programmes and commercial OSAT (Kaynes Semicon, Sanand) plus the India Semiconductor Mission build the first domestic silicon base; fabless design (Signalchip, Saankhya/Tejas) is the open prize. The memory sub-assembly (SSD/module) route is also opening.

risk.title: Display & camera modules
risk.text: India has no front-end display-panel fab and imports ~$4.4 bn of panels; display assembly is ~13.5% and camera ~10% of a phone’s BOM, and both are only ~25% localised. Together with the chipset/memory, non-localised parts are ~55–60% of BOM. Resilience: years.

opp.title: Module sub-assembly is starting
opp.text: Dixon’s 74:26 HKC display-module JV (~₹1,100 cr, 24 mn mobile displays phase-1, commercial Q4FY27) and Minda’s ECMS display-module approval; Dixon Q-Tech camera modules scaling 70→180–190 mn units; TCL CSOT’s Tirupati open-cell plant (India’s only) is on the block. Dixon projects this lifts mobile DVA toward ~40%.

risk.title: Memory price shock
risk.text: DRAM/NAND prices rose ~40–50% YoY on AI data-centre demand, forcing handset price hikes, deferring replacement demand and pushing Q3 CY2026 shipments down 26% to a decade low. Normalisation is not expected before H1-2027. Resilience: structural (a global cycle India cannot control).

opp.title: Premiumisation & value mix
opp.text: Higher prices are shifting mix to premium and lengthening replacement cycles (3.5→4.3 yrs), lifting ASPs ($282, +8%). Finance-led purchasing, trade-in/buyback and accessories attachment (chargers, TWS, cases) are the offsetting demand pools; 4G is re-entering the value band below ₹20,000.

risk.title: Cells & chargers
risk.text: Consumer Li-ion cells are ~fully imported (cell = ~75–80% of battery cost); the global leader (ATL) and the Munoth–Cosmx JV are unlisted, and the charger leader (Salcomp) is unlisted. ACC-PLI, aimed at EV cells, has commissioned only 1.4 GWh of 50 GWh. Resilience: years.

opp.title: Cell & charger localisation
opp.text: ECMS is funding Li-ion cell lines (ATL Haryana; Munoth, with Cosmx taking 26%), anode material (NPSPL/Epsilon), acetylene black (PCBL) and electrolyte additives (Acutaas). Exide and Amara Raja are building EV/industrial cell capacity. Local cell + charger capacity is the deepest import-substitution prize in the handset BOM.

risk.title: Shallow component depth & thin margins
risk.text: Assembly is high-volume and thin-margin (Dixon mobile & EMS ~3.5% operating margin), and PLI-LSEM’s expiry removes a cushion. India is a final-market supplier (US/UAE), not embedded in dense East-Asian component trade, so value addition stays ~23%. Resilience: months–years.

opp.title: MPMS + ECMS reward depth
opp.text: The ₹62,500 cr MPMS pays +1.5% for domestic sourcing and +3% for Indian-brand design/R&D; ECMS (raised to ₹40,000 cr) funds 106 component projects. Together they shift policy from assembly to components — the structural fix for both margin and DVA. Deepest hidden import dependency: the memory (DRAM/NAND) and SoC dies inside every phone, and one layer up, the display panels, image sensors and Li-ion cells that India still cannot make at scale — plus the precision manufacturing equipment (SMT, bonding, injection) used to build the modules.

Accessories (~$7.5 bn, ~8.5% CAGR) and the ~1 bn-device installed base are durable domestic pools.

Dixon Technologies NSE/BSE: DIXON — largest smartphone maker by volume (19% CY2025); FY26 revenue ₹48,893 cr (+26%), mobile & EMS ₹44,257 cr; 32–33 mn smartphones; camera (Q-Tech) & display (HKC) modules
Amber Enterprises NSE/BSE: AMBER — entering handsets via Oppo/OnePlus/realme JV (8 mn units yr-1, to 15–16 mn)
PG Electroplast NSE/BSE: PGEL — mobile mfg (Pune/Greater Noida, ~5 mn units/yr) within an EMS/ODM platform (FY26 revenue ₹5,288 cr)
Kaynes Technology NSE/BSE: KAYNES · Syrma SGS SYRMA · BPL · Centum CENTUM — PCB, flex, coils, passives, filters under ECMS
Uno Minda UNOMINDA (display module) · Motherson MOTHERSON & Hindalco HINDALCO (enclosures) · Permanent Magnets & PCBL (magnets, cell materials)

nodes.name: Shell, Heads & Tubesheet
nodes.fn: The pressure-boundary steel: cylindrical shell, hemispherical/elliptical heads, the thick forged tubesheet and the transition cone. Low-alloy Mn-Mo-Ni steel (SA-508 / SA-533) formed and welded to Class-1 nuclear code.

companies.m: Shell, heads and tubesheet fabrication and assembly at Hazira; the dominant Indian SG fabricator with >50% SG & end-shield share
SG shells and assemblies at Trichy; nuclear SGs supplied since 1976
Special stainless-steel plates (e.g. 304L NAG) and alloy mill forms for the DAE
Heat-exchanger / pressure-vessel vendor on the NPCIL procurement list

nodes.name: Heavy Forgings & Special Steels
nodes.fn: Nuclear-grade forging ingots and finished forgings — SG shells, cones, tubesheets and dished ends. Ingots up to 300 MT, finished forgings up to 120 MT. The single domestic heavy-forging shop is LTSSHF at Hazira.

companies.m: L&T Special Steels & Heavy Forgings (LTSSHF) — the only nuclear-grade heavy-forging facility in South-East Asia; SG shell/cone/tubesheet/dished-end forgings for 700 MWe PHWRs. Now a 100% L&T subsidiary (NPCIL exited its 26% in Feb-2025); Crisil upgraded it to AA-/Stable in May-2026; order book ₹1,107 cr (Mar-2026).
companies.ev: LTSSHF / CRISIL rating rationale May-2026; LTSSHF AR FY26

companies.m: Special steels, superalloys and titanium mill forms; the only titanium-alloy maker in India

nodes.name: Nozzles, Manways & Safe-Ends
nodes.fn: Primary inlet/outlet nozzles, steam-outlet and feedwater nozzles, manways and safe-ends — the penetration points welded to the shell and clad with a corrosion-resistant overlay.

companies.m: Nozzle and safe-end fabrication as part of the SG assembly
Nozzles and headers for nuclear primary-side equipment

nodes.name: Inconel 690 Tube Bundle
nodes.fn: The heat-transfer surface — ~11,000 seamless U-bend tubes of thermally-treated Alloy 690 (UNS N06690), ~130 km of tube per SG. The highest-value, most qualification-gated material in the vessel. Note: PWR/VVER SGs use Alloy 690; India’s PHWR SGs use Alloy-800, whose tubing IS made domestically.
nodes.gap: NO COVERAGE IN SELECTED UNIVERSE for the 690 (PWR/VVER) grade — the qualified seamless Alloy-690 U-bend tube is held by Sandvik (Sweden), Valinox / Vallourec (France) and Sumitomo (Japan). sections.title: Digest — at a glance
sections.note: short summary; full detail below

items: The PWR/VVER/PHWR steam generator — the shell-and-tube heat exchanger that turns reactor heat into steam. A VVER SG weighs ~340 t, carries ~130 km of tube (~11,000 U-bend tubes) and takes ~2 years to fabricate melt-to-despatch; a unit uses four SGs.
India’s SG fleet is dominated by the indigenous 700 MWe PHWR, whose SGs are built domestically (L&T, BHEL, Godrej, Walchandnagar); PWR/VVER SGs (Kudankulam) are imported from Russia.
Spine: nuclear-grade forging (shell, cone, tubesheet, dished ends) → tube-bundle assembly → ~11,000 tube-to-tubesheet welds → internals (separators/dryers) → full NDT → hydro / helium-leak test.
Tube: Alloy-800 (PHWR) is made domestically by NFC/MIDHANI; Inconel 690 (PWR/VVER) is imported.
Key machinery (imported): ultra-heavy forging press, welding automation, heat-treatment furnaces, heavy CNC.
Inconel 690 tube (PWR/VVER only) — Sandvik / Valinox / Sumitomo; no Indian maker. Resilience: years. The PHWR Alloy-800 tube is now domestic (NFC, 81-day cycle).
One nuclear-grade heavy-forging shop (LTSSHF, Hazira) for every SG shell and tubesheet. Resilience: years.
Fabrication machinery (heavy press, welding automation, furnaces, heavy CNC) is imported. Resilience: months–years.
Certification-gated vendor base (ASME N/NPT, AERB Class-1) and the ~2-year fabrication cycle.
Skilled trades (Class-1 welders, TTS-weld operators, NDT inspectors) bind tighter than materials.
SG fabrication — L&T (dominant; >50% SG / end-shield share), BHEL, Walchandnagar, ISGEC; Godrej (unlisted) is a newer SG fabricator.
Heavy forgings — LTSSHF (100% L&T) is the sole domestic source; order book ₹1,107 cr (Mar-2026).
L&T guides 3–3.5× nuclear-revenue growth over five years and a 55–60% share of the nuclear value chain.
Pools that leak to imports: the Inconel 690 tube (PWR/VVER), fabrication machinery, nuclear-grade Inconel weld overlay and primary-side SG instrumentation.
Aftermarket (eddy-current inspection, tube plugging / sleeving, full SG replacement) is a recurring 60-year pool.
India nuclear-plant-equipment market (scope: all nuclear equipment, India): ~$2.8 bn (2026) → ~$7.4 bn (2035) , headline CAGR 11.4% [REPORTED-T3, MarkWide]. Value (nominal); volume [UNAVAILABLE].
Global nuclear-SG market: [CONFLICTING DATA] — ~$1.6 bn–$5.7 bn (2025), 5-yr CAGRs from ~1.5% (Mordor) to ~6.9% (MarketResearchReports); the spread is scope-driven (equipment-only vs design+install).
CEA capex breakup: the SG is ~7% of a ~₹19 lakh cr / 100 GW build (~₹1.4 lakh cr), within a 36% reactor island.
Growth is new-build-led (fleet of 10, then a second fleet of 10, plus SMRs), not replacement-led as in the West.

SHANTI Act 2025 rules still not notified : the DAE/AERB draft SHANTI Rules and Regulations went to public consultation with comments closing 04-Sep-2026 ; final notification remains the gate to private orders. [LIVE]
AEC cleared a nuclear FDI policy (Apr-2026); AEC chairman guided ₹7.5 lakh cr private investment and a 30 GW private share by 2047 (11-Oct-2026). [LIVE]
ASHVINI ₹28,000 cr Mahi Banswara NIMEP tender — technical bids opened 06-Oct-2026. [LIVE]
RAPP-8 initial fuel loading began 19-Sep-2026; Kaiga-5&6 and GHAVP-3&4 SG deliveries in progress. [LIVE]
Inconel 690 seamless U-bend tube (PWR/VVER) has no Indian producer — nearest listed proxy MIDHANI (Superni 690 mill forms, not the qualified tube).
Nuclear SG fabrication machinery has no qualified NSE/BSE maker; the forging shop sits inside L&T (LTSSHF).
Owner (NPCIL) and designer (BARC) are unlisted.

sections.title: Bottlenecks — Risk & Opportunity
sections.note: dual-readable: every risk is a substitution play

risk.title: Inconel 690 tube imported — for PWR/VVER only
risk.text: India’s PHWR SGs use Alloy-800 U-bend tube, which is now made domestically by NFC (Hyderabad) with MIDHANI billet — NFC shipped its 12th set in a record 81-day cycle (Sep-2026). The Inconel 690 (UNS N06690) tube used by PWR/VVER SGs is still made only by Sandvik (Sweden), Valinox/Vallourec (France) and Sumitomo (Japan); India has no qualified 690 maker. Resilience: years (certification-gated) — and it now applies only to the LWR/VVER portion of the fleet.

opp.title: 690 tube qualification + Alloy-800 scale-up
opp.text: MIDHANI casts Superni 690 mill forms; a qualified seamless 690 line would close the residual PWR/VVER import gap, while NFC/MIDHANI scale the already-qualified Alloy-800 PHWR line (from 180 to 81 days).

risk.title: One heavy-forging shop
risk.text: LTSSHF (Hazira) is the only nuclear-grade heavy-forging facility in South-East Asia — a single point of failure for every SG shell, cone, tubesheet and dished end. Its financial profile has strengthened: Crisil upgraded it to AA-/Stable in May-2026 (from A+/Stable; earlier a ‘D’ on the NPCIL loan), and it is now a 100% L&T subsidiary after NPCIL exited its 26% in Feb-2025. Resilience: years.

opp.title: Forging scale-up / second shop
opp.text: Fleet-mode demand (10×700 MWe plus SMRs) and a ₹1,107 cr order book (Mar-2026) justify a second qualified forging source alongside LTSSHF.

risk.title: Certification-gated vendor base
risk.text: Class-1 nuclear qualification (ASME N/NPT, AERB) takes years; only a handful of fabricators are qualified. Resilience: years.

opp.title: N-stamp incumbents scale
opp.text: L&T (first Indian ASME N-stamp, US-NRC-audited) and BHEL capture a widening order book as fleet mode ramps.

risk.title: Fabrication machinery imported
risk.text: The ultra-heavy forging press, welding automation, heat-treatment furnaces and heavy CNC are foreign-built. Resilience: months–years.

opp.title: Machine-tool localisation
opp.text: A domestic heavy-machine-tool and welding-automation base would de-risk the entire heavy-fabrication chain.

risk.title: Skilled trades
risk.text: Class-1 welders, tube-to-tubesheet welding operators, NDT inspectors and QA engineers bind tighter than materials and cannot be bought quickly.

opp.title: Training pipelines
opp.text: BHEL / L&T / Walchandnagar qualification pipelines are a durable moat for incumbents.

risk.title: Owner & design are unlisted
risk.text: Design (BARC), ownership (NPCIL) and the fuel cycle sit inside DAE entities with no NSE/BSE listing. Resilience: structural.

opp.title: SHANTI Act 2025
opp.text: Graded liability, a statutory AERB and private participation open SPV models for the next tranche of reactors. Deepest hidden dependency: the SG is India’s most mature nuclear-equipment node — L&T, BHEL, Godrej and Walchandnagar build it, the heavy forgings (LTSSHF) and the PHWR Alloy-800 tube (NFC/MIDHANI) are now domestic, and L&T alone targets 3–3.5× nuclear-revenue growth over five years. What still leaks: the Inconel 690 tube for PWR/VVER SGs, the fabrication machinery (heavy presses, welding automation, furnaces, heavy CNC) and the owner/designer (NPCIL/BARC, unlisted). The fabrication is investable; the 690 material, the machinery and the IP are not.

sections.title: Bottlenecks — Risk & Opportunity
sections.note: dual-readable: every risk is a substitution play

risk.title: Preform & bare fibre
risk.text: ~65–75% of preform is imported (China, Japan); domestic capacity meets only ~25–35% of demand, and preform captures ~60–70% of the value-chain profit pool. The expansion cycle is 18–24 months. [REPORTED]

opp.title: Domestic preform integration
opp.text: STL is fully integrated (₹3,000 cr capex FY27-29); Finolex has commissioned captive preform (100→200 MT); HFCL is building 600 MT/yr by Oct-2028 (₹1,250 cr; total planned ~₹1,800 cr). [REPORTED]

risk.title: Strength members & FRP/aramid
risk.text: Aramid yarn has no Indian maker (Teijin/DuPont); FRP capacity is concentrated and was named among cost-pressure inputs in BharatNet Phase-III. HDPE rose ₹90→₹175/kg; jelly ₹135→₹250. [REPORTED]

opp.title: Backward integration
opp.text: Aksh runs the world’s largest single FRP-rod facility (~2 mn km/yr); HFCL (Hosur, via HTL) and Polycab (Halol) make FRP/ARP rods and IGFR yarns in-house. [REPORTED]

risk.title: Fibre price spike & BharatNet fixed-price squeeze
risk.text: Spot fibre is 2.8–5× 2025 levels; the CRUofpi index ran 78.6 (Mar-2024) → 263.0 (Mar-2026), the sharpest rise since 2017. Under fixed-price 10-year BharatNet contracts, STL and Polycab invoked force majeure as cable prices nearly doubled. [REPORTED]

opp.title: Multi-year volume certainty
opp.text: ₹65,000 cr programme across 16 packages; HFCL won ₹2,666 cr from RVNL (UP-West, Oct-2026), on top of ₹8,100 cr of BharatNet-3 wins; Polycab ₹6,447 cr, STL+Dilip Buildcon ₹2,631 cr, ITI ₹6,900 cr. [REPORTED]

risk.title: Chinese overcapacity & dumping
risk.text: China’s fibre capacity (~500 mn km) dwarfs its demand and export pricing creates structural pressure; sub-standard fibre has entered as raw material. India’s ADD on SMOF covers only finished fibre, not preform. [REPORTED]

opp.title: Tariff & localisation tailwind
opp.text: India’s ADD on SMOF (CN/KR/ID) runs to Aug-2028; domestic-preference in BharatNet/5G procurement and a proposed “Trusted Fibre” policy favour Indian makers. [REPORTED]

risk.title: Machinery & test equipment
risk.text: Cabling / SZ-stranding lines and OTDR / PMD / CD test gear are imported (Austria, USA, Belgium, Switzerland, Japan) with no Indian pure-play. [INFERENCE]

opp.title: Capacity-expansion pull
opp.text: The ₹1,800 cr+ industry capex wave (HFCL, STL, Finolex, VTL) is a direct demand signal for upstream machinery localisation; SIMCO and Machine & Controls build some lines in India. [INFERENCE]

risk.title: AI data-centre demand skew
risk.text: Data centres are ~18–20% of world fibre demand in 2026, heading to 30–35% in 2027; domestic telco capex stays lumpy and ARPU-sensitive. [REPORTED]

opp.title: High-fibre-count premium
opp.text: IBR / ribbon cables command premium margins — HFCL’s 3456-fibre micro-duct IBR (capacity 1.73 → 19.01 mn fkm) and STL’s 864-fibre ribbon target this segment; HFCL’s OFC+DCI order book is ₹18,500 cr, ~70% hyperscalers. [REPORTED] Deepest hidden import dependency: the glass preform — the semiconductor-grade glass rod from which every fibre is drawn — plus the germanium tetrachloride (GeCl₄) and helium that go into it. Even with HFCL and Finolex building preform lines, India remains a net importer of preform, and it is the one input whose expansion cannot be dialled up to meet a demand spike.

sections.title: Bottlenecks — Risk & Opportunity
sections.note: dual-readable: every risk is a substitution play

risk.title: Preform — the upstream choke point
risk.text: ~65–75% of preform is imported (China, Japan); domestic capacity meets only ~25–35% of demand, and ~60–70% of the value-chain profit pool sits in this one step.

opp.title: India’s second & third integrated players
opp.text: STL is already integrated (₹3,000 cr capex FY27-29); Finolex has commissioned captive preform (100→200 MT) and HFCL is building 600 MT/yr by Oct-2028 (₹1,800 cr total capex).

risk.title: Fibre price spike & global deficit
risk.text: Spot fibre prices are 2.8–5× their 2025 levels; the CRUofpi index ran 78.6 (Mar-2024) to 263.0 (Mar-2026), the sharpest rise since 2017. A ~180 mn fkm global shortfall in 2026 is expected to persist to ~2028.

opp.title: Integrated players win the queue
opp.text: In a glass shortage, whoever makes their own preform fills orders others cannot; STL’s utilisation is ~70% and HFCL’s fibre lines are near ~100%, with order books booked into 2027.

risk.title: Germanium & helium — two input shocks at once
risk.text: China holds >90% of germanium refining and has run it under export licence since Aug-2023 (ban to the US/Japan suspended only to Nov-2026); it also imposed a helium export ban in Jul-2026 after Qatar/Hormuz disruption. India imports almost all its helium.

opp.title: Diversify & recycle
opp.text: Germany, the US and Kazakhstan have smaller germanium capacity; new ex-China projects target +95 t by 2030. Fibre-scrap recycling and India’s Critical Minerals Mission are the medium-term substitutes; helium recovery/recycling is the near-term lever.

risk.title: Draw-tower equipment
risk.text: Towers, induction furnaces and winders are imported (Rosendahl Nextrom, SG Controls); there is no Indian listed equipment pure-play and new preform/draw capacity carries an 18–24-month lead time.

opp.title: Local equipment build
opp.text: SIMCO and Machine & Controls build towers, colouring lines and FRP lines in India — an under-owned, pick-and-shovel play on the fibre capex cycle.

risk.title: Precision ceramic ferrules
risk.text: Sub-micron zirconia ferrules are dominated by China and Japan; India largely grinds imported blanks, so the connector end of the chain stays import-dependent.

opp.title: Make-in-India ferrules
opp.text: Domestic firms are moving from grinding to full powder→sinter→grind manufacturing — a small but strategically placed import-substitution niche.

risk.title: Capacity vs consumption
risk.text: ~100 mn fkm of capacity against ~46 mn fkm of domestic use makes India export-dependent and exposed to the global fibre price cycle and to dumping — hence the anti-dumping duty regime.

opp.title: Global AI demand cycle
opp.text: AI data centres, 5G densification and BharatNet 2.0 have fibre makers sold out; India’s fibre exports surged +158% YoY to $483 mn in Apr–Aug FY27, with the US taking more than half.

risk.title: Consumables & specialty grades
risk.text: UV coating resin, colouring inks and process gases are imported; G.657 and specialty grades are harder to draw, and consistency and yield separate winners from the pack.

opp.title: ADD protection & premium mix
opp.text: The ADD (Aug-2023) covers bend-insensitive G.657, and the data-centre mix (G.657.A2, hollow-core, high-count) carries a steep price premium — a tailwind for domestic drawers. Deepest hidden import dependency: the preform glass itself — India draws world-scale fibre from imported glass, and the germanium tetrachloride (GeCl₄) and helium that go into it. A step that generates over 60% of the value-chain profit pool is controlled by fewer than ten firms worldwide, and only one Indian company is fully backward-integrated into it.

digest.h: Snapshot Optical fibre preform — the ultra-pure silica glass rod drawn into fibre. It is the deepest upstream layer of the optical-fibre chain and holds roughly 60–70% of a finished cable's value. Scope: India, NSE/BSE. Re-analysed 2026-10-21 (delta pass over the 2026-10-08 entry). Process & equipment
items: Deposition (MCVD/OVD/VAD/PCVD) builds doped silica layers into a rod; glassworking, lathes and draw towers are the key (largely imported) equipment.
Feedstock is high-purity silica/SiCl₄ with GeCl₄ core doping; cleanroom-grade glassworking is required.
STL now runs a green-hydrogen preform furnace at Aurangabad (Project Photon Leap, >200 TPA H₂), cutting plant emissions ~30%.
Preform import dependence (~65–75%); resilience: years, shortening as STL/HFCL/Finolex build.
Germanium / GeCl₄ export controls — China >60% of supply (>90% of refining); licence regime since Aug-2023; the ban to the US/Japan is suspended only through Nov-2026. Prices ~9–10× 2023.
Preform price spike: ~$55/kg (mid-2025) → $120–140/kg (mid-2026) → HFCL cites ~$300/kg in Q2 FY27; the global supply deficit is expected to persist to ~2028.
Deposition technology/equipment concentrated in 6–10 firms; no listed Indian exposure.
Preform captures ~60–70% of the chain's value — largely leaked to imports, now being pulled home (STL ₹3,000 cr, HFCL ₹1,800 cr, Finolex).
STL captures it domestically as the only integrated player; HFCL becomes the second by Oct-2028, Finolex the third.
Import-substitution prize ~$300–400 mn/yr; India fibre exports surged +158% YoY to $483 mn in Apr–Aug FY27.
Deposition equipment is a hidden second import layer.

India preform market (scope: preform supplied to domestic drawers, landed cost): ~$320–380 mn (2026) → $850–1,050 mn (2035) , CAGR ~12–15% [REPORTED-T3, IndexBox, May-2026]. Value (nominal); volume 55–65 mn fkm-equiv → 140–170 mn fkm.
Last-year: +14–16% YoY (2026 vs 2025) [REPORTED-T3]. 3-year horizon not separately reported [UNAVAILABLE].
Exports: India optical-fibre/bundle/cable exports +158% YoY to $483 mn in Apr–Aug FY27 (US >half at $266.7 mn) [REPORTED-T1, Ministry of Commerce, Oct-2026].

[CONFLICTING DATA] on other scopes: OFC & accessories $4.8 bn 2026→$12.99 bn 2035 (11.7%, MarkWide); India fibre-optics $323.9 mn 2024→$866.1 mn 2029 (21.7%, MarketsandMarkets); India OFC ~$550 mn 2025→~$1 bn 2031 (~11%, tele.net). Growth is demand-led (BharatNet Phase III, data centres, FTTH), with price/mix positive as data-centre fibre (~$25–27/km) runs above telco D-fibre (~$15/km).

Germanium export ban to the US is suspended only to 27-Nov-2026 (MOFCOM 2025 No. 72); the 28-Sep-2026 Kuala Lumpur extension to 10-Jan-2027 does not name that announcement — unconfirmed. The Chinese licence regime persists. [LIVE]
India's ADD on SMOF to Aug-2028 ; China extended its own ADD on Indian SMOF for 5 yrs to Aug-2031 . [CYCLICAL]
HFCL preform facility commissioning Oct-2028 ; Finolex preform Phase-2; STL ₹3,000 cr capex FY27-29 (capacity +50%). [CYCLICAL]

sections.title: Digest — at a glance
sections.note: short summary; full detail below

items.h: Snapshot A four-subsystem apparatus sector — ophthalmic/optical devices, diagnostic imaging, surgical instruments and patient-care/monitoring/implants. India localises assembly, disposables and lenses well but imports the core imaging hardware, advanced optics and medical-grade materials . ~65% of demand is imported; ~800 manufacturers, ~90% MSME. Process & equipment
items: Assembly spine: precision machining, injection moulding, cleanroom build, sterilisation (EtO/steam/gamma), calibration.
Lens optics: casting/polymerisation, surfacing, spin & PVD coating, edging.
Imaging: gantry/detector/tube assembly, magnet winding & cryogenics, transducer fabrication.
Hidden import: the machines that make the components — tube-winding, detector litho, precision optics.
X-ray tubes & flat-panel detectors — imported (US/DE/JP); Varex localising at AMTZ. Resilience: months–years.
Superconducting MRI magnets & liquid-helium cryogenics — thin domestic base.
Advanced optics & CMOS image sensors (endoscopy, ophthalmic) — imported.
Medical-grade polymers & specialty alloys (PEEK, silicone, L605 CoCr, nitinol) — imported.
Certification lead time (CDSCO/BIS/AERB) & skilled manpower — domestic constraints.
Disposables & infusion therapy — the deepest listed pool (Poly Medicure; also a large exporter).
Spectacle lenses & eyewear retail — GKB Ophthalmics (lens maker) and Lenskart (listed Nov-2025).
Interventional cardiology (stents) — Poly Medicure live; Sahajanand (pre-IPO) and Meril (private) lead volume.
Imaging & monitoring systems — mostly foreign-listed MNCs (GE, Siemens Healthineers, Philips) plus unlisted Indian OEMs.
Dialysis, orthopaedics and renal — Poly Medicure’s fastest-growing verticals.
Components & materials (tube, detector, magnet, optics) leak almost wholly to imports.
All Class C/D devices under CDSCO licensing from 1-Oct-2023; Class A/B from 1-Oct-2022.
PLI medical devices runs FY2023-24 to FY2026-27 (expiry within ~1 year).
Varex 2nd AMTZ line (CsI + glass tubes) commissioned Jul-2025; ramp still early.
Correction from the prior run: Sahajanand Medical Technologies IPO — RHP filed 9-Oct-2026; issue opens 15-Oct-2026 and closes 19-Oct-2026; tentative listing 23-Oct-2026 (was “listing pending”).
Opto Circuits under CIRP since Nov-2022 — distressed, not investable.
IOLs, ophthalmic diagnostics, endoscopy, ventilators, cath labs and robotic surgery have no listed Indian pure-play (private or foreign).
X-ray tubes/detectors, superconducting magnets and medical-grade materials have no NSE/BSE exposure at all.
