sections.title: Bottlenecks — Risk & Opportunity
sections.note: dual-readable: every risk is a substitution play

risk.title: X-ray tubes & flat-panel detectors
risk.text: Imported (USA ~55–66%, Germany, Japan); HHI concentration very high. Every Indian CT/DR/cath-lab OEM depends on them. Resilience: months–years.

opp.title: AMTZ imaging-hardware chain
opp.text: Varex (USA) is building India’s first CsI-coating and medical-glass-tube lines at AMTZ; local tube + detector assembly would move the whole imaging value chain onshore.

risk.title: Superconducting MRI magnets & cryogenics
risk.text: Liquid-helium-cooled magnets and superconducting wire were a pure import; MRI is the highest-value single device in the market.

opp.title: Domestic magnet production
opp.text: AMTZ superconducting-magnet and cryogenics lines let three OEMs build MRI in India, reportedly halving scanner cost (~₹6 cr → ~₹3 cr).

risk.title: Advanced optics & image sensors
risk.text: Endoscope optics, ophthalmic optics and CMOS image sensors are imported (Olympus, Karl Storz, Sony). India assembles but does not make the optics. Resilience: months–years.

opp.title: Indian optics challengers
opp.text: Forus Health and Remidio (fundus/retinal imaging) and Endo-Med (endoscopy) prove Indian optics design; local lens & sensor sourcing is the next step.

risk.title: Medical-grade materials
risk.text: PEEK, silicone, medical PVC/PC, L605 cobalt-chromium, nitinol and piezo ceramics are imported; a device is only as local as its material.

opp.title: Specialty compounding & alloys
opp.text: Domestic polymer compounding and CoCr/nitinol tube-making would unlock stents, implants and disposables upstream — a protected, high-margin niche.

risk.title: Certification lead time & skilled manpower
risk.text: CDSCO/BIS/AERB approvals and NABL-grade testing were a domestic bottleneck; biomedical engineers and regulatory-affairs talent are named binding constraints.

opp.title: Test infrastructure & skills
opp.text: AMTZ common test centres (EMC, biomaterial, gamma) and the IBSC skills programme shorten approval cycles — qualification-gated roles carry durable scarcity value. Deepest hidden import dependency: not the assembled scanner but the components and the machinery that make them — X-ray tube inserts, detector arrays, piezo transducer ceramics, superconducting wire, precision optics and the tube-winding / detector-fab / precision-polishing equipment behind them. India’s localisation so far stops at assembly, lenses and disposables.

sections.title: Value pools & cost waterfall
sections.note: where value is captured · and which pool leaks to imports

items: Upstream materials & specialty components (imaging tube/detector, superconducting magnets, advanced optics, medical-grade polymers) carry the highest value per unit — and are the least indigenous.
Disposables & infusion therapy hold the largest absolute listed pool; India is globally competitive and export-led.
Interventional cardiology (stents, balloons, catheters) carries proprietary margin; India has scale, mostly private.
OEM assembly of imaging & monitoring is scale-driven and thin-margin for unlisted Indian OEMs; the brand margin sits with MNCs.
Aftermarket (service, spares, probes, consumables) is the most resilient pool, riding the installed base of scanners, monitors and dialysis machines.
Poly Medicure — broadest listed device content (infusion, renal, cardiology, critical care, ortho); FY25 net sales ₹1,619.8 cr.
GKB Ophthalmics — the listed lens-making play (semi-finished & Rx lenses).
Lenskart Solutions — vertically integrated eyewear retail + in-house lens making; ₹6,653 cr FY25 revenue.
Hemant Surgical Industries — the listed turnkey & distribution play (OT / ICU / dialysis / imaging).
Small-cap set — KMS Medisurgi, Centenial Surgical Suture, Raaj Medisafe, Avience, Nureca, Tarsons, Fabtech.
X-ray tubes & flat-panel detectors (USA / Germany / Japan).
Superconducting magnets & cryogenics (liquid helium).
Advanced optics & CMOS image sensors (endoscopy, ophthalmic).
Medical-grade polymers & specialty alloys (PEEK, silicone, L605 CoCr, nitinol, piezo ceramics).
Capital equipment (tube-winding, detector-fab, precision optics, cleanroom / sterilisation plant).
Collectively the bulk of India’s ~65% import dependence.

India localises assembly, disposables and lenses well but imports the core imaging hardware, advanced optics and medical-grade materials . ~65% of demand is imported; ~800 manufacturers, ~90% MSME. Process & equipment
items: Assembly spine: precision machining, injection moulding, cleanroom build, sterilisation (EtO/steam/gamma), calibration.
Lens optics: casting/polymerisation, surfacing, spin & PVD coating, edging.
Imaging: gantry/detector/tube assembly, magnet winding & cryogenics, transducer fabrication.
Hidden import: the machines that make the components — tube-winding, detector litho, precision optics.
X-ray tubes & flat-panel detectors — imported (US/DE/JP); Varex localising at AMTZ. Resilience: months–years.
Superconducting MRI magnets & liquid-helium cryogenics — thin domestic base.
Advanced optics & CMOS image sensors (endoscopy, ophthalmic) — imported.
Medical-grade polymers & specialty alloys (PEEK, silicone, L605 CoCr, nitinol) — imported.
Certification lead time (CDSCO/BIS/AERB) & skilled manpower — domestic constraints.
Disposables & infusion therapy — the deepest listed pool (Poly Medicure; also a large exporter).
Spectacle lenses & eyewear retail — GKB Ophthalmics (lens maker) and Lenskart (listed Nov-2025).
Interventional cardiology (stents) — Poly Medicure live; Sahajanand (pre-IPO) and Meril (private) lead volume.
Imaging & monitoring systems — mostly foreign-listed MNCs (GE, Siemens Healthineers, Philips) plus unlisted Indian OEMs.
Dialysis, orthopaedics and renal — Poly Medicure’s fastest-growing verticals.
Components & materials (tube, detector, magnet, optics) leak almost wholly to imports.
All Class C/D devices under CDSCO licensing from 1-Oct-2023; Class A/B from 1-Oct-2022.
PLI medical devices runs FY2023-24 to FY2026-27 (expiry within ~1 year).
Varex 2nd AMTZ line (CsI + glass tubes) commissioned Jul-2025; ramp still early.
Correction from the prior run: Sahajanand Medical Technologies IPO — RHP filed 9-Oct-2026; issue opens 15-Oct-2026 and closes 19-Oct-2026; tentative listing 23-Oct-2026 (was “listing pending”).
Opto Circuits under CIRP since Nov-2022 — distressed, not investable.
IOLs, ophthalmic diagnostics, endoscopy, ventilators, cath labs and robotic surgery have no listed Indian pure-play (private or foreign).
X-ray tubes/detectors, superconducting magnets and medical-grade materials have no NSE/BSE exposure at all.

sections.title: Digest — at a glance
sections.note: A short summary. Structure and inputs live on the tree; process, value pools and watch items are summarised here.

items.h: Snapshot Optical transceivers & modules — the pluggable 100G/400G/800G/1.6T optics in every transport port, switch line-card and AI-cluster fabric. It is the fastest-growing and most import-dependent layer of the optical stack: India is a large and fast-growing demand market (AI data centres, 5G backhaul, DCI) but designs and fabs none of the two chips that matter — the PAM4 DSP and the laser die. Scope: India, NSE/BSE. Re-analysed 2026-10-24 (delta pass over the 2026-10-08 entry). Process & equipment
items: Optical engines are assembled from imported DSPs, laser dies and PICs; TO-can/OSA build, sub-micron active alignment, firmware, thermal packaging, burn-in and high-speed test are the key steps.
Key machinery: die/wire bonders, active-alignment stations, automated optical & electrical test (BERT, OSA, high-speed scopes) and thermal burn-in chambers — imported.
India’s first real module-assembly capacity is being built now: the Dixon–Gemtek JV (Oct-2026) and GX Quantum Photonics (Dec-2026).
Optical DSP / retimer ASICs (PAM4) — Broadcom/Marvell/Credo; no Indian design or fab. Resilience: YEARS.
Light sources EML/VCSEL/DFB — InP/GaAs laser-die fab absent in India; global InP-EML demand exceeds supply ~30% in 2026. Resilience: YEARS–STRUCTURAL.
Silicon-photonics PIC engines — imported; Indian design just starting (IIT-Madras PDK, Apr-2026). Resilience: YEARS.
High-speed 800G/1.6T test & qualification capacity is thin in India; lead times for 800G-class components ran 14–20 weeks.
Import duty ~44% on finished modules (HS 8517 62 90); SFP classification has been litigated.
Value sits in the DSPs, laser dies and PICs — all imported; the top-5 module vendors hold ~72% of global revenue and Chinese firms >70% of 800G+.
India’s listed value-add is module/assembly integration (new), fibre & cable, connectors and network systems.
The AI data-centre build (1.8 GW → 6 GW by 2029) is the domestic pull; DCI is the fastest-growing application.
Localisation path: assembly (Dixon–Gemtek, GX) → OSA/BOSA → PIC/DSP design.

India optical-transceiver market: USD 0.73 bn (2026) → 0.82 bn (2027) → 1.73 bn (2033) , ~13.25% CAGR (2027–33) [REPORTED-T3, MarkNtel]. A second scope puts India optical interconnect at $938.6 mn (2026) → $3,569 mn (2033) , 21% CAGR [REPORTED-T3, GrandView]. Value, nominal; the two scopes differ and are shown, not averaged.
Current-year global read: Ethernet optics $16.5 bn (2025) → $26 bn (2026) , +60% [REPORTED-T2, LightCounting]; ~$80 bn by 2031.
Volume: India data-centre capacity 1.8 GW (H1-2026) → ~6 GW (2029) [REPORTED-T2]; 800G-and-above rose from 19.5% of global module shipments (2024) to >60% (2026) [REPORTED-T3].
Growth is demand/adoption-led: module ASPs fall 12–18%/yr, so value growth is mix-led (800G/1.6T, SiPh, coherent) rather than pure price.
Dixon–Gemtek JV (60:40) to make SFP transceivers + BOSA in India; completion target 3-Feb-2027. [LIVE]
GX Quantum Photonics ₹500 cr SFP/TOSA/ROSA plant — production from Dec-2026; ECMS phase-1 ₹100 cr approved. [LIVE]

US FCC — final rule FCC 26-50 (adopted 22-Jul-2026, published 11-Sep, effective 13-Oct-2026 ) bars new authorisations for devices containing logic-bearing components from Covered-List firms; optical transceivers are not named and the large Chinese vendors stay off the list, though a separate new-model transceiver ban reported in Aug-2026 remains under consideration. Correction from the prior run: this was carried as “considering a ban” — the rule is now in force and narrower than feared. [REPORTED-T2]
India data-centre capacity on track for ~2 GW by end-2026 ; >$38 bn committed in H1-2026. [LIVE]
Aksh Optifibre under CIRP; NCLAT stayed the IRP’s further steps (30-Jun-2026). [LIVE]

No NSE/BSE pure-play across optical DSP, laser dies, photodetectors or PIC design. Nearest listed: Dixon (new module JV), Tejas/HFCL (systems & integration), STL (connectors), HFCL/STL/Birla/Aksh (fibre & cable). New module assembly is otherwise private (GX, CloudPhotonix, LightSpeed Photonics).

sections.title: Bottlenecks — Risk & Opportunity
sections.note: dual-readable: every risk is a substitution play

risk.title: Optical DSP & retimer ASICs
risk.text: No Indian design or fab of PAM4 DSPs; 400G/800G/1.6T engines rely on Broadcom, Marvell and Credo silicon. Export controls and allocation risk sit here, and the AI boom has driven record DSP backlogs.

opp.title: Fabless DSP design
opp.text: Design-led PLI plus India’s chip-design talent base make a fabless optical-DSP play the highest-value localisation frontier — a design-in win at a hyperscaler qualifies the whole module.

risk.title: Light sources — EML / VCSEL / DFB
risk.text: InP/GaAs laser-die fabrication is absent in India; dies come from Coherent, Lumentum, Broadcom, Sumitomo. Global InP-EML demand exceeded supply by ~30% in 2026 and 800G-class component lead times ran 14–20 weeks.

opp.title: Compound-semiconductor seed
opp.text: India’s compound-semi / OSAT push could seed laser-die packaging and test even before wafer fab — the same play that built the LED-packaging base.

risk.title: Module integration was only final assembly
risk.text: Until Oct-2026 India’s value-add was integrating imported engines into housings — thin margin, low IP — with no listed module pure-play.

opp.title: Integration → design — the base is now being built
opp.text: Dixon–Gemtek (60:40 JV, SFP + BOSA, target Feb-2027) and GX Quantum Photonics (₹500 cr, SFP/TOSA/ROSA, from Dec-2026) start the assembly base; HFCL’s data-centre connectivity plant (₹215 cr, 2.7 lakh assemblies/yr, by Sep-2027) deepens it.

risk.title: High-speed test & qualification
risk.text: 800G, 1.6T and coherent test capacity is limited in India; buyers rely on overseas labs, stretching qualification cycles and time-to-deploy.

opp.title: Local test & burn-in as a service
opp.text: Qualification-gated labs carry durable scarcity value and are a cheaper entry point than fab; IIT-Madras’ PPIC test engine (Apr-2026) is a first domestic step.

risk.title: Import dependence, concentration & duty
risk.text: 85–90% of 100G+ demand by value is imported, China-dominant (7 of the top-10 vendors; >70% of 800G+); finished modules carry ~44% total duty incidence and SFP classification has been litigated.

opp.title: Import substitution under ECMS/PLI
opp.text: High-count cable, connectors and preform lines (HFCL ₹1,800 cr; STL ₹3,000 cr) plus the new SFP/BOSA assembly plants target the substitutable layers, with the US FCC’s China-module review as a re-shoring tailwind. Deepest hidden import dependency: the InP/GaAs laser dies and the PAM4 DSP silicon inside every 400G/800G/1.6T module — the two chips India neither designs nor fabs today. Module assembly is now genuinely localising (Dixon–Gemtek, GX); these two layers cannot, in the current window, and they carry the highest value per module.

sections.title: Value pools & cost waterfall
sections.note: where value is captured · and which pool leaks to imports

items: Value sits in the DSPs, laser dies and PICs — all imported; the top-5 module vendors hold ~72% of global module revenue.
India’s value-add is final assembly (now being built), plus fibre/cable, connectors and systems.
The AI data-centre wave (1.8 GW → 6 GW by 2029) is the big domestic opportunity; DCI is the fastest-growing application.
Localisation path: module integration → OSA/BOSA → PIC/DSP design.
Dixon Technologies NSE/BSE: DIXON — [REPORTED] 60:40 JV with Taiwan’s Gemtek to make SFP transceivers + BOSA in India; completion target 3-Feb-2027; the first listed Indian module-assembly exposure.
Tejas Networks NSE/BSE: TEJASNET — [REPORTED] Designs & manufactures optical transport and packet-optical systems; 400G/800G coherent DWDM; hyperscaler/DCI and BSNL 4G; design-led PLI approved.
HFCL NSE/BSE: HFCL — [REPORTED] Data-centre optical connectivity (MMC/SNMT assemblies, ₹215 cr plant by Sep-2027); fibre/cable; ₹29,000 cr order book.
Sterlite Technologies (STL) NSE/BSE: STLTECH — [REPORTED] Optical connectivity & interconnect (connectors, patch cords, MPO, pre-terminated systems); $1.11 bn hyperscaler optical deal.
Polycab India NSE/BSE: POLYCAB — [INFERENCE] Wires & cables major with optical-fibre cable capacity; data-centre fibre a growing but smaller part of the mix.
Birla Cable NSE/BSE: BIRLACABLE · Aksh Optifibre NSE/BSE: AKSHOPTFBR — [REPORTED] Optical-fibre cable makers; Aksh is under CIRP.
ITI Limited NSE/BSE: ITI · Bharat Electronics NSE/BSE: BEL — [INFERENCE] Networking/transmission and optronics, minor segments of larger businesses.
No listed pure-play across DSP, laser dies, photodetectors, PIC design and high-speed test — nearest: Dixon (module JV), Tejas/HFCL (systems), STL (connectors).
Bottleneck nodes: Optical DSP & Retimer ASICs (PAM4), Light Sources (EML/VCSEL/DFB), Silicon Photonics / PIC Engines, Coherent Optics (400ZR/800ZR DCO), Test, Burn-in & Qualification.
The assembly margin stays domestic but is competitive and duty-exposed.

sections.title: Digest — at a glance
sections.note: short summary; full detail below

items.h: Snapshot India is the world's sixth-largest chemicals producer and a fast-growing petrochemical market, yet runs one of the deepest import dependencies of any manufacturing line — ~45% of petrochemical intermediates are imported. Value sits at the integrated upstream and in proprietary specialty chemistry; the thin middle (solvents, commodity intermediates) leaks value to imports. Process & equipment
items: A process industry : feedstock (naphtha/gas/salt) → cracker/reformer/chlor-alkali → intermediates → grades; specialty/fine is batch.
Cracker and reformer technology is licensed (Linde, Lummus, KBR, Technip); compressors from Siemens Energy/MAN — all imported.
Core machinery — reactors, distillation trains, extruders, cold boxes — largely imported; Indian EPC (L&T, Thermax, Praj) supplies the shell.
Ethylene/propylene shortfall gates all downstream polymer capacity (years).
Methanol, acetic acid, acetone, MEK imported — Gulf/China-concentrated (months–years).
EDC/VCM for PVC and fluorspar→HF for fluorochemicals (years).
Chinese dumping in PVC and bulk chemicals — live trade-remedy window.
Catalysts (reforming, Ziegler-Natta) almost fully imported; process-chemistry skills scarce.
Integrated upstream (RIL, IOCL, GAIL, OPaL) captures the feedstock-to-polymer spread — capital-heavy and cyclical.
Specialty & fine chemistry is the high-margin, export-led pool and the clearest China+1 winner (SRF, Navin, Vinati, Aarti, Deepak Nitrite).
Intermediates (phenol/acetone/IPA) are import-substituting and re-rate as domestic capacity lands (Deepak Nitrite).
Polymers are commodity and ADD-protected; PVC is the most import-exposed.
Solvents are thin-margin and import-led — the largest value leak.
Circularity (solvent recovery, recyclates) is an emerging, policy-driven pool.

Correction from the prior run: the suspension-PVC anti-dumping duty was not notified by the MoF; the government instead imposed a Minimum Import Price of US$0.766/kg on S-PVC for six months from 24-Jul-2026, and a separate CVD probe on PVC suspension resins from China was initiated 26-Feb-2026. [LIVE]

PVC follow-through: DGTR widened its countervailing-duty probe on suspension-PVC from China to 13 producer/exporter groups on 06-Oct-2026, withdrawing the earlier three-producer sampling; no duty has been imposed. The six-month MIP lapses ~23-Jan-2027 unless extended. [REPORTED-T2]
QCOs on several petrochemical products rescinded Nov-2025 (PVC Homopolymer QCO revoked 12-Nov-2025) — medium-term import risk. [LIVE]
BHAVYA Rasayan guidelines issued 3-Oct-2026; state proposals due 30-Nov-2026. [LIVE]
IOCL Paradip petchem complex (₹61,077 cr) commissioning 2029; ONGC ethane imports mid-2028.
No NSE/BSE player in styrene, acrylonitrile, MDI/TDI, acetonitrile/DMF or polymerisation/reforming catalysts.
OPaL and HMEL (cracker/polymer capacity) are unlisted; ONGC carries OPaL via subsidiary.

sections.title: Bottlenecks — Risk & Opportunity
sections.note: dual-readable: every risk is a substitution play

risk.title: Ethylene / propylene shortfall
risk.text: Olefins cannot be easily imported (hazardous gases); domestic cracker capacity lags demand and gates PVC and every downstream polymer. Resilience: years.

opp.title: Cracker build-out
opp.text: IOCL Paradip (₹61,077 cr, 2029), RIL and Adani capacity additions are the import-substitution play — with EPC and equipment localisation alongside.

risk.title: Methanol & acetic-acid imports
risk.text: Over 3 MMT of methanol and ~1.2 MMT of acetic acid are imported, Gulf/China-concentrated, because domestic gas is not cheap. Resilience: months–years.

opp.title: Coal-to-methanol & import substitution
opp.text: Coal-based methanol and new solvent capacity (Deepak Chem Tech phenol/acetone/IPA) target the leak; BHAVYA parks de-risk it.

risk.title: EDC / VCM for PVC
risk.text: Unreliable domestic EDC supply caps PVC expansion; India imports ~62% of its PVC resin. Resilience: years.

opp.title: Backward-integrated PVC
opp.text: RIL (doubling), Adani Mundra (1 MMTPA) and Chemplast capture the EDC/VCM chain — import dependency projected to fall toward ~30% by FY27.

risk.title: Fluorspar → HF
risk.text: China-concentrated feedstock feeds every fluorochemical and refrigerant; non-integrated users are exposed. Resilience: months–years.

opp.title: Integrated fluorochemistry
opp.text: Captive HF is the moat — SRF, Gujarat Fluorochemicals and Navin Fluorine already hold it and export from it.

risk.title: Chinese dumping — PVC & bulk chemicals
risk.text: Structural Chinese overcapacity redirected to India compresses domestic realisations and utilisation. Resilience: live.

opp.title: Trade-remedy window
opp.text: Anti-dumping duties (paste PVC in force; suspension PVC final findings Aug-2025) and BIS/QCO create a protected window for domestic capacity to ramp.

risk.title: Catalysts & process technology
risk.text: Reforming and polymerisation catalysts and cracker technology are almost fully imported; process-chemistry skills are scarce and cannot be bought quickly. Resilience: months–years.

opp.title: CDMO / CRDMO capability
opp.text: India's specialty CDMO base (SRF, PI, Navin, Anupam) is a durable, export-led moat and a catalyst-manufacturing white space. Deepest hidden dependency: the feedstock and the intermediate middle. Crude, naphtha and gas are imported, and the intermediate layer (methanol, acetic acid, acetone, EDC/VCM, styrene, acrylonitrile, catalysts) is either imported or thinly domestic — the capital to close it sits with a handful of diversified majors, while OPaL and HMEL are unlisted. India's investable edge is at the two ends: integrated upstream majors and export-led specialty chemistry.

sections.title: Digest — at a glance
sections.note: A short summary of the analysis. Structure and inputs are on the tree; process, value pools and watch items are summarised here.

items.h: Snapshot The physical transmission line itself — conductors, towers, insulators, hardware and OPGW, foundations, right-of-way and erection. The NEP 2022–32 outlay is ₹9.16 L cr; India added 12,139 ckm of lines in FY26 against a downward-revised 15,382 ckm target, and the FY27 ISTS target has risen to 25,146 ckm. Process & equipment
items: Stranded conductor drawing, tower fabrication and hot-dip galvanising, insulator firing, hardware fittings and OPGW, then stringing and erection EPC.
Tower capacity is concentrated: KEC ~4.8 lakh t/yr, Skipper 3.75–4.5 lakh t/yr, Transrail ~1.84 lakh t/yr.
Conductor-grade rod is domestic; OPGW fibre and composite long-rod insulators are import-linked.
Right-of-way / forest clearance — the binding constraint; new Oct-2026 market-rate compensation rules are the unlock.
Tower-fabrication capacity and certified stringing crews (skills).
OPGW fibre and composite / hollow insulators — imported; FY26 line-add fell ~21% short.
Line-materials integrators and turnkey EPC — KEC, KPIL, L&T, Transrail, Skipper.
Asset owners — PGCIL, Adani Energy Solutions, IndiGrid — earn a 35-yr TSA / TBCB annuity.
Premium conductors (HTLS / AL59) and aftermarket reconductoring (APAR, 272+ projects).
Power Ministry ISTS RoW compensation guidelines (7 Oct 2026).
MoEFCC revised forest RoW norms (10 Jun 2026) — HTLS cuts RoW up to 26%.
Four China-owned plants exempt to bid until 2028 (3 Jul 2026).
OPGW fibre, composite long-rod and hollow insulators, and compression hardware are largely unlisted; no listed pure-play insulator maker.

sections.title: Digest — at a glance
sections.note: short summary; full detail below

items: Bare PCBs and the components that populate them — the substrate layer beneath India's ~USD 115 bn electronics production.
India consumes ~₹35,000 cr (USD 4.2 bn) of PCBs but makes only ~10–15% locally; the rest is imported, mainly from China, Taiwan and Korea.
Bare-board line: CCL cut & inner-layer imaging → lamination → CNC drilling → PTH / plating → outer imaging & etching → solder mask → surface finish (ENIG / HASL) → electrical test.
Key machinery — CNC drillers, LDI / exposure, plating & etching lines, multilayer presses, AOI and flying-probe testers — is almost entirely imported (China, Taiwan, Italy, Germany, Japan).
Assembly (PCBA) is the domestic stronghold: SMT, reflow, AOI / X-ray and box-build.
Copper-clad laminate (CCL) & prepreg — 100% imported until 2026; India's first CCL plant (Wipro) starts 2026. Resilience: months→years.
Copper foil & glass fabric — imported; a thin domestic base. Resilience: years.
HDI / flex and ≥8-layer boards — imported; new ECMS capacity from FY27. Resilience: years.
PCB machinery & drills — imported; DGTR anti-dumping probe on Chinese PCB drills/routers (Sep 2025). Resilience: months.
Capacitors (MLCC / film) — ~20% domestic. Resilience: structural.
Value sits upstream of assembly: laminate (~30% of PCB BOM), copper foil, HDI / flex fabrication and capital equipment.
Domestic bare-PCB fabrication is small and thin-margin but protected by the 30% anti-dumping duty (Mar 2024).
The ECMS ₹40,000 cr outlay is redirecting value into laminate, HDI and equipment — Amber, Kaynes, Syrma and Wipro are the main vehicles.
Listed pure-play capture is thin: BPL and Fine-Line are small; most PCB capacity is unlisted.
EMS / PCBA (Dixon, Kaynes, Syrma) is where listed exposure actually sits, but the board itself still leaks to imports.
India PCB demand ~₹35,000 cr FY25; ELCINA projects ~USD 14 bn by FY30 [REPORTED-T2].
Value CAGR ~15% (2025–2034) [CALCULATED] from IMARC sizes; volume CAGR [UNAVAILABLE].
Domestic bare-PCB output to rise from ~13% of demand (FY24) to ~31% (FY29) — Avendus [REPORTED-T2].
[CONFLICTING DATA]: imported share cited at 88% (ELCINA), ~90% (Ind-Ra), 85–90% (Jefferies) vs “45% met domestically” (Vaishnaw, Aug 2026) — scopes differ.
ECMS 5th tranche, 17-Aug-2026: 106 projects approved, outlay raised to ₹40,000 cr. [LIVE]
Amber–Korea Circuit JV (₹3,250 cr) at YEIDA for HDI / flex + substrates; Kaynes Chennai PCB line due to start ~Sep 2026.
30% anti-dumping duty on bare PCB (≤6-layer) runs to Mar 2029; ADD probe on PCB drills/routers open. [LIVE]
Customs: BCD on populated PCBA cut 20%→15% (Budget 2025); bare PCB BCD 0% plus the anti-dumping duty.
HDI, flex, CCL, copper foil, glass fabric and PCB-equipment nodes have no NSE/BSE pure-play — capacity is unlisted or foreign-owned.
Only small listed bare-PCB names (BPL, Fine-Line) and passives (Gujarat Poly, Shivalik) exist in the selected universe.

sections.title: Bottlenecks — Risk & Opportunity
sections.note: dual-readable: every risk is a substitution play

risk.title: Copper-clad laminate (CCL) & prepreg
risk.text: 100% imported until 2026; CCL is ~30% of a PCB's bill of materials and the single largest upstream gap. Resilience: months→years.

opp.title: First domestic CCL plants
opp.text: Wipro Electronic Materials ₹500 cr (Karnataka, 2026, 6 mn sheets/yr); Amber CCL Mysuru (₹800 cr); MeitY reports 80% laminate self-sufficiency by Aug 2026.

risk.title: HDI / flex & ≥8-layer boards
risk.text: Imported; the ≥8-layer and mobile boards are exempt from the anti-dumping duty, so high-value boards face no protection. Resilience: years.

opp.title: ECMS HDI / flex build-out
opp.text: Kaynes ₹4,995 cr Thoothukudi (74-layer / HDI / flex); Amber Ascent ₹991 cr Hosur + Ascent-K JV ₹3,215 cr (YEIDA); Syrma–Shinhyup JV.

risk.title: PCB machinery & drills
risk.text: CNC drillers, imaging, plating lines and presses are almost fully imported from China / Taiwan / Europe; a single delayed line gates a plant's ramp. Resilience: months.

opp.title: Capital-goods ECMS tier
opp.text: Jyoti CNC and Ind-Sphinx won ECMS capital-goods approvals (Aug 2026); DGTR opened an anti-dumping probe on Chinese PCB drills / routers (Sep 2025).

risk.title: Passive components
risk.text: Capacitors are only ~20% domestic and connectors ~75%; MLCC and film capacitors remain foreign-concentrated. Resilience: structural.

opp.title: Passive / electro-mech ECMS round
opp.text: ECMS now covers capacitors, connectors, relays, speakers and metallised film (SRF); listed proxies are Gujarat Poly (MLCC) and Shivalik Bimetal (shunt resistors). Deepest hidden import dependency: the substrate beneath the substrate — electro-deposited copper foil and woven glass fabric, the two inputs to the copper-clad laminate. India has no PCB-grade ED-foil line and only two (foreign-owned) glass-fibre makers, so even a "localised" CCL plant imports its own feedstock.

sections.title: Digest
sections.note: short summary

items.h: Snapshot India's bulk-drug / API complex — the upstream active-ingredient layer that feeds the world's largest generic-formulation industry. A hybrid process industry : fermentation routes (antibiotics, vitamins) plus multi-step chemical-synthesis routes (paracetamol, statins, ARVs). India is the world's 3rd-largest pharma producer by volume with ~500 API makers (≈8% of the global API industry), yet still imports 30–35% of its API requirement — China supplies ~74% of those imports. Process & equipment
items: Fermentation: large-scale bioreactors (350 kL class), sterilisation, then solvent extraction, crystallisation and drying; needs cheap glucose, steady power and very large water volumes (the Pen G plant draws ~10 mn L/day).
Chemical synthesis: multi-step reactors, hydrogenation, distillation, crystallisation, milling and drying.
Both routes lean on solvent recovery, effluent treatment (ETP/ZLD) and cGMP analytical QC.
China KSM / intermediate dependence — ~74% of API imports; STRUCTURAL at the material layer.
Fermentation economics — Chinese APIs run 35–40% cheaper; viability is subsidy-set, MONTHS–YEARS.
Solvents & feedstock (propylene, methanol, ammonia) — shock-exposed, MONTHS.
Fermentation equipment & process know-how — largely foreign-sourced, YEARS.
Schedule M / GMP compliance at MSME units — MONTHS, now deadline-bound.
Value is migrating upstream (KSMs, intermediates, fermentation) and downstream (CRDMO, HPAPI, complex APIs); the middle — commodity APIs — is thin-margin and China price-set.
CRDMO is the premium pool (Divi's, Neuland, Laurus, Syngene) — but India's CRDMO is only $3–3.5 bn of a $145 bn global market.
Fermentation re-entry (Pen G, clavulanic acid) is real but subsidy-dependent — PLI incentive plus a minimum import price, not yet cost-competitive on its own.
The largest localisation prize sits in KSMs, advanced intermediates and solvents , where India currently has almost no listed pure-play.
Subsidy/scheme money — not market price — currently determines whether a fermentation project clears.
India API market ~$15–16 bn , growing 5–7% CAGR through FY28 [REPORTED-T2].
Broader-scope estimate: $14.18 bn (2025) → $15.28 bn (2026) → $22.18 bn (2031) , a 7.74% value CAGR (nominal) [CALCULATED from reported sizes].
Volume CAGR is lower than value — the mix is shifting to complex / high-potent APIs, so growth is partly price-and-mix, not physical.
Context: India's pharma market is ~$60 bn, projected $130 bn by 2030; exports $30.5 bn in FY25.

US Section 232 — correction from the prior run: the final phase took effect 29-Sep-2026 , so the 100% duty on covered patented drugs/APIs now applies to all companies, not only the Annex III list. Generics remain outside the tariff , but the stated plan is a 100% duty on generics from Aug-2028 and 200% thereafter. India is among 20 jurisdictions eligible for a 0% rate on designated specialty pharmaceuticals (BIS notice, 22–23-Sep-2026). [REPORTED-T1]
PLI bulk-drugs tenure not extended (13-Mar-2026); a revamped, R&D-plus-infrastructure scheme is proposed.
Minimum import price on Pen G, 6-APA and amoxicillin (from Dec-2025) — a one-year CIF floor.
Proposed separate bulk-drug wholesale licensing regime (DCGI trader registry).
Revised Schedule M GMP: mandatory for 01-Jan-2026 .

Power semiconductors — the pool that leaks entirely; CG Semi (CGPOWER) is the only listed OSAT exposure.

sections.title: Bottlenecks — Risk & Opportunity
sections.note: dual-readable: every risk is a substitution play

risk.title: No Indian power-semiconductor fab
risk.text: Every IGBT/SiC device in an Indian PCS is imported; CG Semi is OSAT assembly/test; Dholera makes logic, not power; a fab is 3–5+ years and US$1–5 bn away. Resilience: critical.

opp.title: OSAT today, fab tomorrow
opp.text: CG Semi's Sanand OSAT (Jul-2026) is the first step; the India Semiconductor Mission and power-device demand make a domestic device line the logical next node.

risk.title: Grid-forming control IP
risk.text: GFM (VSM, droop, synthetic inertia, black-start) IP is held by SMA, GE Vernova, Sungrow and Tesla; Indian competence is nascent. Resilience: high.

opp.title: The CEA mandate creates a market
opp.text: Making grid-forming PCS mandatory from Jul-2027 creates a captive domestic market for whoever builds the control stack locally.

risk.title: Magnetics & film capacitors
risk.text: Magnetics materials and DC-link film capacitors are largely imported; domestic quality/scale is a work in progress. Resilience: medium-high.

opp.title: Passive localisation
opp.text: Rising PCS volume plus the ≥60% localisation draft pull passive-component and magnetics manufacturing into India.

risk.title: Central PCS & silicon-import cost
risk.text: Central inverters >1 MW and SiC platforms are imported; long-term BESS duty deferment can disadvantage domestic integrators. Resilience: high.

opp.title: Localisation policy
opp.text: The ≥60% PCS/EMS localisation draft and the 20% DCR route procurement to domestic builders; six Chinese firms may only participate via JVs. Deepest hidden dependency: the power semiconductor itself — India can assemble a PCS cabinet but makes none of the IGBT/SiC devices or the grid-forming control IP inside it, so the two highest-value, hardest-to-copy layers remain entirely foreign.

sections.title: Digest — at a glance
sections.note: short summary; full detail below

items: India's transformer market is ~₹40,000 cr (FY26), riding the ₹9.16 lakh cr T&D build-out; ~86,000 MVA was added in FY25 alone.
Demand is strong and visibility long, but lead times (24–42 months at EHV) and imported inputs (CRGO, bushings, OLTC) gate delivery.
Core cutting: CRGO coils (0.18–0.35 mm) slit and cut-to-length to ±0.1 mm with burr ≤0.02 mm, then step-lap mitered.
Winding: HV disc/interleaved coils and LV foil coils from paper/nomex-insulated copper or aluminium.
Drying & impregnation: vapour-phase or vacuum drying to <0.5% moisture, then vacuum oil filling.
Testing: routine (ratio, impedance, loss, dielectric) per IS 2026/IEC 60076; impulse/short-circuit at accredited labs.
CRGO electrical steel — ~90% imported; live anti-dumping probe. Resilience: structural.
HV bushings (OIP/RIP) — significant import dependence; RIP cores imported. Resilience: import-substitution underway.
On-load tap changer (OLTC) — advanced vacuum OLTCs >80% imported (Reinhausen-led). Resilience: concentrated foreign supply.
CTC/copper winding conductor — capacity a choke point; copper 85–90% of CTC cost.
EHV testing infrastructure — limited accredited HV/short-circuit capacity lengthens lead times.
Power-transformer OEMs are the largest pool; CG Power's Power segment at 21.9% PBIT margin.
EHV/765 kV and HVDC transformers carry high entry barriers and pricing power.
Backward integration (CTC, pressboard, RIP bushing) is a margin lever.
Bushing value sits with condenser-graded RIP makers (60–70% premium over OIP).
Transformer market ~₹40,000 cr in FY26, up from ~₹33,000 cr in FY25 — +21% YoY [CALCULATED from Eninrac, FY26].

DGTR CRGO/amorphous anti-dumping finding; a precedent duty was imposed on Chinese CRNO in Dec 2025.
BIS licence renewals for foreign CRGO suppliers.
Copper price swings — 35–45% of active material cost.
New capacity: CG Power to ~110,000 MVA by end-2026; Hitachi Energy ₹2,000 cr Karjan plant.
No NSE/BSE-listed OLTC pure-play (Reinhausen, Hitachi, Huaming are foreign/unlisted).
Bushings: only Yash Highvoltage, and it trades on the BSE SME platform.

industries.title: India Reactor Coolant Pumps & Primary Loop

nodes.name: Reactor Coolant Pump (PCP / RCP)
nodes.fn: The vertical, single-stage centrifugal pump that circulates pressurised D₂O past the core to the steam generators — casing, an impeller welded to the shaft, a hydrostatic radial bearing, a thrust bearing, a squirrel-cage induction motor and (in seal-less designs) a canned stator/rotor.
nodes.importDep: Indigenised (KSB is the sole domestic PCP supplier)

companies.m: Sole domestic supplier of primary coolant pumps (RSR 400/2); nuclear order book ₹1,235 cr at Jun-2026, down from ₹1,313 cr at Dec-2025 (GHAVP 1&2, Kaiga 5&6, Kudankulam); first fully indigenous 700 MWe PCP under execution; Shirwal capacity 1,200→1,450 pumps/yr by 2027
companies.ev: KSB press releases; SEBI Reg-30; ICICI Direct (Aug-2026)

nodes.name: Casing, Impeller & Pressure Boundary
nodes.fn: The pump casing (cast CF8A or forged SA-508-3 with stainless cladding on wetted surfaces), the impeller welded to the shaft, and the suction/discharge nozzles — an integral part of the reactor-coolant pressure boundary.

companies.m: Heavy castings, forgings and pressure-boundary fabrication for nuclear primary-side equipment
Special steels, superalloys and titanium mill forms for the DAE

nodes.name: PCP Motor, Flywheel & Drive
nodes.fn: The squirrel-cage induction motor (~6 MW class, 6.6 kV) driving the pump, with a flywheel for coastdown inertia after loss of power; canned-motor designs add a thin corrosion-resistant stator can.

companies.m: Motors for reactor coolant pumps (220 & 500 MWe); 6 MW primary circulating pump motor for KAPS-3&4

nodes.name: Shaft Seal System (Class-1 Mechanical Seals)
nodes.fn: Three full-pressure mechanical seals in series plus a standstill seal, a thermal-barrier heat exchanger and the gland/seal-injection supply — the single most demanding pressure-boundary application in the pump, and a common cause of forced outage.
nodes.gap: NO COVERAGE IN SELECTED UNIVERSE — Class-1 RCP mechanical seals are held by Framatome (Jeumont), Flowserve and John Crane. No NSE/BSE pure-play.
nodes.near: Nearest listed proxy: KSB Limited (in-house mechanical-seal manufacturing at Shirwal).

nodes.name: Bearings & Wear Surfaces
nodes.fn: A hydrostatic radial bearing and a Kingsbury double-acting thrust bearing (oil-lubricated) for shaft-seal pumps, or water-lubricated bearings (WLBs) for seal-less designs; cobalt-free hardfacing on wear surfaces to cut Co-60 activation.

companies.m: Indigenous manufacturer of water-lubricated bearings for nuclear reactors; precision internals

nodes.name: Primary Loop Piping, Headers & Valves

companies.m: Reactor headers, primary heat transport systems and nuclear-island pressure boundary
Reactor header assemblies and piping & valves for 700 MWe PHWRs

Primary pressurising, shutdown-cooling and auxiliary nuclear pumps

sections.title: Bottlenecks — Risk & Opportunity
sections.note: dual-readable: every risk is a substitution play

risk.title: Single-source PCP qualification
risk.text: KSB is the sole qualified domestic supplier of primary coolant pumps to NPCIL. A single point of failure for every 700 MWe unit. Resilience: years (certification-gated).

opp.title: A second qualified source
opp.text: Flowserve (US) is licensed under 10 CFR Part 810 to transfer PCP technology to CORE Energy Systems for manufacture at Coimbatore — the first such US authorisation for India.

risk.title: Test-bed capacity is the live bind
risk.text: GHAVP PCP testing (started Apr–May 2026) was paused on third-party test-bed equipment; management guided resolution by end-Aug-2026 and resumption in Sep-2026 — the gate on the first fully indigenous 700 MWe PCP. Resilience: months.

opp.title: Domestic dynamic-test facilities
opp.text: KSB already built a 220 MWe PCP dynamic-test facility; a second qualified test bed de-risks the whole fleet schedule.

risk.title: Class-1 seals & bearings are the deepest import
risk.text: RCP mechanical seals are held by Framatome (Jeumont), Flowserve and John Crane; no NSE/BSE pure-play. Resilience: years.

opp.title: Seal & bearing localisation
opp.text: KSB runs an in-house mechanical-seal line at Shirwal; MTAR makes indigenous water-lubricated bearings for reactors.

risk.title: One heavy-forging shop
risk.text: LTSSHF (L&T Special Steels & Heavy Forgings) is the only nuclear-grade heavy-forging facility in the region — now a 100% L&T subsidiary after NPCIL exited its 26% stake (Feb-2025) and rated AA-/Stable (May-2026; corrected from the prior CRISIL-D note). A single point of failure for casings, headers and vessels. Resilience: years.

opp.title: Forging scale-up
opp.text: Fleet-mode demand (10×700 MWe + SMRs) justifies a second qualified forging source and an LTSSHF recapitalisation.

risk.title: Fabrication & test machinery imported
risk.text: The 5-axis CNC, Hirth gear grinders, EDM, seal-making and dynamic test-bed equipment are foreign-built. Resilience: months–years.

opp.title: Machine-tool & test-bed localisation
opp.text: A domestic heavy-machine-tool and test-rig base would de-risk the entire pump-fabrication chain.

risk.title: Skilled trades
risk.text: Nuclear-qualified welders, NDT inspectors and process engineers bind tighter than materials and cannot be bought quickly.

opp.title: Incumbent qualification pipelines
opp.text: KSB / BHEL / L&T qualification pipelines are a durable moat as fleet mode ramps.

risk.title: Owner & design are unlisted
risk.text: Design (BARC), ownership (NPCIL) and the fuel cycle sit inside DAE entities with no NSE/BSE listing. Resilience: structural.

opp.title: SHANTI Act 2025
opp.text: Graded liability, a statutory AERB and limited private participation open SPV models for the next tranche of reactors and SMRs. Deepest hidden dependency: the pump is India’s most investable nuclear-equipment node — KSB (PCP), BHEL (motors) and L&T (headers, forgings) are listed and qualified — yet the two highest-value layers, the Class-1 seal & design IP and the fabrication/test machinery , are imported or held inside the incumbent, and the owner (NPCIL) and designer (BARC) are unlisted. The pump is investable; the seal IP and the tooling are not.

sections.title: Digest — at a glance
sections.note: short summary; full detail below

items.h: Snapshot India’s robotics ecosystem spans four families — industrial robots, AMR/AGV, drones/UAV and humanoid & service robots — over a shared core of actuators, drives, sensors, power and software. India is the world’s 6th-largest robot installer (9,120 units, 2024) with a stock of ~52,600, but imports the core: reducers, magnets, encoders and power semiconductors. No dedicated robotics PLI exists; the National Strategy on Robotics is still a draft. Process & equipment
items: Robot build = cast/forge/machine housings → wind stators → assemble actuator (motor + reducer + encoder + brake) → fit controller → integrate cell (fixtures, EOAT, vision) → EOL test.
Core process equipment is imported: 5-axis CNC, gear/thread grinding (Klingelnberg, Gleason, Nidec, Höfler), vacuum/atmosphere heat-treat furnaces, magnet presses and CMMs (ZEISS, Mitutoyo).
Drone and cobot assembly is lighter — PCB SMT, composite lay-up and DGCA/ISO test rigs.
Reducers (harmonic/RV) — effectively 100% imported; no robotics-grade domestic maker.
Rare-earth NdFeB magnets — ~95% imported; first Indian plant targeted Q1 2028.
Power electronics (IGBT/MOSFET/MCU) and encoders/torque sensors — no Indian capability.
Precision machine tools & metrology — fully imported; they make the reducers.
Value sits upstream in reducers, motors, sensors, magnets and control silicon — the pools India imports.
Indian assembly/integration is competitive and thin-margin; ARAPL is the only listed robotics pure-play.
Software/autonomy and service (RaaS, AMC, retrofits) are the fastest-growing domestic capture layer.
Drones: four listed players; ~50–60% of subsystem value still imported.
Drone PLI 2.0 finalised early 2026; Mission Drone Shakti (₹10,000 cr) proposed in Budget 2026.
National Strategy on Robotics still un-adopted; TAG review Feb-2026.
Electronics PLI lapses 2026 — IFR flags a possible 2026 robot-installation pause.

sections.title: Bottlenecks — Risk & Opportunity
sections.note: dual-readable: every risk is a substitution play

risk.title: Harmonic / strain-wave reducers
risk.text: Effectively 100% imported — no large-scale domestic robotics-grade producer. A 50–100 Nm unit lands at ₹35,000–₹1,20,000 (2026); lead times 12–24 weeks. Every robot joint needs one. Resilience: years / structural.

opp.title: Domestic reducer industry from zero
opp.text: China’s Leaderdrive scale (206k units 2023 → 1.59 mn planned 2027) shows the shape; India’s humanoid programme would need reducer volumes exceeding any single Chinese supplier — a first-mover prize.

risk.title: Rare-earth NdFeB magnets
risk.text: ~95% imported; China holds ~94% of sintered output and 87–91% of rare-earth processing. Every servo motor needs magnets. First Indian plant targeted Q1 2028. Resilience: years / structural.

opp.title: Domestic magnet capacity
opp.text: National rare-earth/magnet scheme + motor makers (Bharat Bijlee, CG Power, Sona Comstar) create a captive domestic demand base; the magnet plant is the missing link.

risk.title: Servo motors, drives & power silicon
risk.text: >60% of AC servo systems imported; ~34% domestic motor capability; power electronics (IGBT/MOSFET) and control MCU/DSP have no Indian capability. India does licensed assembly, not indigenous design. Resilience: months–years.

opp.title: Servo & power-electronics localisation
opp.text: Bharat Bijlee (SynchroTorq PM servo, 4,000+ packages) and CG Power (motors + Emotron drives) are scaling; India Semiconductor Mission could anchor power-semi. The design, not the assembly, is the gap.

risk.title: Encoders, torque sensors & LiDAR
risk.text: No Indian manufacturer of robotics-grade encoders or joint torque sensors disclosed; the dominant encoder chip is made in Austria. LiDAR and depth sensors are imported. Resilience: years.

opp.title: Precision sensing entry
opp.text: High-value, low-volume, qualification-gated — a natural niche for Indian precision-electronics firms once machine-tool and metrology capability matures.

risk.title: Precision machine tools & metrology
risk.text: The gear/thread grinders (Klingelnberg, Gleason, Nidec, Höfler) and CMMs (ZEISS, Mitutoyo) that make reducers, screws and gears are fully imported — the deepest hidden dependency in a “localised” robot. Resilience: years / structural.

opp.title: Machine-tool & metrology build-out
opp.text: Without domestic gear grinding and metrology, no reducer plan can qualify. MTAR’s defence/space-grade screws are a beachhead; volume is unproven.

risk.title: Drones — subsystem imports
risk.text: ~50–60% of drone subsystem value is imported (flight controllers, ESCs, BLDC motors, optics); complete-drone imports are banned, so much “domestic” output is assembly. Resilience: months–years.

opp.title: Component indigenisation cascade
opp.text: PLI 2.0, Mission Drone Shakti (₹10,000 cr proposed) and ANRF MAHA Drones (component R&D) target exactly these subsystems; Zen’s Vector Technics (51%) is an early listed step.

risk.title: Skills & standards
risk.text: Scarce engineers in AI, actuators, control and integration; no unified testing/standards framework (a non-tariff export barrier). Capacity can be bought; qualified process engineers cannot.

opp.title: Training & accredited labs
opp.text: RPTO/robotics training and BIS/ISO-aligned test labs carry durable scarcity value; a National Robotics Mission would fund both. Deepest hidden import dependency: the precision machine tools and metrology that make the reducers, screws and gears — and the magnet and power-semiconductor supply behind the motors. India’s robotics position is “strong at the edges, empty at the core”: integration, software and assembly are real, but every high-value joint, magnet and encoder is imported.

sections.note: where value is captured · and which pool leaks to imports

items: Upstream: reducers, motors, encoders/sensors, magnets and control silicon — the pools India imports.
Downstream: application engineering, vision, software and service (RaaS, AMC, retrofit) — the domestic capture layer.
Assembly of arms/cells is competitive and thin-margin.
Drones: airframe/assembly domestic, subsystems imported.
ARAPL NSE: AFFORDABLE — India’s first listed robotics co; order book >₹140 cr (Nov-2025); AMR brand Humro (RaaS, leasing).
Bharat Bijlee NSE: BBL — indigenously developed SynchroTorq PM servo motors (4,000+ packages).
CG Power NSE: CGPOWER — motors, drives (Emotron), automation.
Sona Comstar NSE: SONACOMS — ₹62.6 cr robotics-components capex; NEURA Robotics partnership.
Zen / ideaForge / Paras / DroneAcharya — the four listed drone-sector names.
Reducers, NdFeB magnets, encoders/torque sensors, power semiconductors, LiDAR and precision machine tools have no listed Indian pure-play.
Bottleneck nodes: harmonic/RV reducers, servo motors, drives, power electronics, encoders, magnets, LiDAR, drone flight-controllers, machine tools.

sections.title: Bottlenecks — Risk & Opportunity
sections.note: dual-readable: every risk is a substitution play

risk.title: Space-grade solar cells (III-V)
risk.text: 70–80% of materials imported (US, EU, Japan); ITAR/ECCN licensing can delay procurement 6–12 months. India has zero gallium and germanium refining capacity. Resilience: years.

opp.title: MOCVD epitaxy + array qualification
opp.text: Dhruva’s Solis+ rollable arrays and BEL’s panel work sit on a domestic gap in epitaxial wafers; a five-year ISRO offtake could seed TRL-7/8 domestic cell and anti-radiation-coating capacity.

risk.title: ADCS & precision sensors
risk.text: Star trackers (Sodern, France), reaction wheels, gyros and radiation-hardened OBCs are imported. “Made in India” satellites often assemble foreign subsystems. Resilience: years.

opp.title: Five-year subsystem orders
opp.text: Placing 5-year orders with 2–3 Indian firms per category (gyros, star trackers, reaction wheels, atomic clocks, optical payloads, OBCs) is the model to build the missing component base.

risk.title: Atomic clocks (NavIC)
risk.text: First-generation NavIC clocks were imported from SpectraTime (now Safran); clocks have failed on 5 of 11 NavIC satellites — a navigation-integrity risk. Resilience: structural.

opp.title: Indigenous rubidium clocks
opp.text: CSIR-CEERI / ISRO have demonstrated indigenous clocks on TDS-01; qualifying a domestic supplier is a strategic, high-margin prize.

risk.title: Launch cadence
risk.text: India flies ~12 missions/yr against a stated need for 50–60 to reach the 2033 target. Skyroot’s Vikram-1 reached orbit on 18 Jul 2026 — India’s first private orbital launch. Resilience: months–years.

opp.title: Industry-built launchers
opp.text: HAL’s ₹511 cr SSLV ToT and the HAL–L&T PSLV consortium (₹860 cr, 5 vehicles) shift serial production to industry; Skyroot’s Vikram-1 and Agnikul’s Agnibaan open the private launch market.

risk.title: Satcom ground-segment localisation
risk.text: DoT security norms mandate 20% ground-segment indigenisation within 5 years, yet high-end RF, modems and antennas are still largely imported. Resilience: months.

opp.title: Gateway & VSAT build-out
opp.text: NSIL’s rate-contract RFPs for C/Ku/Ka gateways and VSAT terminals, plus L&T’s GSAT gateway execution, are a recurring domestic integration market for BEL, Avantel and Nelco. Deepest hidden import dependency: the radiation-hardened silicon (OBCs, FPGA, memory) and precision electro-mechanical subsystems — star trackers, reaction wheels, atomic clocks and space-grade solar cells — that sit inside almost every Indian satellite and launch vehicle, regardless of how Indian the final integration looks.

nodes.name: Wafer-fab process tools (deposition, etch, clean, CMP, implant)
nodes.fn: The capital tools that build a wafer layer by layer — the deepest import dependency in the entire stack.
nodes.near: No NSE/BSE tool OEM. Nearest: ASM Technologies (contract manufacturing for tool OEMs). Foreign: Applied Materials, Lam Research, Tokyo Electron, ASML.

nodes.name: Lithography & optical column (DUV / EUV)
nodes.fn: Patterning. The single most concentrated node in world manufacturing — and the one India cannot buy its way past.

nodes.name: Deposition (CVD / ALD / PVD / epitaxy)

nodes.name: Etch & dry clean
nodes.fn: Removes material selectively; chamber materials and RF power determine yield.
nodes.near: Lam Research, Tokyo Electron, Applied Materials. No listed Indian exposure.

nodes.name: Metrology & inspection
nodes.fn: Measures whether the last step worked — the node Semicon 2.0 names as India's most accessible equipment entry point.
nodes.near: KLA, ASML (HMI e-beam), Hitachi High-Tech, Onto. Semicon 2.0 funds R&D and pilot lines here; no listed Indian player yet.

sections.title: Digest — at a glance
sections.note: short summary; full detail below

items: The upstream layer of the chip industry: the tools that pattern a wafer and the materials it consumes — not the chips themselves.
India's position is near-zero. Every process tool, wafer, photoresist, mask and most gases and wet chemicals are imported; Semicon 2.0 creates a dedicated pillar to change that.
Front-end spine: lithography → deposition → etch → implant → diffusion → CMP → clean → metrology, repeated 400–1,400 times per wafer.
Sub-fab spine: vacuum, abatement, gas cabinets, chillers and ultrapure water — unglamorous and completely imported.
Back-end spine: dicing, die attach, wire bond, moulding, singulation, ATE — the tools India's new OSATs have all bought abroad.
Materials are consumables, not capex: they recur every wafer, which is why qualification, not capital, is the barrier.
Lithography — ASML sole EUV supplier; DUV export-controlled. Resilience: STRUCTURAL.
Photoresist, photomask blanks and 300mm silicon wafers — three-to-five supplier oligopolies, 2–3 year requalification. Resilience: YEARS.
Specialty gases and high-purity wet chemicals — 12–22 of 50+ gases made locally; Fujifilm's first plant lands FY2028. Resilience: MONTHS–YEARS.
Packaging materials — leadframe, bonding wire, moulding compound, substrate: no qualified Indian producer. Resilience: MONTHS–YEARS.
Skills — orbital welders for 5N/6N gas lines: 200–300 needed per project, trained from scratch. Resilience: YEARS.
Value sits with the tool OEM and with proprietary consumables that recur per wafer — slurry, resist, quartzware, targets, chamber parts.
India's current capture is the commoditised slice: civils, cleanroom fit-out, cryogenic tanks, gas supply, installation labour.
The realistic entry is tool contract manufacturing and precision sub-assemblies — ASM Technologies' model, now funded by an ECMS approval.
Localisation alone does not cut cost: NITI Aayog found Indian arms of global suppliers price at import parity, so the saving arrives only at genuine Indian scale.
The largest single material line item is the leadframe at ~35–40% of OSAT material cost — the highest-value localisation target in the back end.
Global equipment: $135.1 bn (2025 actual) → $165.9 bn (2026F, +23.2%) → $229.5 bn (2028F). 3-year CAGR 19.3% [CALCULATED]; last-year +15.4% [CALCULATED]; 5-year [UNAVAILABLE].
Global materials: $73.2 bn in 2025, +6.8% last year [REPORTED-T1]; 3- and 5-year CAGR [UNAVAILABLE] from this pass.
All growth figures are nominal USD, value only — equipment has no meaningful unit series to separate volume from price.
India: no published equipment/materials market size [UNAVAILABLE]. The visible pipeline is ₹1.64 lakh cr of committed projects and $11–12 bn of announced equipment/materials proposals.
10 Nov 2026 — China's suspension of its October-2025 rare-earth package expires; reverts to licensing with a presumption against approval.
27 Nov 2026 — China's US-specific gallium / germanium / antimony suspension expires.
Dec 2026 — Tata–PSMC Dholera trial production target; first commercial wafer guided to 2028.
FY2028 — Fujifilm's ₹800 cr Dholera materials plant targets commercial production.
No NSE/BSE-listed company exists in process tools, deposition/etch, metrology, back-end equipment, wet chemicals, or wafers and SiC substrates.
Closest listed exposures: ASM Technologies (tool contract manufacturing) and INOX India (cryogenic gas delivery).

risk.text: Hoya/AGC/Shin-Etsu make the blanks; five suppliers make most 300mm wafers. Neither exists in India at any scale. Resilience: STRUCTURAL.

risk.title: Specialty gases
risk.text: 12–22 of 50+ gases are made locally; 20–25 will still be imported after INOX Air Products' expansion. Resilience: MONTHS–YEARS.

opp.title: Gas purification and the Dholera hub
opp.text: INOX Air Products' ~₹500 cr specialty-gas hub plus Linde's Dholera plant are the build; purification capacity, not gas molecules, is the gap.

risk.title: High-purity wet chemicals
risk.text: No qualified Indian producer; Fujifilm's first plant targets FY2028, and NITI Aayog found local arms of global suppliers price at import parity. Resilience: MONTHS.

opp.title: Genuinely Indian chemical manufacture
opp.text: India's specialty-chemical base can supply the plant; the barrier is sub-ppb purification and fab qualification, not chemistry.

risk.title: Packaging materials
risk.text: Leadframe ~95% imported at ~35–40% of material cost; bonding wire 100%; moulding compound ~90%; organic substrate 100%. Resilience: MONTHS–YEARS.

opp.title: Leadframe stamping & plating
opp.text: The highest-value localisation target in the back end; copper strip and precision stamping already exist in India, qualification does not.

risk.title: Qualified skills
risk.text: A single project needs 200–300 orbital welders for 5N/6N gas lines; material qualification takes 9–18 months and a new vendor plant three years. Resilience: YEARS.

opp.title: Training plus bonded warehouses
opp.text: INOX India's skill centre is the template; a bonded stocking hub turns a 75–90 day import exposure into 7–14 days without needing the factory.

sections.title: Value pools & cost waterfall
sections.note: where value is captured · and which pool leaks to imports

items: Tool OEM margin — the largest pool in the chain, protected by patents and process know-how rather than materials.
Recurring consumables — resist, slurry, quartzware, targets and chamber parts are billed per wafer, so they compound with fab utilisation.
Qualification itself — once a material is designed into a process, it is rarely displaced; that is the moat, not the chemistry.
Civils, cleanroom fit-out, cryogenic tanks, gas supply, UPW and installation labour — the low-margin, commoditised end.
Tool contract manufacturing is the one higher-value foothold, and it is small: ASM Technologies' whole FY26 revenue is ₹528.5 cr.
Material value leaks almost entirely: material is ~45–50% of OSAT cost and 60–70% of that is imported.
NITI Aayog (May 2026) found Indian arms of global suppliers price at import parity, tariffs included — so a "made in India" component can cost what the import costs.
Cost competitiveness arrives only when manufacture is genuinely Indian and at scale, which is why the leadframe (the biggest single line item) matters more than headline fab announcements.

Front-end spine: lithography → deposition → etch → implant → diffusion → CMP → clean → metrology, repeated 400–1,400 times per wafer.
Sub-fab spine: vacuum, abatement, gas cabinets, chillers and ultrapure water — unglamorous and completely imported.
Back-end spine: dicing, die attach, wire bond, moulding, singulation, ATE — the tools India's new OSATs have all bought abroad.
Materials are consumables, not capex: they recur every wafer, which is why qualification, not capital, is the barrier.
Lithography — ASML sole EUV supplier; DUV export-controlled. Resilience: STRUCTURAL.
Photoresist, photomask blanks and 300mm silicon wafers — three-to-five supplier oligopolies, 2–3 year requalification. Resilience: YEARS.
Specialty gases and high-purity wet chemicals — 12–22 of 50+ gases made locally; Fujifilm's first plant lands FY2028. Resilience: MONTHS–YEARS.
Packaging materials — leadframe, bonding wire, moulding compound, substrate: no qualified Indian producer. Resilience: MONTHS–YEARS.
Skills — orbital welders for 5N/6N gas lines: 200–300 needed per project, trained from scratch. Resilience: YEARS.
Value sits with the tool OEM and with proprietary consumables that recur per wafer — slurry, resist, quartzware, targets, chamber parts.
India's current capture is the commoditised slice: civils, cleanroom fit-out, cryogenic tanks, gas supply, installation labour.
The realistic entry is tool contract manufacturing and precision sub-assemblies — ASM Technologies' model, now funded by an ECMS approval.
Localisation alone does not cut cost: NITI Aayog found Indian arms of global suppliers price at import parity, so the saving arrives only at genuine Indian scale.
The largest single material line item is the leadframe at ~35–40% of OSAT material cost — the highest-value localisation target in the back end.
Global equipment: $135.1 bn (2025 actual) → $165.9 bn (2026F, +23.2%) → $229.5 bn (2028F). 3-year CAGR 19.3% [CALCULATED]; last-year +15.4% [CALCULATED]; 5-year [UNAVAILABLE].
Global materials: $73.2 bn in 2025, +6.8% last year [REPORTED-T1]; 3- and 5-year CAGR [UNAVAILABLE] from this pass.
All growth figures are nominal USD, value only — equipment has no meaningful unit series to separate volume from price.
India: no published equipment/materials market size [UNAVAILABLE]. The visible pipeline is ₹1.64 lakh cr of committed projects and $11–12 bn of announced equipment/materials proposals.
10 Nov 2026 — China's suspension of its October-2025 rare-earth package expires; reverts to licensing with a presumption against approval.
27 Nov 2026 — China's US-specific gallium / germanium / antimony suspension expires.
Dec 2026 — Tata–PSMC Dholera trial production target; first commercial wafer guided to 2028.
FY2028 — Fujifilm's ₹800 cr Dholera materials plant targets commercial production.
No NSE/BSE-listed company exists in process tools, deposition/etch, metrology, back-end equipment, wet chemicals, or wafers and SiC substrates.
Closest listed exposures: ASM Technologies (tool contract manufacturing) and INOX India (cryogenic gas delivery).

sections.title: Digest
sections.note: short summary · full detail below

items: Shakti is the Indian Navy's indigenous capital-warship EW suite — DRDO/DLRL-designed, BEL-built — giving wideband ESM (intercept, direction-finding, radar fingerprinting) and DRFM-based ECM jamming.

Part of DRDO's seven-system Samudrika family (ship-borne Shakti, Nayan, Tushar; air-borne Sarang, Sarakshi, Sarvadhari, Nikash). Fitted to P-15B destroyers, P-17A frigates, Talwar-class and INS Vikrant.
RF/digital LRUs are SMT-assembled, die-attached and wire-bonded in cleanrooms; antennas and arrays are precision-machined and hermetically sealed.
Spine: MMIC/HEMT fab (GaN-on-SiC) → T/R-module and microwave-module assembly → LRU build → array integration → EMC/EMI + environmental qualification → sea trials & Navy/DGQA acceptance.
Key machinery: MOCVD reactors, RF wafer fabs, pick-and-place/SMT lines, wire/die bonders, RF anechoic & EMI/EMC chambers, vector network analysers.
GaN/GaAs MMIC and SiC substrate — ~75% imported; DRDO GAETEC output is limited. Resilience: years.
RF test equipment, BAW/SAW filters, specialty gases, MOCVD reactors — 90–100% imported. Resilience: years.
FPGA/DSP and high-speed ADC/DAC — imported (US/foreign). Resilience: months–years.
Cognitive-EW software — India at TRL 4–5 vs China 6–7. Resilience: years.
Prime integration is the largest pool and is captured by BEL (listed) as DRDO's ToT partner — ~85% of system value is captured domestically at integration.
RF subsystems and T/R modules are the fastest-climbing private pool (Astra Microwave, Centum, Data Patterns, Apollo Micro).
Software/cognitive-EW is the highest-margin, fastest-appreciating pool (BEL, Data Patterns).
The pools that leak to imports are the deepest ones: GaN MMIC, RF chips, FPGA, test gear, laminates, connectors.
Localisation opportunity sits at the MMIC/fab and cognitive-software layers — where no listed pure-play exists yet.
India EW market: ₹3,200 cr (FY24) → ₹9,200 cr (FY35) committed baseline ; ₹15,000–22,000 cr under upside scenarios. [REPORTED-T3 / SCENARIO]
India defence-electronics: ~$6.85 bn (2024) → ~$11.35 bn (2032), ~6.2% CAGR; EW ~22.6% of it (2024). [REPORTED-T2 / CALCULATED]
EW systems 5-yr CAGR 8–10% (industry est.) [REPORTED-T3]; a rival estimate puts EW at $923 mn (2025) → $1.47 bn (2035), ~4.8% CAGR [CONFLICTING DATA].
Value is nominal; no separate physical/volume series is published for EW — volume [UNAVAILABLE]. Growth is driven by budget/mix, not unit count.
Oct-2026: single-tender RFP to BEL for a Shakti system to replace Ellora Mk-II on a Shivalik-class frigate. [LIVE]
BEL flagged Shakti Phase IV and Shatrughat / Samghat EW solutions as near-term orders (May-2026 call). [LIVE]
Pragyashakti tri-service EW software framework — launched 30-Oct-2025, 25-month build. [LIVE]

No NSE/BSE pure-play for GaN/GaAs MMIC, FPGA/ADC silicon, RF test equipment, MIL connectors, RF laminates, radomes/mechanical or hermetic packaging — exposure is via unlisted DRDO fabs, startups and foreign-listed OEMs.

items: Shakti is the Indian Navy's indigenous capital-warship EW suite — DRDO/DLRL-designed, BEL-built — giving wideband ESM (intercept, direction-finding, radar fingerprinting) and DRFM-based ECM jamming.

Part of DRDO's seven-system Samudrika family (ship-borne Shakti, Nayan, Tushar; air-borne Sarang, Sarakshi, Sarvadhari, Nikash). Fitted to P-15B destroyers, P-17A frigates, Talwar-class and INS Vikrant.
RF/digital LRUs are SMT-assembled, die-attached and wire-bonded in cleanrooms; antennas and arrays are precision-machined and hermetically sealed.
Spine: MMIC/HEMT fab (GaN-on-SiC) → T/R-module and microwave-module assembly → LRU build → array integration → EMC/EMI + environmental qualification → sea trials & Navy/DGQA acceptance.
Key machinery: MOCVD reactors, RF wafer fabs, pick-and-place/SMT lines, wire/die bonders, RF anechoic & EMI/EMC chambers, vector network analysers.
GaN/GaAs MMIC and SiC substrate — ~75% imported; DRDO GAETEC output is limited. Resilience: years.
RF test equipment, BAW/SAW filters, specialty gases, MOCVD reactors — 90–100% imported. Resilience: years.
FPGA/DSP and high-speed ADC/DAC — imported (US/foreign). Resilience: months–years.
Cognitive-EW software — India at TRL 4–5 vs China 6–7. Resilience: years.
Prime integration is the largest pool and is captured by BEL (listed) as DRDO's ToT partner — ~85% of system value is captured domestically at integration.
RF subsystems and T/R modules are the fastest-climbing private pool (Astra Microwave, Centum, Data Patterns, Apollo Micro).
Software/cognitive-EW is the highest-margin, fastest-appreciating pool (BEL, Data Patterns).
The pools that leak to imports are the deepest ones: GaN MMIC, RF chips, FPGA, test gear, laminates, connectors.
Localisation opportunity sits at the MMIC/fab and cognitive-software layers — where no listed pure-play exists yet.
India EW market: ₹3,200 cr (FY24) → ₹9,200 cr (FY35) committed baseline ; ₹15,000–22,000 cr under upside scenarios. [REPORTED-T3 / SCENARIO]
India defence-electronics: ~$6.85 bn (2024) → ~$11.35 bn (2032), ~6.2% CAGR; EW ~22.6% of it (2024). [REPORTED-T2 / CALCULATED]
EW systems 5-yr CAGR 8–10% (industry est.) [REPORTED-T3]; a rival estimate puts EW at $923 mn (2025) → $1.47 bn (2035), ~4.8% CAGR [CONFLICTING DATA].
Value is nominal; no separate physical/volume series is published for EW — volume [UNAVAILABLE]. Growth is driven by budget/mix, not unit count.

sections.title: System Overview
sections.note: Metallisation turns a passivated wafer into a current-delivering cell by printing (or plating) a conductive grid. Gold-bordered nodes below are the HIGH-priority subsystems carried into the drill-down tree — the silver powder, the glass frit, the front-side paste, the printing step, the copper-substitution pathways and the upstream silver metal. This is the node where the module’s largest cost line sat through 2026, and where the technology is now actively migrating away from silver.

sections.title: Bottlenecks — Risk & Opportunity
sections.note: dual-readable: every risk is a substitution play

risk.title: Certification-gated vendor base
risk.text: Class-1 nuclear qualification takes years; a small pool of ASME-qualified suppliers gates the schedule. Resilience: years.

opp.title: N-stamp incumbents scale
opp.text: L&T, Kirloskar Brothers and KSB can capture a widening order book as fleet mode ramps — KSB’s nuclear order book already stands at ₹1,235 cr (Jun-2026).

risk.title: Heavy forging capacity
risk.text: A single integrated nuclear-grade forging shop (L&T–NPCIL JV) is the pinch point for large RPV/SG forgings. Resilience: years.

opp.title: Indigenous ApuRVA alloy
opp.text: Already developed with Indian industry — an export and SMR-module opportunity.

risk.title: Reactor C&I electronics
risk.text: ECIL is effectively the sole fully-integrated nuclear C&I house — and it is unlisted. Resilience: months.

opp.title: Indigenous NUCON platform
opp.text: Sanctions-tested and could extend to SMR digital I&C — a private-sector white space.

risk.title: Fuel-cycle front-end
risk.text: Uranium, enrichment, zircaloy and heavy water sit in unlisted DAE units; some UOC is imported. Resilience: months–years.

opp.title: NFC / UCIL / IREL expansion
opp.text: Plus thorium and ANEEL-fuel optionality (L&T–CCTE) — the import-substitution case. PFBR first criticality (Apr-2026) advances the thorium route.

risk.title: Skilled trades
risk.text: Class-1 welders, NDT inspectors and QA engineers bind tighter than materials and cannot be bought quickly.

opp.title: Training pipelines
opp.text: BHEL / MTAR / L&T qualification pipelines are a durable moat for incumbents.

risk.title: Liability & financing
risk.text: Private capital stayed cautious on first projects under the old liability regime. Resilience: structural.

opp.title: SHANTI Act 2025
opp.text: Graded liability (₹100–3,000 cr), supplier liability removed, statutory AERB and private participation unlock SPV models — AEC expects 30 GW from private players by 2047. Deepest hidden dependency: the qualified-vendor base and the unlisted fuel cycle. Most of the critical path — reactor design/IP (BARC/NPCIL), fuel fabrication (NFC), uranium (UCIL), zircon (IREL), heavy water (HWB) and reactor C&I (ECIL) — runs through entities with no NSE/BSE listing. The technology is indigenous; the investability is not.

sections.title: Digest — at a glance
sections.note: A short summary of the analysis. Structure and inputs are on the tree; process, value pools and watch items are summarised here.

items.h: Snapshot The wafer-to-cell conversion step — texturing, diffusion, passivation, metallisation, firing and test. India has built 37.8 GW of ALMM-listed cell capacity (8-Oct-2026) but only ~ 16–18 GW is effective; silicon wafers are >99% imported ; capex is ~₹470 cr/GW; TOPCon has displaced PERC as the default new line. Import dependence has moved up the chain, not disappeared. Process & equipment
items: Texturing, POCl₃/BBr₃ diffusion, Al₂O₃/SiN passivation, screen-printed metallisation and co-firing — a ~15–20 step wet-chemistry + high-temperature sequence.
Turnkey cell lines are imported (>90% of capex), mostly Chinese OEMs; metallisation is the largest direct cost after the wafer (~24% of conversion cost).
Silicon wafers — >99% imported; India wafer capacity ~2 GW.
Silver paste and high-purity silver — ~90% imported; silver-bar imports restricted since 16-May-2026.
Cell-line machinery — >90% foreign; process gases and fine-mesh screens largely imported.
Cell OEMs are the largest listed pool — Premier, Waaree, Websol, Emmvee, Tata Power (TP Solar), Reliance.
Premier is India’s largest cell maker (10.6 GW after the 7 GW Naidupeta line, Sep-2026); Waaree holds 5.4 GW.
Wafers/polysilicon and paste/screens have no listed Indian pure-play — the localisation prize.
ALMM List-II in force 1-Jun-2026; net-metering/open-access exemption ends 31-Dec-2026.
ALMM-III (ingots/wafers) targeted 1-Jun-2028; US AD ~123% / CVD ~126% on Indian cells.
Wafers, ingot/polysilicon, silver paste, screens and cell-line equipment have no listed Indian pure-play; nearest exposure is via integrated OEMs.

sections.title: System Overview
sections.note: Cell fabrication turns an imported wafer into a current-producing device through a ~15–20 step sequence of wet chemistry, high-temperature diffusion, deposition and metallisation. Gold-bordered nodes are the HIGH-priority subsystems carried into the drill-down tree — the wafer input, the deposition and metallisation steps, the cell-line machinery and the silver paste.

sections.title: Bottlenecks — Risk & Opportunity
sections.note: dual-readable: every risk is a substitution play

risk.title: Incoming wafer
risk.text: >99% of India’s silicon wafers are imported (China ~97% of global output); domestic wafer capacity is ~2 GW — the binding input constraint. Resilience: years / structural.

opp.title: Wafer localisation — ALMM-III (1-Jun-2028)
opp.text: Waaree’s 10 GW ingot-wafer complex at Nagpur (₹6,200 cr) and Tata Power’s 10 GW plan (₹6,500 cr) lead a ~100 GW announced pipeline; the mandate triggers once ≥3 units and ≥15 GW are enlisted.

risk.title: Metallisation paste (Ag / Al)
risk.text: Silver paste is ~90% import-dependent (China ~90–92% of global production); India has near-zero domestic paste. Silver-bar imports (≥99.9%, HS 71069221/29) moved to “Restricted” on 16-May-2026 and now need DGFT authorisation. Resilience: months–years.

opp.title: Paste & silver thrifting
opp.text: Silver-paste imports hit US$184m in FY26 (+64.5% YoY, ~65% from China); a domestic paste/refined-silver play is the open white space, and copper-metallisation is the substitution race (see the Silver Paste drill-down).

risk.title: Cell-line machinery
risk.text: >90% of cell-line capex is foreign — turnkey lines and process tools (diffusion, PECVD/LPCVD, ALD, printers, firing furnaces) come mainly from Chinese OEMs, now under export pressure. Resilience: years.

opp.title: Domestic equipment & consumables
opp.text: An unlisted white space — wet-bench, PECVD, printers, screens, ribbon. RENA/centrotherm (Germany) and China S.C serve India today; no NSE/BSE pure-play exists.

risk.title: Process gases & wet chemicals
risk.text: Cell-grade silane, ammonia, POCl₃/BBr₃ and high-purity wet chemicals (KOH, HF, HNO₃) are substantially imported; supply is concentrated and qualification is line-specific. Resilience: months.

opp.title: Industrial-gas localisation
opp.text: Linde India is the only listed gas exposure; local bulk-gas and on-site nitrogen plants (e.g. Praxair/Linde) are the substitution route.

risk.title: ALMM-II demand timing
risk.text: List-II is live (1-Jun-2026) at 37.8 GW enlisted but only ~16–18 GW effective; module lines have been under-fed, and the 31-Dec-2026 net-metering/open-access exemption creates a demand pull-forward cliff. Resilience: months–years.

opp.title: Effective-capacity ramp
opp.text: Premier’s 7 GW Naidupeta TOPCon line (Sep-2026) and Waaree’s 10 GW Unn plant are converting enlisted into operating capacity — the value pool that stays with the domestic builder.

risk.title: Trade exposure
risk.text: US preliminary AD ~123% / CVD ~126% on Indian cells (final order 26-Oct-2026) squeezes exports, while China’s WTO challenge (Dec-2025) contests India’s tariff/PLI stack. Resilience: structural.

opp.title: Domestic-demand anchoring
opp.text: ALMM-II plus 44 GW of annual domestic demand makes the home market the anchor; EU FTA (concluded 27-Jan-2026) is the diversification route. Where value sits: Cell OEMs — Premier, Waaree, Websol, Emmvee, Tata Power (TP Solar), Reliance. Silver-paste and screen makers are foreign/unlisted; recycling is emerging.

digest.h: Snapshot The wafer-to-cell conversion step — texturing, diffusion, passivation, metallisation, firing and test. India has built 37.8 GW of ALMM-listed cell capacity (8-Oct-2026) but only ~ 16–18 GW is effective; silicon wafers are >99% imported ; capex is ~₹470 cr/GW; TOPCon has displaced PERC as the default new line. Import dependence has moved up the chain, not disappeared. Process & equipment
items: Texturing, POCl₃/BBr₃ diffusion, Al₂O₃/SiN passivation, screen-printed metallisation and co-firing — a ~15–20 step wet-chemistry + high-temperature sequence.
Turnkey cell lines are imported (>90% of capex), mostly Chinese OEMs; metallisation is the largest direct cost after the wafer (~24% of conversion cost).
Silicon wafers — >99% imported; India wafer capacity ~2 GW.
Silver paste and high-purity silver — ~90% imported; silver-bar imports restricted since 16-May-2026.
Cell-line machinery — >90% foreign; process gases and fine-mesh screens largely imported.
Cell OEMs are the largest listed pool — Premier, Waaree, Websol, Emmvee, Tata Power (TP Solar), Reliance.
Premier is India’s largest cell maker (10.6 GW after the 7 GW Naidupeta line, Sep-2026); Waaree holds 5.4 GW.
Wafers/polysilicon and paste/screens have no listed Indian pure-play — the localisation prize.
ALMM List-II in force 1-Jun-2026; net-metering/open-access exemption ends 31-Dec-2026.
ALMM-III (ingots/wafers) targeted 1-Jun-2028; US AD ~123% / CVD ~126% on Indian cells.
Wafers, ingot/polysilicon, silver paste, screens and cell-line equipment have no listed Indian pure-play; nearest exposure is via integrated OEMs.
