sections.title: Bottlenecks — Risk & Opportunity
sections.note: dual-readable: every risk is a substitution play

risk.title: Solar cells (ALMM-II live)
risk.text: ALMM List-II for cells in force since 1-Jun-2026; enlisted capacity 37.8 GW (12th rev, 8-Oct-2026) but only ~16–18 GW effective; ~one-third of ~140 SME module makers halted; 6–8 month waits; domestic-cell modules cost ~3–4¢/W more. Resilience: months–years.

opp.title: Cell capacity ramp
opp.text: The single biggest listed value pool — Premier (3.6→10.6 GW), Waaree (5.4 GW), Websol, Emmvee, plus Reliance's integrated entry.

risk.title: Wafers & polysilicon
risk.text: ~100% polysilicon and >90% wafer import; China curbs equipment and wafer technology exports. India wafer capacity ~2 GW. Resilience: years / structural.

opp.title: ALMM-III (1-Jun-2028) + polysilicon VGF
opp.text: First-mover scarcity premium — Waaree (10 GW ingot-wafer Nagpur), Tata Power (10 GW plan), Reliance, Indosol; a polysilicon VGF of ₹7,000–8,000 cr (target 35–40 GW) is under consideration.

risk.title: Cell-line machinery
risk.text: >90% of cell-line capex is foreign; turnkey lines supplied mainly by Chinese OEMs now under export pressure. Resilience: years.

opp.title: Domestic equipment & consumables
opp.text: An unlisted white space — screen printers, PECVD, pastes, ribbon, screens.

risk.title: Solar glass & ancillaries
risk.text: ~70% of glass demand imported; domestic ~2,600 TPD vs ~11,000 TPD demand; anti-dumping duties on China/Vietnam and CVD on Malaysia glass; encapsulant, backsheet and frames largely imported.

opp.title: Localisation wave
opp.text: Borosil expansion to 1,600 TPD (₹1,100 cr, Mar-2027); Vishakha Renewables DRHP (₹1,250 cr, Adani-backed) for glass/frames/encapsulant/backsheet.

risk.title: Inverters
risk.text: Chinese suppliers (Sungrow ~26%, Sineng, TBEA, Hopewind) dominate; no Indian pure-play listed. Data-sovereignty and BIS/BEE norms tightening.

opp.title: Domestic power electronics
opp.text: Waaree Power (4.15 GW string inverters, Oct-2026); a listed entry point remains the gap.

risk.title: Export-market trade exposure
risk.text: US imposed final CVD ~126.09% and AD ~123.04% on Indian cells/modules in 2026 (final ITC injury vote now 14-Oct-2026; AD/CVD orders due 2-Nov-2026); China filed a WTO challenge to India's tariff regime and PLI in May 2026. Resilience: years / structural.

opp.title: China+1 / non-Chinese supply
opp.text: US and EU buyers seeking non-Chinese wafers and modules; Indian upstream (wafer/poly) could export trade-compliant material — Indosol is targeting US cell lines.

risk.title: Skilled manpower
risk.text: Cell and wafer process know-how is scarce; capacity can be bought, process engineers cannot.

opp.title: Training + JV route
opp.text: Slowest to fix, but qualification-gated roles carry durable scarcity value. Deepest hidden import dependency: the turnkey cell-line and polysilicon/wafer equipment — and the technology licence behind it. China added solar manufacturing equipment and wafer technology to its export-control catalogue (from 2023) and, per Reuters (Apr-2026) and industry reporting (Jul-2026), is restricting equipment sales and technical support to India — the real reason domestic cell plants ramp slower than policy expects.

sections.title: Digest — at a glance
sections.note: short summary; full detail below

items.h: Snapshot The steam turbine proper — the rotating machine that converts steam to shaft power. India builds supercritical sets at 660/700/800 MW through BHEL (46 SC steam generators / 39 SC turbine-generators contracted, the highest in India) and via licensed / JV lines (Toshiba JSW, L&T-MHI); the AUSC target is 310 bar / 710°C using Alloy 617(M) rotors. The live cycle is the supercritical / ultra-supercritical thermal build-out plus the 700 MWe PHWR fleet. Process & equipment
items: CrMoV and 9–12% Cr rotor forgings, Ni-superalloy hot-stage blades, and precision machining of the turbine proper; large rotor forgings are the gating input.
BHEL's HEEP (Haridwar) still tenders imported HP rotor forgings — a tender for “Forging for HP Rotor without weld overlay (rough machined)” opened 24-Mar-2026.

Large rotor forgings are imported — NTPC's approved HP/IP/LP shaft-forging vendors are all foreign (JCFC, Saarschmiede, JSW Pacific, Schmiedewerke Gröditz, Buderus, Creusot, Kobe, Energomash, Doosan, AST). Resilience: years.
AUSC superalloy (Alloy 617(M)) is not yet commercial; the 800 MW demo still awaits final approval and dissimilar-metal-weld rotors are unproven at scale. Resilience: years.
Hot-stage blading is a Ni-superalloy item; the rest of the blading is domestic. Resilience: months–years.
Heavy fabrication machinery (ultra-heavy press, heavy CNC, balancing / overspeed rigs, heat-treatment furnaces) is foreign-built. Resilience: months–years.
BHEL NSE: BHEL — the dominant utility turbine maker and the sole Indian nuclear-steam-turbine supplier; outstanding order book ₹2,57,571 cr (Sep-2026).
Toshiba JSW Power Systems JSW Energy, NSE: JSWENERGY, ~20.7% associate — Chennai plant manufacturing 500–1,000 MW supercritical / USC steam turbine-generators.
L&T-MHI (LMTG) NSE: LT — Hazira plant (4,000 MW/yr) building 500–1,000 MW supercritical / USC turbine-generators under one roof.
Triveni Turbine NSE: TRITURBINE — industrial STs to 100 MW; FY26 revenue ₹2,181 cr; aftermarket 38% of order booking.
Siemens Energy India NSE: ENRIN — Vadodara plant; industrial STs; in-house rotor and blade manufacturing.

India steam turbine market (scope: utility + industrial steam turbines, India): ~$3.33 bn (2022) → ~$4.38 bn (2030) , headline CAGR ~3.5% [CALCULATED] from [REPORTED-T3, Grand View Research]. Value (nominal); volume [UNAVAILABLE].

[CONFLICTING DATA] on India steam-turbine size: IMARC ~$0.97 bn (2025, 4.15% CAGR to 2034), TechSci ~$0.83 bn (2025, 7.61% CAGR to 2031), Arizton ~$1.57 bn (2024) — the spread is scope-driven (utility vs industrial; equipment vs services).

Volume driver: India had 47,545 MW of thermal capacity under construction at 30-Jun-2026 , of which 44,020 MW is supercritical and 34,500 MW ultra-supercritical (~78%); 120 SC/USC units (83,710 MW) already commissioned [REPORTED-T1, CEA].

Growth is new-build-led (supercritical / USC thermal + PHWR fleet + SMR optionality); aftermarket is the steadier pool. Value growth is unit-count and mix (USC uprating) driven, not price [INFERENCE].
AUSC 800 MW demo still awaiting final Government approval (VGF ~₹6,000 cr mooted; Korba at ~₹15,000 cr considered) — no progress since the Mar-2025 PIB note. [LIVE]
BHEL Q2 FY27 (14-Oct-2026): revenue ₹9,300 cr (+23.8%), PAT ₹810 cr standalone (+120%), outstanding OB ₹2,57,571 cr (+17.3% YoY); Q2 order inflow slowed to ~₹4,000 cr. [CYCLICAL]
BHEL board approved ₹500 cr for thermal + nuclear TG manufacturing at Haridwar HEEP (14-Oct-2026). [CYCLICAL]
L&T-MHI developing 700 MW / 220 MW nuclear turbine-generator technology under the Make-in-India BSR scheme; Toshiba JSW (JSW Energy) supplying 4×800 MW STGs for Salboni. [LIVE]
Large rotor forgings and heavy fabrication machinery have no qualified NSE/BSE exposure.

sections.title: Bottlenecks — Risk & Opportunity
sections.note: dual-readable: every risk is a substitution play

risk.title: Large rotor forgings are imported
risk.text: The HP/IP/LP rotor forging (CrMoV, 9–12% Cr and the Ni-based AUSC rotor) is sourced from abroad — NTPC’s approved shaft-forging vendors are all foreign (JCFC, Saarschmiede, JSW Pacific, Schmiedewerke Gröditz, Buderus, Creusot, Kobe, Energomash, Doosan, AST), and BHEL’s HEEP re-tendered an imported HP rotor forging (rough-machined) in Mar-2026. India’s own heavy-forging base is real but not yet a frontier substitute. Resilience: years.

opp.title: Scale the domestic rotor-forging chain
opp.text: LTSHF and Bharat Forge’s 16,000-t press plus MIDHANI’s superalloys are the platform; supercritical and fleet-mode demand justifies qualifying an indigenous large-rotor line.

risk.title: AUSC superalloy not yet commercial
risk.text: India’s AUSC programme (310 bar / 710°C / 720°C, Alloy 617(M) rotors, Alloy 625 castings, dissimilar-metal-welded rotors) has finished R&D but the 800 MW demo still awaits final Government approval; large Ni-alloy forgings are globally immature. Resilience: years.

opp.title: AUSC materials & dissimilar-weld rotors
opp.text: An 800 MW AUSC demo with indigenous Ni-alloy forging and dissimilar-metal-weld capability lifts efficiency and opens an export material market.

risk.title: Hot-stage blading is a superalloy item
risk.text: The highest-temperature blade rows need Ni-based superalloy, an emerging capability in India; the rest of the blading is domestic. Resilience: months–years.

opp.title: Blade superalloy qualification
opp.text: MIDHANI superalloy mill forms plus domestic blade shops could close the hot-stage blade gap.

risk.title: Heavy fabrication machinery imported
risk.text: The forging press, heavy multi-axis CNC, rotor-balancing and overspeed rigs and heat-treatment furnaces are foreign-built. Resilience: months–years.

opp.title: Heavy machine-tool localisation
opp.text: A domestic heavy-machine-tool and balancing-rig base would de-risk the whole turbine chain.

risk.title: Skilled trades
risk.text: Precision blading machinists, rotor-balancing and NDT engineers and turbine-commissioning engineers bind tighter than materials.

opp.title: Incumbent training moats
opp.text: BHEL, L&T and Siemens Energy India qualification pipelines are a durable barrier to entry. Deepest hidden dependency: India machines and assembles the turbine well, but the two highest-value inputs — the large rotor forging and the balancing/heavy-machining equipment — are imported. The fabrication is investable; the frontier material is not.

sections.title: Bottlenecks — Risk & Opportunity
sections.note: dual-readable: every risk is a substitution play

risk.title: Transformer core (CRGO electrical steel)
risk.text: ~90% imported (China / Japan / Korea / Russia). Annual consumption ~4.0–4.5 lakh t against ~40,000–50,000 t domestic output. DGTR opened an anti-dumping probe on 22-Jun-2026 (complainant: JSW-JFE Electrical Steel Nashik); GTRI warns duties could raise transformer cost without cutting dependence. CRGO is 25–30% of transformer cost.

opp.title: CRGO — localisation play
opp.text: JSW-JFE (Nashik) and SAIL (Bokaro) are the domestic route; PLI specialty-steel (Scheme 1.1) lowered the CRGO threshold to ₹3,000 cr / 50,000 t. No NSE/BSE pure-play — nearest listed proxy is JSW Steel. [DERIVED]

risk.title: EHV bushings
risk.text: A global bushing shortage has stretched transformer deliveries and stalled substation completion (APAR Q3 FY26 earnings call; management expects normalisation over ~6 months). Capacitor-graded bushings above 245 kV are predominantly imported (Trench, Modern/HSP).

opp.title: EHV bushings — localisation play
opp.text: CG Power has partial in-house capability; domestic qualification of 765 kV bushings is the substitution play. No listed pure-play. [DERIVED]

risk.title: OLTC / tap changers
risk.text: >80% of advanced vacuum OLTCs are imported; Reinhausen alone holds ~35–40% and the top five ~65%. EMR (Easun-MR JV), Amson and Trishul serve the domestic retrofit market; OLTC lead times now run past 24 months. No NSE/BSE pure-play.

opp.title: OLTC — localisation play
opp.text: Building the vacuum-interrupter supply chain and IEC 60214-1 grid-grade certification is the gap to close. No listed pure-play. [DERIVED]

risk.title: Numerical relays / IEDs & HVDC valve design
risk.text: Core IED technology is foreign (ABB / Hitachi / Siemens / GE / Schneider). HVDC thyristor/IGBT valves are made by BHEL (Bhopal converters, Bengaluru valves) but the design IP is licensed (Hitachi / Alstom / Siemens / GE); ~65–70% of power-semiconductor components are imported.

opp.title: Valve & IED design — localisation play
opp.text: Closing this runs through the device layer — domestic high-power MOSFET/IGBT/SiC fabs (e.g. the approved Odisha SiC fab) and indigenous IED design. Listed exposure is via MNC subsidiaries. [DERIVED]

risk.title: SF₆ / SF₆-free gas
risk.text: CEA now requires SF₆-free GIS for new substations above 220 kV (bids after 1-Jul-2026; approved gases g3 (3M) and AirPlus (ABB)). Green GIS costs 6–8× conventional and relies on imported components and gases; fluoronitrile (C4FN) is made in India by Laxmi Organic (~60 t/yr).

opp.title: SF₆-free gas — localisation play
opp.text: Hitachi Energy (EconiQ) and Siemens Energy (Blue) hold the listed positions; domestic fluoronitrile and gas-handling scale is the substitution play. [DERIVED]

risk.title: Qualified capacity & certified manpower
risk.text: Capacity at the top of the range is held by a short list of qualified names; a new entrant needs 2–3 years to become bid-eligible. Delivery timelines (Ministry of Power, Mar-2026): 220 kV 11–15 months, 400 kV ~15 months, 765 kV 20–24 months. 765 kV serial production is limited to 3–4 firms.

opp.title: Qualified capacity — expansion play
opp.text: Announced/under-construction transformer capacity is large (IEEMA/MOFSL: 375 GVA FY25 → 650 GVA FY27E; Hitachi ₹2,000 cr LPT plant FY28; Voltamp Unit-III; Indo Tech to 50,000 MVA). The binding constraint is certified winding/test manpower, which cannot be bought quickly. [DERIVED] Where value sits: transformer & switchgear OEMs (Hitachi Energy India, CG Power, GE Vernova T&D, Siemens Energy India, BHEL, Voltamp, TRIL, Indo Tech) and HVDC terminal consortia; then aftermarket service, retrofit and GIS upgrades. The GEC-III order cycle to FY33 broadens the pipeline.

nodes.name: Baseband SoC & Modem
nodes.fn: The application + modem SoC at the heart of every handset, dongle, router and radio — India imports essentially all of it.
nodes.near: Global: Qualcomm, MediaTek, Unisoc and Apple hold roughly 75-80% of India smartphone SoC value. Domestic design attempts — Saankhya Labs (Tejas sub), Signalchip and WiSig Networks — are all unlisted.

nodes.name: RF Transceiver / RFIC
nodes.fn: Converts baseband to and from radio frequency; sits between the modem and the RF front-end in handsets and radios.
nodes.near: Global: Qualcomm, Broadcom, Marvell, NXP. No NSE/BSE exposure.

nodes.name: DSP / Baseband Processing IP
nodes.fn: Vector DSP cores and accelerators (FFT, LDPC) that process baseband for radios and handsets.

companies.m: Owns Saankhya Labs (majority-owned, non-material unlisted sub); its SDR chipsets run an indigenous multi-core DSP architecture. [REPORTED]

nodes.name: RF Front-End Module (FEM)
nodes.fn: Integrated PA + LNA + filter + switch block between antenna and transceiver; a rising share of handset and radio BOM.
nodes.near: Context (unlisted): A 20-company Indian fabless RF cohort includes Axiro, FermionIC, AGNIT, MMRFIC, Saankhya, WiSig and Silizium Circuits.

companies.m: Unlisted subsidiary Axiro Semiconductor designs RF and mmWave front-end and GaN solutions; IP now held in India. A minor segment of the listed entity. [REPORTED + INFERENCE]

nodes.name: Power Amplifier (GaAs / GaN)
nodes.fn: Boosts the transmit signal; compound-semiconductor (GaAs/GaN) devices dominate, especially for 5G massive-MIMO radios.

companies.m: Via unlisted Axiro — GaN-based RF and microwave amplifier and phased-array solutions for 5G/6G and satcom. Minor segment. [REPORTED + INFERENCE]

nodes.name: Low-Noise Amplifier (LNA)
nodes.fn: Amplifies weak received signals with minimal added noise; the first active stage after the antenna.
nodes.near: Silizium Circuits (unlisted) completed a GaAs 5G LNA / front-end design funded by DoT DCIS, DLI, C2S-Samridh and TTDF; fabrication and packaging were done abroad. Axiro (CG Power sub) also plays here.

nodes.name: RF Filter (SAW / BAW)
nodes.fn: Selects the wanted band and rejects interference; acoustic-wave filters are a high-value, IP-heavy node.
nodes.near: Global: Broadcom (BAW), Qorvo, Murata, Skyworks. No NSE/BSE pure-play.

nodes.name: Compound-Semiconductor Substrate (GaAs / GaN)
nodes.fn: The wafer material under every RF and power device; India has no compound-semiconductor substrate line.
nodes.near: GaAs/GaN substrates are largely imported (IQE, Sumitomo, AXT). No NSE/BSE substrate maker.

nodes.name: OSAT / Advanced Packaging
nodes.fn: Assembly, test, marking and packaging of the die into a usable chip — historically done almost entirely abroad, now building domestically.
nodes.near: Context: five of twelve ISM plants are in commercial production (Micron, Kaynes, CG Semi, CDIL, Suchi) — all back-end ATMP/OSAT.

companies.m: India's oldest IC assembly & test house (BSE-listed since 1988); wafer sort, assembly, test and turnkey services. [REPORTED]

Wholly-owned Kaynes Semicon runs the Sanand OSAT, in commercial production since 31-Mar-2026; shipped India's first commercially packaged multi-chip module (Oct 2025). A minor segment of the listed entity. [REPORTED + INFERENCE]
CG Semi (CG–Renesas–Stars JV, Sanand) began commercial chip packaging on 4-Jul-2026. A minor segment of the listed entity. [REPORTED + INFERENCE]

nodes.name: Test, Marking & Certification
nodes.fn: Wafer sort, final test, reliability and band certification — the last gate before a chipset ships.

companies.m: Turnkey wafer sort, assembly, final test, reliability testing and product characterisation. [REPORTED]
Kaynes Semicon performs assembly, test, marking and packaging at Sanand. [REPORTED]

nodes.name: EDA Tools, IP & Design Services
nodes.fn: Design tools and reusable IP cores gate every chip; India supplies design services but owns little of the tool and core-IP layer.
nodes.near: Context (T1): DLI has 24 approved projects, 25 tape-outs and 140+ reusable IP cores; ChipIN gives ~1 lakh engineers EDA-tool access.

companies.m: Semiconductor and system design services — SoC design, semiconductor IP and turnkey ASIC. [REPORTED]

nodes.name: Base-Station & RAN Silicon
nodes.fn: Baseband and radio silicon inside 5G RUs / BBUs — India assembles and increasingly designs RAN, but buys much of the silicon.
nodes.near: Context (unlisted): WiSig Networks opened commercial orders for a made-in-India O-RAN 32TR Massive-MIMO radio (IMC 2026; volume 2027); Signalchip designs 5G/4G base-station SoCs.

companies.m: Supplies an indigenous 4G/5G RAN (BSNL ~100,000 sites) with in-house baseband/radio and Saankhya chipsets. [REPORTED]
Jio built an about 80% indigenous 5G radio/core stack; the underlying silicon is sourced from NXP / Intel / Qualcomm. [REPORTED + INFERENCE]

sections.title: Digest — at a glance
sections.note: A short summary. Structure and inputs live on the tree; process, value pools and watch items are summarised here.

items.h: Snapshot Telecom chipsets — baseband SoCs, RF transceivers and the RF front-end modules inside every handset, router and radio — are the highest-value node in the telecom stack and the one India imports almost entirely. India designs some of this silicon (Saankhya, Signalchip, WiSig, Silizium) and now packages chips at scale, but it neither fabs the dies nor owns the design toolchain. Scope: India, NSE/BSE. Re-analysed 2026-10-25 (delta pass over the 2026-10-08 entry). Process & equipment
items: Design (EDA/IP) → wafer fab (still absent in India; Dholera due 2028) → OSAT assembly, test and packaging — the only reachable domestic layers today.

Key machinery: EDA tool grid, mask/MPW prototyping, wafer sort and final-test, wire-bond and flip-chip bonders, burn-in — largely imported; the first Indian OSAT lines are now running at Sanand, Surat and Mohali.
RF front-end needs compound-semiconductor (GaAs/GaN) epitaxy and SAW/BAW filter lines — none in India yet.
Baseband / modem SoC chokehold — Qualcomm, MediaTek and Unisoc hold ~75–80% of India smartphone SoC value. Resilience: YEARS–STRUCTURAL.
RF front-end & compound semiconductors — no GaAs/GaN substrate, epitaxy or SAW/BAW line. Resilience: YEARS.
No commercial fab — Dholera (28–110 nm) commissions 2028; every Indian-designed chip is fabbed abroad. Resilience: YEARS.
EDA tools and core IP — foreign duopoly (Synopsys/Cadence/Siemens) plus Arm. Resilience: STRUCTURAL.
Design-to-revenue gap — 24 DLI projects, 25 tape-outs, but almost no commercial silicon revenue yet; sovereign demand is thin.
Chip design is the main value driver — up to ~50% of value-add and 20–50% of BOM cost — and India’s listed exposure is still thin.
Value sits in the baseband SoC, the RF FEM and the RF filter, all imported; India captures design services, OSAT packaging and RAN system integration.
The localisation prize is the RF front-end (compound semi) and OSAT/packaging — both now the focus of Semicon 2.0.
OSAT costs in India run ~20–30% below peers — a genuine cost edge in the one layer India can scale fastest.

India semiconductor market US$62 bn (2026) → US$155 bn (2031) , ~20% CAGR (value, nominal) [REPORTED-T3, Kotak MF]. A second scope: ~US$64 bn (2026) → US$200 bn (2035) [REPORTED-T3, EY-IESA]. Scopes shown, not averaged.
Telecom is the second-largest end-segment of that demand after mobile: ~US$13.2 bn by FY30 [REPORTED-T3, IDTA].

Volume/import read: 90–95% of India’s semiconductor consumption is imported; imports were US$30.3 bn in FY25 , a 23% CAGR from FY17 [REPORTED-T3]. OSAT/ATMP capacity 15 mn chips/day (CY26) → 48 mn/day (CY28) [REPORTED-T3].
Growth is demand- and policy-led, not price-led; the memory-price squeeze cut India smartphone shipments −20% YoY in Q3 2026 (a decade low), so unit volumes and market value are moving differently.
Semicon 2.0 (₹1,27,500 cr) notified Aug-2026 — design IP must be co-owned by a state agency and stay in India. [LIVE]
IMC 2026 : government targets indigenous alternatives for 10–20 critical imported network technologies, chipsets included; 136 TTDF R&D projects (~₹500 cr). [LIVE]
Tata–PSMC Dholera fab on track for first wafer in 2028; Tata Jagiroad OSAT pilot output reported 3-Oct-2026. [LIVE]
Kaynes and CG Semi Sanand OSAT lines in commercial production; WiSig opened commercial orders for a made-in-India O-RAN 32TR Massive-MIMO radio (volume 2027). [LIVE]

No NSE/BSE pure-play across baseband, RFIC, FEM, filters, substrates, fab or EDA. Nearest listed adjacents: OSAT/packaging (SPEL, Kaynes, CG Power), design services (MosChip) and RAN systems (Tejas, Reliance/Jio).

sections.title: Bottlenecks — Risk & Opportunity
sections.note: dual-readable: every risk is a substitution play

risk.title: Baseband / modem chokehold
risk.text: Qualcomm, MediaTek and Unisoc supply over 80% of India’s smartphone SoCs (MediaTek ~45% of units in Q3 2026, Qualcomm dominant in premium); design-in is locked by IP, reference designs and band certification.

opp.title: Policy-funded design
opp.text: Saankhya’s 5G SoC (DLI-approved), Signalchip’s 5G/4G base-station SoCs, WiSig’s NB-IoT SoC and the TTDF Chipset Mission’s 5G modem + RF brief are the first serious domestic attempts; Semicon 2.0 puts design first among six pillars.

risk.title: RF front-end & compound semiconductors
risk.text: GaAs/GaN substrates, SAW/BAW filters and power amplifiers are largely imported; India has no substrate, epitaxy or filter line, so the highest-value block of the radio BOM leaks abroad.

opp.title: First domestic RF designs
opp.text: Silizium Circuits’ GaAs LEO/GNSS and 5G LNA/FEM designs (DCIS + DLI + TTDF funded), Axiro’s GaN lines and a 20-company Indian fabless RF cohort point at the RF front-end as the most reachable import-substitution prize.

risk.title: Packaging was absent
risk.text: India historically had no advanced packaging; chip assembly and test were done entirely offshore, adding cost and lead time and capping domestic value-add.

opp.title: OSAT build-out is now real
opp.text: Five of twelve ISM plants are in commercial production — Micron (Feb-2026), Kaynes Semicon (Mar-2026), CG Semi (Jul-2026), CDIL and Suchi (Sep-2026) — alongside incumbent SPEL. Indian OSAT costs run ~20–30% below peers.

risk.title: EDA & IP dependency
risk.text: Design flows, reusable IP cores and tools are foreign-controlled (Synopsys, Cadence, Siemens EDA, Arm), carrying export-control and pricing risk; India supplies design services but owns little of the tool and core-IP layer.

opp.title: Design-services depth → owned IP
opp.text: MosChip, Tata Elxsi and the design-services base, with ~20% of the world’s chip-design engineers, are what DLI (24 projects, 25 tape-outs, 140+ IP cores) and Semicon 2.0’s state-co-owned-IP rule aim to convert into owned silicon.

risk.title: Fab gap & thin sovereign demand
risk.text: There is no commercial fab in India yet — Dholera commissions only in 2028 — and domestic anchor demand is weak, pushing Tata, Kaynes and CG Semi to chase overseas customers instead.

opp.title: Mature-node fab and a widening ecosystem
opp.text: Tata–PSMC Dholera (28–110 nm, 50k wafers/month) targets telecom-relevant mature nodes from 2028; Applied Materials (US$5 bn), Lam Research (~₹10,000 cr), Fujifilm, JSR, Sumitomo and INOX are building the equipment/materials layer India lacked. Deepest hidden import dependency: the design toolchain, the foundry and the compound-semiconductor substrate. Even a chip fully designed in India is still built on foreign EDA, fabbed on a foreign wafer, and — until the Sanand/Surat/Mohali OSAT lines, only recently — packaged abroad.

digest.h: Snapshot Telecom chipsets — baseband SoCs, RF transceivers and the RF front-end modules inside every handset, router and radio — are the highest-value node in the telecom stack and the one India imports almost entirely. India designs some of this silicon (Saankhya, Signalchip, WiSig, Silizium) and now packages chips at scale, but it neither fabs the dies nor owns the design toolchain. Scope: India, NSE/BSE. Re-analysed 2026-10-25 (delta pass over the 2026-10-08 entry). Process & equipment
items: Design (EDA/IP) → wafer fab (still absent in India; Dholera due 2028) → OSAT assembly, test and packaging — the only reachable domestic layers today.

Key machinery: EDA tool grid, mask/MPW prototyping, wafer sort and final-test, wire-bond and flip-chip bonders, burn-in — largely imported; the first Indian OSAT lines are now running at Sanand, Surat and Mohali.
RF front-end needs compound-semiconductor (GaAs/GaN) epitaxy and SAW/BAW filter lines — none in India yet.
Baseband / modem SoC chokehold — Qualcomm, MediaTek and Unisoc hold ~75–80% of India smartphone SoC value. Resilience: YEARS–STRUCTURAL.
RF front-end & compound semiconductors — no GaAs/GaN substrate, epitaxy or SAW/BAW line. Resilience: YEARS.
No commercial fab — Dholera (28–110 nm) commissions 2028; every Indian-designed chip is fabbed abroad. Resilience: YEARS.
EDA tools and core IP — foreign duopoly (Synopsys/Cadence/Siemens) plus Arm. Resilience: STRUCTURAL.
Design-to-revenue gap — 24 DLI projects, 25 tape-outs, but almost no commercial silicon revenue yet; sovereign demand is thin.
Chip design is the main value driver — up to ~50% of value-add and 20–50% of BOM cost — and India’s listed exposure is still thin.
Value sits in the baseband SoC, the RF FEM and the RF filter, all imported; India captures design services, OSAT packaging and RAN system integration.
The localisation prize is the RF front-end (compound semi) and OSAT/packaging — both now the focus of Semicon 2.0.
OSAT costs in India run ~20–30% below peers — a genuine cost edge in the one layer India can scale fastest.

India semiconductor market US$62 bn (2026) → US$155 bn (2031) , ~20% CAGR (value, nominal) [REPORTED-T3, Kotak MF]. A second scope: ~US$64 bn (2026) → US$200 bn (2035) [REPORTED-T3, EY-IESA]. Scopes shown, not averaged.
Telecom is the second-largest end-segment of that demand after mobile: ~US$13.2 bn by FY30 [REPORTED-T3, IDTA].

Volume/import read: 90–95% of India’s semiconductor consumption is imported; imports were US$30.3 bn in FY25 , a 23% CAGR from FY17 [REPORTED-T3]. OSAT/ATMP capacity 15 mn chips/day (CY26) → 48 mn/day (CY28) [REPORTED-T3].
Growth is demand- and policy-led, not price-led; the memory-price squeeze cut India smartphone shipments −20% YoY in Q3 2026 (a decade low), so unit volumes and market value are moving differently.
Semicon 2.0 (₹1,27,500 cr) notified Aug-2026 — design IP must be co-owned by a state agency and stay in India. [LIVE]
IMC 2026 : government targets indigenous alternatives for 10–20 critical imported network technologies, chipsets included; 136 TTDF R&D projects (~₹500 cr). [LIVE]
Tata–PSMC Dholera fab on track for first wafer in 2028; Tata Jagiroad OSAT pilot output reported 3-Oct-2026. [LIVE]
Kaynes and CG Semi Sanand OSAT lines in commercial production; WiSig opened commercial orders for a made-in-India O-RAN 32TR Massive-MIMO radio (volume 2027). [LIVE]

No NSE/BSE pure-play across baseband, RFIC, FEM, filters, substrates, fab or EDA. Nearest listed adjacents: OSAT/packaging (SPEL, Kaynes, CG Power), design services (MosChip) and RAN systems (Tejas, Reliance/Jio).

sections.title: Digest — at a glance
sections.note: short summary; full detail below

items.h: Snapshot India’s telecom network-infrastructure stack — the equipment, fibre, silicon, towers and services behind the world’s second-largest subscriber base (1,348 mn telephone subscribers, Jun-2026). The demand side is monetising (industry ARPU ₹187.12; a 12–15% tariff hike expected within months), while the supply side stays import-heavy: roughly 60% import substitution at product level, but >80% of critical components sourced from China. Scope: India, NSE/BSE. Process & equipment
items: Equipment is assembled in India (SMT/pick-and-place, RF test) but built around imported chipsets, RF front-ends and high-speed optics.
Optical fibre runs preform → draw → cable; draw towers, preform lathes (MCVD/OVD/VAD) and cabling lines are the key machinery — all being expanded now (HFCL, Finolex, STL).
Towers are erected on site; site power (SMPS, batteries, DG, solar) is the largest operating cost, with ~46,000 solarised sites at Indus.
Fibre preform: ~65–75% imported (Japan/China/Korea); only STL is fully backward-integrated, HFCL and Finolex are building. Resilience: years (shortening).
Telecom chipsets / baseband + RF: almost fully imported (~$4–5 bn/yr); no listed pure-play. Resilience: structural.
RAN BOM only ~4% localised; optical transceivers ~$0.6 bn/yr imported (USA/Taiwan/China).
High-end DCS/optics silicon and MTCTE/trusted-source (NSCS) gating; test gear imported.
Preform captures ~70% of the optical-fibre chain’s profit — largely leaked to imports, now being pulled home by HFCL (§1,800 cr), Finolex and STL.
Indian RAN/OFC assembly value is thin and competitive; equipment margin sits upstream in silicon and photonics.
Towers and services are domestic and annuity-like (Indus, Airtel, Jio) — value stays home.
Localisation opportunity: preform & specialty fibre (HFCL/Finolex/STL), optical transceivers (Dixon–Gemtek, GX Quantum Photonics), RF front-end design (fabless + Kaynes OSAT).

India telecom & network equipment (TANE), scope: telecom/network equipment, India: $25 bn (FY25) → $50 bn (FY32) , CAGR ~10% [REPORTED-T3, NITI Aayog / KPMG, Oct-2026]. Value (nominal); volume [UNAVAILABLE]. Growth led by physical build-out (5G densification, fibre/data-centre), so the volume mix is positive.

Mobile network traffic (scope: India mobile traffic): ~17% CAGR 2025→2030 vs operator revenue ~2.7% [REPORTED-T3, KPMG]. Value (nominal) vs volume — the traffic/revenue gap is the monetisation problem.
Last-year: telecom gross revenue ₹4,04,067 cr FY26 (+8.59%) ; AGR ₹3,34,659 cr (+10.44%) [REPORTED-T1, TRAI Yearly Indicators 2025-26].
[CONFLICTING DATA] on the equipment-market CAGR (different scopes): ~10% [NITI Aayog/KPMG], 10.41% [MarketsandData, $22.5 bn FY24→$49.7 bn FY32], 3.66% [IMARC, $25.4 bn 2025→$35.5 bn 2034].

Telecom PLI 2.0 — successor to the ₹12,195 cr scheme (ends 31-Mar-2027) at a proposed ₹6,000–7,000 cr, focused on components and design-led manufacturing; DoT’s proposal is with the Finance Ministry and Cabinet approval is still pending (MoS Communications, 08-Oct-2026), with Q1 FY28 the launch target and a TTDF 2.0 announced alongside. [LIVE]
Jio Platforms IPO — RHP 14-Oct-2026, price band ₹1,065–1,119, issue ₹30,213 cr, opens 21-Oct, lists 28-Oct; capex cycle peaking. [LIVE]
Telecom Manufacturing Zone (TMZ) Gwalior — Asia’s first; ~₹5,500 cr, 24 companies, 170 acres; DoT proposed ~₹500 cr common testing lab. [CYCLICAL]

Anti-dumping: India’s ADD on single-mode fibre from China/Indonesia/Korea (5 yrs from Aug-2023) stays; China extended its own ADD on Indian SMOF for 5 yrs from 14-Aug-2026 — a new export barrier. [LIVE]

No listed pure-play: telecom chipsets (baseband/RF) and test & measurement/MTCTE certification — nearest are domestic fabless + Kaynes OSAT, and foreign T&M vendors. High-speed optical DSPs remain an import-only pool.

sections.title: Bottlenecks — Risk & Opportunity
sections.note: dual-readable: every risk is a substitution play

risk.title: Optical fibre preform
risk.text: ~65–75% imported (Japan, China, Korea); only STL is fully backward-integrated. Preform holds ~70% of the profit pool, and only 6–10 companies worldwide make it. Global fibre is in shortage as AI data centres absorb supply, lifting fibre/preform prices 20–25%. Resilience: years (shortening).

opp.title: Second & third integrated player
opp.text: HFCL has approved a ~₹1,800 cr preform/fibre/cable programme (600 MT preform, 43.1 mn fkm fibre, 62 mn fkm cable by 2028); Finolex commissioned 100 MT (to 200 MT) preform and is doubling fibre/OFC to 8 mn fkm; STL remains fully integrated. Anti-dumping duty on single-mode fibre protects the domestic industry.

risk.title: Telecom chipsets — baseband & RF
risk.text: Almost fully imported; no listed pure-play in India. NITI Aayog reports >80% of critical components (4G/5G antennas, signal processors) come from China. The RF front-end is one of the highest-value parts of a 5G radio. Resilience: structural.

opp.title: Fabless design + OSAT
opp.text: Domestic fabless (Saankhya Labs/Tejas, Signalchip, WiSig, Aheesa) under DLI / C2S / TTDF (23 design projects approved by MeitY), plus commercial OSAT at Kaynes Semicon (Sanand, from Mar-2026) — the 5G-modem-and-RF chipset mission is the open prize.

risk.title: RAN localisation
risk.text: 4G/5G RAN BOM only ~4% localised; switches 3%, GPON ONT 12%; average domestic value addition ~27.8%. Most of the radio is imported even when “made in India”. Resilience: months–years.

opp.title: PLI 2.0 & Telecom Manufacturing Zone
opp.text: A proposed ₹6,000–7,000 cr PLI 2.0 targets components and design-led manufacturing; the Gwalior TMZ (~₹5,500 cr, 24 firms, 170 acres) and the BSNL indigenous stack prove the capability and create a component cluster.

risk.title: Optical transceivers
risk.text: ~$0.6 bn/yr imported (USA ~50%, Taiwan ~25%, China ~15%); high-speed 400G/800G optics concentrated abroad as data-centre demand surges. Resilience: months.

opp.title: Module integration → photonics
opp.text: Dixon–Gemtek JV (60:40) for SFP/BOSA modules, GX Quantum Photonics’ ~₹500 cr Bhiwadi photonics fab (production from late-2026) and CloudPhotonix (Noida, up to 800G) are building India’s first transceiver base — the AI data-centre interconnect wave is a large, fast-growing domestic opportunity.

risk.title: Tower energy & certification
risk.text: Diesel and battery replacement are the tower cost battleground (battery supplies were disrupted by geopolitics in FY27 Q1); every product is gated by MTCTE & trusted-source (NSCS) approval — test gear is imported. Resilience: months.

opp.title: Solar + lithium + ESCo
opp.text: Indus has ~46,000 solarised sites and cut diesel 13% YoY (Q1 FY27); Airtel solarised ~27,000 sites in two years. The energy-management, lithium-battery and testing-lab (§500 cr common testing lab proposed at TMZ) cycles are durable recurring markets. Deepest hidden import dependency: the RF front-end silicon and high-speed optical DSPs inside every radio, router and transport box — and, one layer up, the specialty fibre grades, germanium dopant and precision optical sub-assemblies (laser dies, BOSA/TOSA/ROSA) that India still cannot make at scale.

Preform captures ~70% of the optical-fibre chain’s profit — largely leaked to imports, now being pulled home by HFCL (§1,800 cr), Finolex and STL.
Indian RAN/OFC assembly value is thin and competitive; equipment margin sits upstream in silicon and photonics.
Towers and services are domestic and annuity-like (Indus, Airtel, Jio) — value stays home.
Localisation opportunity: preform & specialty fibre (HFCL/Finolex/STL), optical transceivers (Dixon–Gemtek, GX Quantum Photonics), RF front-end design (fabless + Kaynes OSAT).

India telecom & network equipment (TANE), scope: telecom/network equipment, India: $25 bn (FY25) → $50 bn (FY32) , CAGR ~10% [REPORTED-T3, NITI Aayog / KPMG, Oct-2026]. Value (nominal); volume [UNAVAILABLE]. Growth led by physical build-out (5G densification, fibre/data-centre), so the volume mix is positive.

Mobile network traffic (scope: India mobile traffic): ~17% CAGR 2025→2030 vs operator revenue ~2.7% [REPORTED-T3, KPMG]. Value (nominal) vs volume — the traffic/revenue gap is the monetisation problem.
Last-year: telecom gross revenue ₹4,04,067 cr FY26 (+8.59%) ; AGR ₹3,34,659 cr (+10.44%) [REPORTED-T1, TRAI Yearly Indicators 2025-26].
[CONFLICTING DATA] on the equipment-market CAGR (different scopes): ~10% [NITI Aayog/KPMG], 10.41% [MarketsandData, $22.5 bn FY24→$49.7 bn FY32], 3.66% [IMARC, $25.4 bn 2025→$35.5 bn 2034].

Telecom PLI 2.0 — successor to the ₹12,195 cr scheme (ends 31-Mar-2027) at a proposed ₹6,000–7,000 cr, focused on components and design-led manufacturing; DoT’s proposal is with the Finance Ministry and Cabinet approval is still pending (MoS Communications, 08-Oct-2026), with Q1 FY28 the launch target and a TTDF 2.0 announced alongside. [LIVE]
Jio Platforms IPO — RHP 14-Oct-2026, price band ₹1,065–1,119, issue ₹30,213 cr, opens 21-Oct, lists 28-Oct; capex cycle peaking. [LIVE]
Telecom Manufacturing Zone (TMZ) Gwalior — Asia’s first; ~₹5,500 cr, 24 companies, 170 acres; DoT proposed ~₹500 cr common testing lab. [CYCLICAL]

Anti-dumping: India’s ADD on single-mode fibre from China/Indonesia/Korea (5 yrs from Aug-2023) stays; China extended its own ADD on Indian SMOF for 5 yrs from 14-Aug-2026 — a new export barrier. [LIVE]

No listed pure-play: telecom chipsets (baseband/RF) and test & measurement/MTCTE certification — nearest are domestic fabless + Kaynes OSAT, and foreign T&M vendors. High-speed optical DSPs remain an import-only pool.

Airtel Business — connectivity, cloud, security, IoT and CPaaS for enterprises [REPORTED]
Jio Business — enterprise connectivity and cloud within the conglomerate [INFERENCE]

Airtel Xstream AirFiber — second-largest 5G-FWA base [REPORTED]

M2M share ~17% (Dec-2025) [REPORTED]

Global CPaaS platform (A2P SMS, WhatsApp, RCS); now part of the Proximus Group [REPORTED]

sections.title: Bottlenecks — Risk & Opportunity
sections.note: dual-readable: every risk is a substitution play

risk.title: Spectrum cost & auction demand
risk.text: Reserve prices stay high while competition thins — the 2024 auction sold only ~1.3% of the spectrum on offer (₹11,341 cr). Resilience: policy-led, multi-year.

opp.title: Cheaper capacity ahead
opp.text: TRAI has proposed opening auctions to ISPs and M2M providers and adding 37–40 GHz (mmWave) at ~14% below 26 GHz pricing — a lower cost of raw capacity.

risk.title: RAN & core import dependence
risk.text: India’s 5G networks run predominantly on Nokia and Ericsson gear; domestic RAN is only now emerging. Resilience: slow.

opp.title: India-made network gear
opp.text: Tejas Networks, ITI and HFCL scale local RAN / optical under PLI — a protected import-substitution runway.

risk.title: ARPU vs data explosion
risk.text: ARPU is ₹194.57 while the average subscriber consumes 25.70 GB/month and revenue per GB is ₹7.87 — heavy data growth without commensurate pricing. Resilience: structural.

opp.title: Tariff repair & mix
opp.text: Industry tariff increases, 5G monetisation and a shift toward enterprise / FWA can lift ARPU without losing volume.

risk.title: Vodafone Idea viability
risk.text: Vi keeps losing subscribers (199.59 mn, net −4.0 mn in Dec-2025) and the Government of India is its largest shareholder (~23%) after AGR dues. Resilience: uncertain.

opp.title: Restart benefits the chain
opp.text: Any AGR relief or fresh capex by Vi flows straight to towers (Indus captures 70%+ of Vi rollouts) and equipment vendors.

risk.title: Tower tenancy consolidation
risk.text: Indus’ tenancy ratio has fallen to 1.65x and industry tower additions are moderating as operator rollouts mature. Resilience: cyclical.

opp.title: 5G loading & sharing
opp.text: 5G loading (~35–40% of towers radiating 5G) and a Vi rollout restart support rental growth; Indus gains share from rival towercos.

risk.title: Revenue leakage at 5G scale
risk.text: 5G is ~40% of wireless data (29,094 PB) but ARPU uplift is thin; billing / assurance gaps leak value as services multiply. Resilience: manageable.

opp.title: AI-driven assurance & CPaaS
opp.text: Subex (RA / fraud) and Tanla / Route Mobile (CPaaS, anti-spam) monetise the complexity — software value rising with network value. Deepest hidden import dependency: the silicon inside the network — the 5G RAN, core and transport equipment that India’s operators buy is dominated by Nokia and Ericsson, and the semiconductors inside them are imported. Local RAN is the open prize.

industries.title: India Telecom Towers
meta: Derived from: Telecom → Telecom Towers & Passive Infrastructure

metrics.label: Indus revenue at risk
metrics.sub: Reliance Jio tenancy renewal, H2 FY27

nodes.name: TowerCo Operation, Sharing & Tenancy
nodes.fn: Owns, deploys and leases passive sites to multiple MNOs — the tenancy-ratio business that monetises every other BOM node. Revenue is rent per tenant plus an energy pass-through that currently runs at a loss.

companies.m: 270,480 macro towers and 440,153 co-locations across 22 circles at 30-Sep-2026; tenancy ratio 1.63; Q2 FY27 revenue ₹8,516 cr (+4.0% YoY), EBITDA margin 54.4%, PAT ₹1,793 cr (−2.5%); Crisil AAA; Bharti Airtel holds ~51.3% [REPORTED-T1]

~2.58 lakh sites and 315,000+ tenancies (Q1 FY27 presentation) — the largest tower group by site count; Q1 FY27 revenue ₹6,025 cr (flat YoY), PAT ₹375 cr (+66%), distribution ₹4.02/unit; converting to a public InvIT, draft offer document filed 6-Aug-2026 [REPORTED-T1]
companies.ev: Altius Q1 FY27 presentation · exchange filings

companies.m: Rajasthan and North-East circles; 25,704 network towers at Mar-2024, of which 5,092 owned and 19,782 leased; related-party ceiling for Indus transactions renewed at ₹2,000 cr/yr in Aug-2026 [REPORTED-T1]
companies.ev: Company annual report · shareholder notice FY27

companies.m: ~26,000 towers; financially stressed long-tail towerco — the residual distressed asset in the sector [REPORTED-T3]
Parent of Indus (51.3%); board approval to raise the stake by a further ~4.8%. Tower ownership itself is immaterial to consolidated revenue [REPORTED-T1]

nodes.name: Macro Tower Structure (Lattice & Monopole)
nodes.fn: The galvanised steel lattice tower or monopole itself — the load-bearing physical asset. Steel plus galvanising is the single largest material input per site, and fabrication was supply-constrained in Q1 FY27.
nodes.importDep: Largely domestic — steel and galvanising in India; gas supply for fabrication is externally exposed

companies.m: Galvanised steel structures ~65% of ₹1,511.9 cr FY26 revenue; telecom towers, monopoles and portable towers; order book ~₹2,500 cr; FY27 revenue target ~₹1,800 cr; Q2 FY27 revenue ₹427 cr (Q1 FY27 ₹295.5 cr); EMC merged Jul-2026 [REPORTED-T1/T2]

nodes.name: Foundation, Civil Works & Tower Erection
nodes.fn: RCC foundations, plinth, earthing and site civil works plus tower erection — executed by tower EPC contractors on a per-site basis.

companies.m: EPC segment ₹95.6 cr of ₹295.5 cr Q1 FY27 consolidated revenue; offers tower EPC and installation alongside manufacturing [REPORTED-T1]
Broad infrastructure / EPC capability applicable to telecom site civil works; towers a negligible slice of a ₹3.9 lakh cr order book [INFERENCE]

nodes.name: Site Power System (SMPS / DC Power Plant)
nodes.fn: Switch-mode rectifiers, DC distribution, controllers and AMF — converts grid/AC into the 48 V DC that runs the radio and charges the battery. Energy is both the largest opex line and a negative-margin pass-through.
nodes.importDep: Partial — rectifier modules and power semiconductors imported

companies.m: SMPS-based telecom power systems (EXTS range); historically ~70% of the BSNL/MTNL power-plant requirement; won over ₹140 cr of DC power-system orders for FY27 execution; also supplies BharatNet-3 racks via the HFCL consortium [REPORTED-T2]

nodes.name: Batteries (VRLA Lead-Acid & Li-ion)
nodes.fn: Backup energy at the site — VRLA lead-acid in legacy sites, lithium (LFP) in new deployments. The lead-acid to lithium pivot is the live substitution play, and cell supply was disrupted in Q1 FY27.

companies.m: Crossed 1 GWh cumulative lithium telecom deployment across ~50,000 sites; ~35% telecom battery share; Telangana lithium cell plant under construction — localising the cell, not just the pack [REPORTED-T2]
VRLA telecom ranges (NEPST / NMST 200–6000 Ah; GTB tubular gel) for BTS and tower companies; Li-ion cell programme via Exide Energy Solutions [REPORTED-T2]

nodes.name: Diesel Genset & Fuel Management
nodes.fn: Standby DG sets for grid-outage and off-grid sites, plus fuel logistics — the residual diesel dependence that operators are actively cutting through solarisation.

companies.m: DG sets 7.5–3750 kVA including CPCB IV+ compliant range; pan-India service network [REPORTED-T2]
Power-gen gensets; targeting ~₹19,000 cr operating revenue by FY30, with data-centre and infra demand driving growth [REPORTED-T2]

nodes.name: Solar & Green Energy (ESCo Model)
nodes.fn: Rooftop and ground solar, solar-hybrid DC systems and the Energy-Service-Company model that shifts energy capex to opex and cuts diesel burn.

companies.m: Rooftop and group-captive solar plus ESCo solutions; 1,900+ MW rooftop installed; green-energy solutions for telecom / commtech customers [REPORTED-T2]
Solar modules; group track record includes telecom and rooftop projects via Waaree Renewable Technologies (WAAREERTL) [REPORTED-T2]

nodes.name: Shelter & Outdoor Enclosure
nodes.fn: BTS shelters, battery shelters and IP55/IP65 outdoor cabinets that house power, radio and battery equipment.
nodes.near: Context (unlisted): Eterna Global Solutions, Akash Prefabs, BSMC Power Systems, Indo East Corporation. Enclosure bodies are fabricated locally; active cooling is specified separately by the OEM or operator.

nodes.name: Cooling / Thermal Management (DC Air-Cons)
nodes.fn: DC air-conditioners, heat exchangers and free-cooling units that keep shelters and cabinets within equipment temperature limits — a direct energy consumer at every site.
nodes.near: Context (unlisted): Advance Cooling Systems, FlexSol, BSMC Power Systems. Indoor-to-outdoor conversion and free-cooling retrofits cut AC load and therefore diesel.

nodes.name: In-Building Solutions / Small Cells / DAS
nodes.fn: Indoor coverage and densification for 5G — small cells, DAS and street-furniture deployments that supplement the macro layer. The July-2026 rules put complete IBS inside the DCIP authorisation.

companies.m: Made-in-India 5G indoor and outdoor small cells plus FWA CPE; in-building solutions; Qualcomm small-cell platform partnership [REPORTED-T2]
Crest Digitel (under Altius) is a leading indoor-coverage provider; Altius offers IBS and small-cell sites [REPORTED-T2]

nodes.name: Active Sharing & DCIP Layer (new, 2026 rules)
nodes.fn: The commercial layer opened by the Telecommunications (Authorisation for Telecommunication Network) Rules, 2026: a Digital Connectivity Infrastructure Provider may own and share specified active elements — RAN, complete in-building solutions, WLAN, last-mile transmission — alongside passive infrastructure. This is the towerco moving up the stack, from rent to hosting.
nodes.conc: Not yet formed — no reported revenue

companies.m: Holds IP-1 scope today; DCIP scope would let it lease active elements. No reported DCIP revenue — authorisation framework only, notified 20-Jul-2026 [INFERENCE]
IBS / DAS exposure through Crest Digitel is the closest existing proxy to active sharing; the DCIP authorisation is the route to operating complete IBS [INFERENCE]

nodes.name: Remote Monitoring, IoT & Energy Management
nodes.fn: Site controllers, NMS/SNMP telemetry and energy-management / tamper monitoring that drive uptime and opex. Increasingly bundled into the DC power system and into the towerco’s own NOC.
nodes.near: Context: controllers and NMS are embedded in DC power systems (e.g. Exicom EXTS, SNMP/Modbus); energy-management and AI-led site optimisation is run in-house at Indus and Altius.

nodes.name: Lean / Ultra-Lean Towers & Cell-on-Wheels
nodes.fn: Lightweight, rapid-deploy towers and COWs for capacity add-ons and temporary coverage — a growing part of the mix as 5G needs fewer but denser sites, and the cheapest route to a new tenancy.

companies.m: 14,037 lean co-locations at 30-Sep-2026 (+13 in the quarter); ~2,200 lean towers acquired from Bharti Airtel [REPORTED-T1]
Lean and ultra-lean towers, Cell-on-Wheels and camouflage towers in portfolio [REPORTED-T2]

Active sharing is the new pool: the July-2026 DCIP authorisation lets a towerco host RAN and complete IBS.

H2 FY27 — Jio tenancy renewal decision; up to 15% of Indus revenue.
Dec-2026 — Ambit expects a 15% tariff hike, the next capex trigger.
FY27 — Indus Africa rollouts in Nigeria, Uganda and Zambia.

sections.title: Bottlenecks — Risk & Opportunity
sections.note: dual-readable: every risk is a substitution play

risk.title: Contract renewal at the top of the book
risk.text: Up to 15% of Indus revenue rides on the Reliance Jio tenancy renewal, with ~5,000 exits already modelled in H2 FY27; Vodafone Idea is over 30% of revenue and its capex depends on the SBI-led $3.5 bn debt raise. [REPORTED-T2]

opp.title: Africa is the deliberate second leg
opp.text: Indus has approvals and anchor orders in Nigeria, Uganda and Zambia, with annual capex under 4% of EBITDA and debt funding; higher customers-per-tower (4.54k vs 1.06k in India) means faster payback. [REPORTED-T2]

risk.title: Tower fabrication is gas-exposed
risk.text: Tower manufacturing was hit at the start of Q1 FY27 by constrained gas supplies from West Asia, and battery supply was affected even after tower supply recovered. [REPORTED-T2]

opp.title: Domestic galvanising capacity
opp.text: Salasar runs one of the world’s larger galvanising baths, holds a ~₹2,500 cr order book and targets ₹1,800 cr FY27 revenue, with monopole capability up to 3 m diameter. [REPORTED-T2]

risk.title: Energy is the largest cost and a negative-margin pass-through
risk.text: The energy spread was −4.6% in Q1 FY27 and −4.8% in Q2 FY26; power and fuel exceeded energy reimbursement in every recent quarter. Ambit names power and water linkages, not utilisation, as the main towerco risk. [REPORTED-T2]

opp.title: Solarisation and ESCo
opp.text: Indus reached ~46,000 solar-access sites and cut diesel 13% YoY in Q1 FY27; an ESCo structure moves the capex off the towerco balance sheet. [REPORTED-T1]

risk.title: Battery chemistry transition
risk.text: The VRLA-to-LFP pivot moves the value from a domestic lead-acid duopoly to imported cells; cell supply was disrupted in Q1 FY27 and China’s material-export regime remains the exposure. [REPORTED-T2]

opp.title: Cell localisation, not pack assembly
opp.text: Amara Raja has crossed 1 GWh of lithium telecom deployment and is building a Telangana cell plant; Exide is scaling Li-ion through Exide Energy Solutions — the first domestic cell, not the first domestic pack, is the prize. [REPORTED-T2]

risk.title: Tenancy ratio and ARPT are both deflating
risk.text: The industry tenancy ratio fell to 1.42 in FY25 from 1.47 in FY23 as new sites came up single-tenant; Indus revenue per tower fell 2.0% YoY. Crisil sees only 1.46–1.48 by Mar-2028. [REPORTED-T2]

opp.title: 5G loading and densification
opp.text: 5G BTS reached 593,244 by end-Sep-2026 and 5G subscribers 463 mn; loading existing sites and small-cell densification add revenue at low incremental cost, and Vi’s ₹450 bn capex plan is the swing factor. [REPORTED-T1]

risk.title: Regulation now decides the business model
risk.text: The Network Authorisation Rules 2026 replaced IP-I with IP and created DCIP, but bar IRU-style asset transfers — a firmer posture that limits long-term financing structures for passive assets. [REPORTED-T1]

opp.title: A licence to move up the stack
opp.text: DCIP scope covers RAN, complete IBS, WLAN and last-mile transmission, so a towerco can lease active elements it was previously forbidden to own — the first genuine revenue-line extension since tower sharing itself. [REPORTED-T1] Deepest hidden dependency: not the steel and not the shelter — the LFP cell , the rectifier power semiconductor and the gas supply behind the galvanising line . India fabricates the tower, assembles the battery and builds the power plant; the three layers that decide cost, uptime and schedule all sit outside the country or outside the industry’s control.

sections.title: Digest — at a glance
sections.note: short summary; full detail below

items: The backhaul and core of India’s networks: DWDM/OTN, packet transport, IP/MPLS routers, Ethernet switches and the optics and silicon inside them.
India designs and builds the systems; the transceivers, ASICs and coherent DSPs inside them are imported. Scope: India, NSE/BSE.
SMT assembly of line cards and backplanes, shelf build, then optical alignment and traffic test — the same spine at Tejas, HFCL, ITI and the Flex-run Cisco and Ciena lines.
The gating asset is the test bench, not the placement machine; MTCTE/ITSAR lab capacity queues every launch.
Optical transceivers — 85–90% imported by value; no Indian laser-chip, TOSA/ROSA or DSP source. YEARS.
Switch/router and OTN silicon — US-designed, no carrier-grade Indian design house or fab. YEARS–STRUCTURAL.
PCBAs — ~80% imported, 15% BCD, Chapter 85 exemptions lapsed in Budget 2026. MONTHS.
BharatNet dependence — completes March 2027; private transport capex has not replaced it. CYCLICAL.
Value sits in the optics and silicon; India captures integration, software and a rising share of design.
Tejas won the router and OTN nodes outright and still lost ₹207 cr in Q2 FY27 — winning the box does not win the margin.
HFCL re-rated on fibre and DCI, not transport: ~64% of its ₹28,911 cr book is OFC/DCI.
The component pool is opening: Dixon–Gemtek (SFP/BOSA) and GX Quantum Photonics, both ECMS-backed.
India OTN $1.78 bn (2025) → $2.81 bn (2031), 7.88% CAGR 2026–31, value nominal [REPORTED-T2]; last year +7.9% [CALCULATED]; volume CAGR [UNAVAILABLE].
Second estimate $1.33 bn (2025) → $3.18 bn (2035) at 9.1% — [CONFLICTING DATA], scopes differ, not averaged.
India routers and switches $2.66 bn (2025) → $6.03 bn (2033), 10.85% — wider scope, not additive to OTN.
Q2 FY27 revenue: Tejas +55%, HFCL +143.6%, Netweb +335.7% YoY [REPORTED-T1] — but in fibre and AI systems, not transport.
31 Mar 2027 — PLI 1.0 ends and BharatNet Phase-3 is due; successor with the Finance Ministry, targeted Q1 FY28.
Dec 2026 / 3 Feb 2027 — GX production start and Dixon–Gemtek JV close.
Early Nov 2026 — HFCL board decision on vertical restructuring.
31 Dec 2026 — NCCS and MTCTE relaxations expire.
No NSE/BSE pure-play in transceivers, ASICs, DSPs, timing or backplanes; nearest are Tejas, HFCL, ITI, Netweb, Dixon (JV), Exicom.

risk.title: Switch/router and OTN silicon
risk.text: Core switching ASICs, OTN switch fabrics and coherent DSPs are designed in the US and imported; there is no Indian carrier-grade design house or fab. Resilience: YEARS to STRUCTURAL. [REPORTED]

opp.title: Design, not fabrication, is the entry
opp.text: Cisco now runs silicon design in India alongside six manufactured product lines; the component-focused PLI successor and the ₹25,000 cr design incentive fund target exactly this gap. [REPORTED]

risk.title: PCBA and multilayer boards
risk.text: ~80% of PCBAs in network gear are imported and the 15% BCD on telecom PCBAs raises landed cost; Budget 2026 lapsed a swathe of Chapter 85 exemptions from 31 Mar 2026, adding cost to imported parts. Resilience: MONTHS. [REPORTED]

opp.title: Local PCBA and board capacity
opp.text: The ₹40,000 cr ECMS outlay explicitly covers PCBs and connectors, and Cisco’s Chennai line is moving to deeper local sourcing — the PCB drill-down under this entry tracks the board side. [REPORTED]

risk.title: BharatNet dependence
risk.text: Both indigenous router vendors built their books on one programme: Tejas has shipped 17,000+ of a planned ~60,000 routers, HFCL has taken RVNL awards worth ₹2,167 cr and ₹2,666 cr, and the programme completes in March 2027. Private-operator transport capex has not replaced it. Resilience: CYCLICAL. [REPORTED]

opp.title: Exports and data centres
opp.text: Tejas is shipping an end-to-end 5G network to South America and 400G/800G coherent DWDM to private operators; HFCL reports ~57% of its order book as export. The next leg is hyperscale DCI, not rural middle-mile. [REPORTED]

risk.title: Balance-sheet and execution capacity
risk.text: Tejas carries ₹4,384 cr net debt and ₹2,314 cr of inventory against a ₹2,315 cr order book, and lost ₹207 cr in Q2 FY27; ITI’s statutory auditors issued a disclaimer of conclusion on the Q1 FY27 results. Resilience: CYCLICAL. [REPORTED]

opp.title: Consolidation and capital discipline
opp.text: HFCL is reviewing its verticals with E&Y and a board decision is expected by early November 2026; a cleaner separation of products from EPC would make the transport-equipment pool directly investable. [REPORTED] Deepest hidden import dependency: the coherent DSP and the switch ASIC sitting inside every DWDM line card and IP/MPLS router — US-designed silicon with no Indian design house or fab, and no certification path around it. India assembles boxes around imported silicon; the control-plane chip is the true chokepoint, and unlike optics there is not yet even a module-assembly beachhead. [INFERENCE]

items: The backhaul and core of India’s networks: DWDM/OTN, packet transport, IP/MPLS routers, Ethernet switches and the optics and silicon inside them.

items.h: Snapshot The turbine-island auxiliaries — the feedwater train (condensate pumps, LP/HP feedwater heaters, deaerator, boiler feed pumps), the moisture separator reheater, the lube/control-oil system and the turbine-governing + DCS/control layer that supervise the turbo-generator. sections.note: dual-readable: every risk is a substitution play

risk.title: High-end DCS & governing platforms imported
risk.text: The digital control and turbine-governing platforms are dominated by a few global OEMs; BHEL builds its own EHC but the top-end DCS stack is import-led. Resilience: months.

opp.title: Listed automation players localise
opp.text: Honeywell Automation India, ABB India and Siemens Energy India can extend localisation into turbine-island control and protection — a ~$350 mn (2030) India power-DCS pool.

risk.title: High-spec deaerator internals imported
risk.text: Large tray-type / membrane deaerator internals are import-dependent (est. 55–65% of Indian consumption), even though BHEL and L&T build the vessels domestically. Resilience: months.

opp.title: Internals localisation
opp.text: Domestic fabrication of high-performance tray / spray internals would close a deaerator gap in a 6–8% CAGR India market and serve the 47.5 GW thermal pipeline.

risk.title: Mechanical seal & control-valve IP
risk.text: High-end mechanical seals and control-valve internals carry imported IP and precision. Resilience: months.

opp.title: Seal & valve localisation
opp.text: A domestic high-end seal and control-valve base would de-risk the feedwater and governing sub-systems across thermal and nuclear sets.

risk.title: BFP localised only in 2021
risk.text: KSB’s 700 MWe nuclear main BFP was India’s first; scale-up and nuclear-grade qualification depth are still maturing, with Kirloskar Brothers a developing second source. Resilience: months.

opp.title: Second-source the BFP line
opp.text: KBL’s tested PCP prototype and KSB’s Shirwal expansion (+20% capacity) give India two qualified nuclear-pump lines for fleet-mode 700 MWe and supercritical demand. Where value sits: the auxiliaries are the most thoroughly localised layer of the turbine island — feedwater heaters, deaerators, BFPs and oil systems are covered by KSB, BHEL, Kirloskar Brothers, WPIL, L&T, ISGEC and Thermax. The residual import gap is the high-end DCS / governing platform , high-spec deaerator internals and specialty seal / valve IP.

sections.title: Digest — at a glance
sections.note: short summary; full detail below

items.h: Snapshot The turbine generator and electrical train — the machine that converts shaft power to electricity, plus the generator transformer, GCB, switchgear and protection that export it to the grid. India builds AC generators up to 250 MVA (TD Power Systems) and is the sole indigenous supplier of nuclear turbo-generators (BHEL). Value now turns on BHEL’s record order book and TD Power’s export-led generator boom. Process & equipment
items: Generator rotor forging, non-magnetic retaining rings, stator-bar copper, CRGO transformer core steel, and hydrogen/water cooling.
The retaining ring (cold-expanded) and the large generator rotor forging are the gating inputs; CRGO gates the generator transformer.
Generator retaining rings are imported — cold-expanded non-magnetic 18Mn-5Cr forgings made by only a few mills worldwide, none in India. Resilience: years.
Generator rotor forging shares the constrained heavy-forging base. Resilience: years.
CRGO transformer steel is ~90% imported; a DGTR anti-dumping probe (22-Jun-2026) could lift generator-transformer cost. Resilience: months.
High-end protection/relay platforms and hydrogen seal/gas systems are foreign-dominated specialty sub-systems. Resilience: months.
BHEL NSE: BHEL — dominant utility generator maker and sole Indian nuclear turbo-generator supplier; outstanding OB ₹2,57,571 cr (Sep-2026).
TD Power Systems NSE: TDPOWERSYS — India’s largest independent AC-generator maker (to 250 MVA); FY27 guidance ₹2,600 cr; 10-yr Siemens Energy 2-pole generator pact; entering >100 MW.
Transformer / switchgear OEMs — CG Power, Hitachi Energy India, Siemens Energy India, ABB India cover the electrical train.
MIDHANI NSE: MIDHANI — special steels and non-magnetic grades — retaining-ring qualification not evidenced.
India turbo-generators (scope: utility / industrial turbo-generators, India): ~$340 mn (2023) → ~$462 mn (2030) , CAGR ~4.6% [REPORTED-T3, BlueWeave]. Value (nominal); volume [UNAVAILABLE].

sections.title: Bottlenecks — Risk & Opportunity
sections.note: dual-readable: every risk is a substitution play

risk.title: Generator retaining rings imported
risk.text: The high-strength, non-magnetic retaining ring that holds the rotor end-winding is a cold-expanded 18Mn-5Cr forging (ASTM A289); only a handful of mills worldwide can make it and none is in India, so a supply disruption is hard to re-route. Resilience: months–years.

opp.title: Retaining-ring qualification
opp.text: MIDHANI already makes non-magnetic special steels (e.g. DMR-64); qualifying a retaining-ring grade would close a critical, mid-size import gap in a machine India otherwise builds end-to-end.

risk.title: Generator rotor forging imported
risk.text: The large generator rotor forging shares the same constrained heavy-forging base as the turbine rotor; there is no fully qualified domestic source. Resilience: years.

opp.title: Shared rotor-forging line
opp.text: A qualified indigenous large-forging line would serve both turbine and generator rotors, and the 100 GW nuclear + supercritical order book justifies it.

risk.title: CRGO transformer steel ~90% imported
risk.text: The generator transformer’s grain-oriented core steel is ~90% imported (China, Japan, Korea, Russia); a DGTR anti-dumping probe (22-Jun-2026) could lift cost and slow grid-linked projects. Resilience: months.

opp.title: Domestic CRGO capacity
opp.text: JSW JFE (Nashik) is the sole domestic CRGO producer, targeting ~3.5 lakh t by FY28 under PLI — the clearest localisation play in the electrical train.

risk.title: High-end DCS / protection platforms imported
risk.text: Protection relays and digital control platforms are dominated by a few global OEMs. Resilience: months.

opp.title: Listed automation players scale
opp.text: ABB India, Hitachi Energy India and Siemens Energy India can localise more of the protection and control stack.

risk.title: Hydrogen-cooling seals & gas systems
risk.text: Generator hydrogen cooling and seal-oil systems are specialty, safety-critical sub-systems with limited domestic depth. Resilience: months.

opp.title: Specialty seal & gas-system localisation
opp.text: A domestic hydrogen-seal and gas-system supply base would de-risk large turbo-generators. Where value sits: the generator is a high-value, largely domestic build — TD Power Systems and BHEL cover the stator, rotor and exciter, and the electrical train (transformer, GCB, switchgear) is well served by BHEL, Siemens Energy India, CG Power and Hitachi Energy India. The narrow gaps are the retaining ring and the generator rotor forging , plus the imported CRGO behind the transformer.

items.h: Snapshot The turbine island (turbomachinery) — the steam turbine, generator, condenser and auxiliaries that turn thermal and nuclear heat into electricity. India's utility steam-turbine fleet is BHEL-led (the sole Indian nuclear-steam-turbine maker, ~50% of the installed base). The live cycle is the supercritical / ultra-supercritical thermal build-out plus the 10×700 MWe PHWR fleet. Process & equipment
items: CrMoV and 9–12% Cr rotor forgings, Ni-superalloy blades, titanium condenser tubes, generator rotor forgings and retaining rings.
Large rotor forgings remain the gating imported input; AUSC Alloy 617(M) rotors are validated on BHEL's high-temperature spin test rig.
Large rotor forgings are imported — NTPC's approved HP/IP/LP shaft-forging vendors are all foreign (JCFC, Saarschmiede, JSW Japan, Doosan, Creusot, Kobe, Energomash, AST).
AUSC superalloy is not yet commercial; the 800 MW demo still lacks final approval.
Heavy fabrication machinery (ultra-heavy press, heavy CNC, balancing / overspeed rigs, heat-treatment furnaces) is imported.
Generator retaining rings and titanium condenser tubes are imported.
BHEL NSE: BHEL — sole Indian nuclear-steam-turbine maker; outstanding order book ₹2.57 lakh cr (Sep-2026), power segment ~81%.
L&T / L&T-MHI (LMTG) NSE: LT — Hazira TG plant (4,000 MW/yr); developing 700 MW / 220 MW nuclear turbine technology under Make-in-India.
Siemens Energy India NSE: ENRIN — industrial steam turbines 1–250 MW; ~55% of India's large-ST installed base served via services.
Triveni Turbine NSE: TRITURBINE — industrial ST to 100 MW; FY26 revenue ₹2,181 cr; aftermarket 38% of orders.
TD Power Systems NSE: TDPOWERSYS — generators; FY26 revenue ₹1,878 cr, order book ₹1,973 cr.

India turbo-generator market: ~$340 mn (2023) → ~$462 mn (2030) , ~4.6% CAGR [REPORTED-T3, BlueWeave].

Volume driver: India has 44,020 MW of supercritical thermal capacity under construction (34,500 MW ultra-supercritical, ~78%), with 120 SC/USC units (83,710 MW) already commissioned as of Jun-2026 [REPORTED-T1, CEA]; coal capacity requirement ~307 GW by 2034-35 vs ~212 GW (2023).

opp.text: LTSHF and Bharat Forge’s 16,000-t press, plus MIDHANI’s superalloys, are the platform; fleet-mode 700 MWe and supercritical demand justifies qualification of an indigenous large-rotor line.

risk.title: AUSC superalloy not yet commercial
risk.text: India’s Advanced Ultra-Supercritical (AUSC) programme — 310 bar / 710°C, Alloy 617(M) rotors and Alloy 625 castings — has finished R&D but not reached commercial deployment; large Ni-alloy forgings are a globally immature technology. Resilience: years.

opp.title: AUSC materials & dissimilar-weld rotors
opp.text: An 800 MW AUSC demo with indigenous Ni-alloy forging and dissimilar-metal-weld capability would move India up the efficiency ladder and open an export material market.

risk.title: Heavy fabrication machinery imported
risk.text: The ultra-heavy forging press, heavy multi-axis CNC, rotor balancing and heat-treatment furnaces, and tube-to-tubesheet welding automation are foreign-built. This is the deepest hidden import dependency in a “localised” industry. Resilience: months–years.

opp.title: Heavy machine-tool localisation
opp.text: A domestic heavy-machine-tool and welding-automation base would de-risk the entire turbine and generator manufacturing chain.

risk.title: Generator retaining rings & titanium condenser tubes imported
risk.text: Generator retaining rings (high-strength non-magnetic steel) and condenser titanium tubes are specialty import items; a supply disruption is hard to re-route. Resilience: months–years.

opp.title: Specialty-tube & ring qualification
opp.text: MIDHANI and the specialty-steel chain could qualify retaining-ring and titanium-tube grades, closing two mid-size import gaps.

risk.title: Skilled trades bind tighter than materials
risk.text: Precision blading machinists, rotor-balancing and NDT engineers, Class-1 welders and turbine-commissioning engineers cannot be bought quickly at any price and gate execution timelines.

opp.title: Incumbent training moats
opp.text: BHEL, L&T and Siemens Energy India’s qualification pipelines are a durable moat and a barrier to new entrants.

risk.title: Nuclear owner & designer are unlisted
risk.text: Ownership (NPCIL) and design (BARC) sit inside DAE entities with no NSE/BSE listing; only the equipment supply chain is investable. Resilience: structural.

opp.title: Fleet-mode order book
opp.text: 10×700 MWe PHWR fleet mode plus the 2047 100 GWe target give the listed OEM chain multi-decade visibility.

risk.title: AUSC still not approved
risk.text: India’s 800 MW Advanced Ultra-Supercritical demo — the route to Ni-alloy (Alloy 617M) rotors and higher efficiency — has completed R&D but still lacks final investment approval; VGF of ~₹6,000 cr was mooted and the site has moved toward Korba (~₹15,000 cr). Large Ni-alloy forgings remain globally immature. Resilience: years.

opp.title: AUSC materials & rotor validation
opp.text: BHEL’s high-temperature spin test rig now validates Alloy 617M monometallic and bimetallic welded rotors; approval of the demo would open an indigenous superalloy-rotor and dissimilar-weld market. Default stress test (most binding bottleneck × most plausible shock): a decision-dated disruption or export restriction on imported large turbine rotor forgings (Japan / China origin). Affected nodes: rotor & forgings, blading, generator rotor. Resilience class: YEARS (single-source plus certification-gated requalification). Who loses: OEMs and owners absorb cost and schedule slip. Who benefits: domestic forging capacity (LTSHF, Bharat Forge, MIDHANI) and aftermarket life-extension plays. Lead indicators: JSW/Doosan order backlog and lead-time disclosures, Bharat Forge / LTSHF capex and press-capacity announcements, BHEL order-execution commentary. Inverted reading: the same shock is the strongest possible case for qualifying an indigenous large-rotor line. Deepest hidden dependency: India builds and commissions the turbine island well — BHEL is the sole Indian nuclear-steam-turbine maker with a record ₹2.57 lakh cr order book (Sep-2026) and a new ₹500 cr nuclear/thermal TG capex at Haridwar; L&T-MHI, KSB, TD Power and Triveni cover the TG, pump and generator layers, and L&T-MHI is now developing 700 MW nuclear turbine technology. Yet the two highest-value inputs, the large rotor forging and the fabrication machinery , are still imported, and the nuclear owner (NPCIL) and designer (BARC) are unlisted. The fabrication is investable; the frontier material and the IP are not.

digest.h: Snapshot The turbine island (turbomachinery) — the steam turbine, generator, condenser and auxiliaries that turn thermal and nuclear heat into electricity. India's utility steam-turbine fleet is BHEL-led (the sole Indian nuclear-steam-turbine maker, ~50% of the installed base). The live cycle is the supercritical / ultra-supercritical thermal build-out plus the 10×700 MWe PHWR fleet. Process & equipment
items: CrMoV and 9–12% Cr rotor forgings, Ni-superalloy blades, titanium condenser tubes, generator rotor forgings and retaining rings.
Large rotor forgings remain the gating imported input; AUSC Alloy 617(M) rotors are validated on BHEL's high-temperature spin test rig.
Large rotor forgings are imported — NTPC's approved HP/IP/LP shaft-forging vendors are all foreign (JCFC, Saarschmiede, JSW Japan, Doosan, Creusot, Kobe, Energomash, AST).
AUSC superalloy is not yet commercial; the 800 MW demo still lacks final approval.
Heavy fabrication machinery (ultra-heavy press, heavy CNC, balancing / overspeed rigs, heat-treatment furnaces) is imported.
Generator retaining rings and titanium condenser tubes are imported.
BHEL NSE: BHEL — sole Indian nuclear-steam-turbine maker; outstanding order book ₹2.57 lakh cr (Sep-2026), power segment ~81%.
L&T / L&T-MHI (LMTG) NSE: LT — Hazira TG plant (4,000 MW/yr); developing 700 MW / 220 MW nuclear turbine technology under Make-in-India.
Siemens Energy India NSE: ENRIN — industrial steam turbines 1–250 MW; ~55% of India's large-ST installed base served via services.
Triveni Turbine NSE: TRITURBINE — industrial ST to 100 MW; FY26 revenue ₹2,181 cr; aftermarket 38% of orders.
TD Power Systems NSE: TDPOWERSYS — generators; FY26 revenue ₹1,878 cr, order book ₹1,973 cr.
KSB NSE: KSB — nuclear pumps; nuclear order book ₹1,235 cr (Jun-2026).

India steam turbine market (scope: utility + industrial steam turbines, India): ~$3.33 bn (2022) → ~$4.38 bn (2030) , headline CAGR ~3.5% [CALCULATED] from [REPORTED-T3, Grand View Research]. Value (nominal); volume [UNAVAILABLE].
[CONFLICTING DATA] on India steam-turbine size: Arizton ~$1.57 bn (2024) and TechSci ~$0.83 bn (2025, industrial-only) — the spread is scope-driven (utility vs industrial; equipment vs services).
India turbo-generator market: ~$340 mn (2023) → ~$462 mn (2030) , ~4.6% CAGR [REPORTED-T3, BlueWeave].

Volume driver: India has 44,020 MW of supercritical thermal capacity under construction (34,500 MW ultra-supercritical, ~78%), with 120 SC/USC units (83,710 MW) already commissioned as of Jun-2026 [REPORTED-T1, CEA]; coal capacity requirement ~307 GW by 2034-35 vs ~212 GW (2023).

Growth is new-build-led (supercritical thermal cycle + PHWR fleet + SMR optionality); aftermarket is the steadier pool. Value growth is unit-count and mix (USC uprating) driven, not price [INFERENCE].
AUSC 800 MW demo still awaiting final approval (VGF ~₹6,000 cr mooted; Korba at ~₹15,000 cr under consideration) — no progress since the Mar-2025 PIB note. [LIVE]
BHEL board approved ₹500 cr for thermal + nuclear TG manufacturing at Haridwar HEEP (14-Oct-2026). [CYCLICAL]
L&T-MHI is developing 700 MW / 220 MW nuclear turbine & generator technology under the Make-in-India BSR scheme — a potential second nuclear-turbine source to BHEL. [LIVE]
NPCIL fleet-mode turbine-island EPC executing (Kaiga-5&6 and GHAVP-3&4 awarded; Mahi Banswara via ASHVINI tendering). [CYCLICAL]
Large rotor forgings and heavy fabrication machinery have no qualified NSE/BSE exposure.

sections.title: Digest — at a glance
sections.note: short summary; full report in chat

items.h: Snapshot India's auto-component industry turned over ₹6.73 lakh crore in FY25 and flipped a rare $453 mn trade surplus, but that became a ~$200 mn deficit in H1 FY26 as US tariffs stalled exports and China imports jumped. Two-wheelers are the most localised chain; every EV powertrain node hides an import wall. Process & equipment
items: Spine: melting → forging/casting → precision machining → heat treatment → assembly → test/homologation.
Forging presses, HPDC die-casting machines, CNC tools and cell-fab/SMT lines are all imported — the deepest hidden dependency.
EV adds motor winding, power-module assembly, cell electrode coating/formation and pack EOL testing.
Rare-earth permanent magnets — single-source (China >90% of processing). Resilience: years.
Li-ion cells & active materials — ACC-PLI has commissioned ~1.4 GWh of 50 GWh, zero disbursals.
Automotive semiconductors (MCU/SoC, SiC/IGBT, sensors) — near-total import.
Electrical steel and capital equipment (presses, CNC, cell lines).
Upstream materials, cells, magnets and semiconductors capture the highest value — and leak to imports.
Electronics & software carry the fastest-rising content-per-vehicle and proprietary margins.
Forging/casting/fasteners are globally competitive but capital-heavy and margin-thin — the export franchise (Bharat Forge, Ramkrishna, Sundram).
Broadest value-added content stays domestic with Uno Minda and Samvardhana Motherson; deepest EV-tech with Sona Comstar.
Aftermarket (₹99,948 cr) is the most resilient domestic pool, riding the ageing parc.

Correction from the prior run: the PM E-DRIVE e-2W demand incentive now runs to 31 Mar 2028 (S.O. 4424(E), 10 Aug 2026), not 31 Jul 2026; supported-vehicle cap raised to 45,79,120 and scheme outlay to ₹11,900 cr.

Correction from the prior run: the India–US interim deal that would cut auto-part tariffs (~50% → 0–18%, Feb-2026) is still unsigned, but commerce minister Goyal said on 15-Oct-2026 that the first tranche is finalised with legal drafting under way (he had called it “concluded” in substance on 10-Oct-2026; FM Sitharaman had called the talks a “plateau”, 5-Oct-2026; USTR Greer said a deal was “not imminent”, 2-Oct-2026). Indian exports to the US currently face a 10% tariff, with up to 100% risked under the Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act 2026.
REPM scheme (₹7,280 cr, 6,000 MTPA) tenders expected 2026; production ~2 years out.
China eased light-RE magnets to four Indian firms; heavy magnets still restricted.
No NSE/BSE pure-play in rare-earth magnets, cell active materials, automotive semiconductors or electrical steel; nearest exposure is via conglomerates or unlisted arms.
